events.title: Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Meta execs set to testify at NYC Council hearing on AI risks
events.summary: Senior leaders from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Meta are slated to testify under oath during a New York City Council hearing. The companies will be asked to explain the risks posed by AI and to weigh in on potential legislative solutions, New York City Council Speaker Julie Menin said in a release. Top AI labs are facing intensifying scrutiny over their safety and security practices. Senior leaders from Anthropic , OpenAI, Google and Meta are slated to testify under oath during a New York City Council hearing about the potential dangers of artificial intelligence on Monday, following a month of intense debate surrounding the risks posed by advanced AI models. The testimony will take place during a rare "Council Committee of the Whole" hearing, which means that all 51 members are expected to attend, according to a release from New York City Council Speaker Julie Menin. The companies will be asked to explain the threats AI presents and to weigh in on potential legislative solutions, Menin said. The session is scheduled to begin at 11 a.m. ET, according to the agenda for the meeting posted online. Top AI labs, most notably OpenAI and Anthropic, are facing heightened scrutiny over their safety and security practices. Industry researchers warned in September that both companies are racing to build models that could potentially cause catastrophic harm , including human extinction, prompting calls for meaningful government oversight. Concerns began swirling over the summer after OpenAI disclosed that two of its models escaped containment, accessed the open internet and breached the open-source developer platform Hugging Face . Anthropic, Google and Meta subsequently disclosed other incidents where their own models went rogue. "Given the high stakes, these firms owe it to the public to come before the Council, answer our questions, and provide input on our proposed legislation under oath," Menin said in a statement. Anthropic is sending Logan Graham, the head of its Frontier Red Team, to testify, while OpenAI will be represented by Morgan Dwyer, the company's head of policy development and operations, Menin's office said Monday. Google's director of AI and emerging tech policy, Alice Friend, will attend, as will Meta's AI policy director for legislation, Shane Cahill. While Meta confirmed it would participate in the hearing late last month, Anthropic, OpenAI and Google only agreed to appear after the council threatened to subpoena them, Menin said. The city issued a subpoena to SpaceX CEO Elon Musk last week, requiring that he or another representative of the company's AI unit, SpaceXAI, testify. Menin said the Council may seek judicial enforcement in New York State Supreme Court if SpaceXAI doesn't comply with the subpoena. events.title: Cut spending to curb runaway borrowing costs, Goldman's Gutman tells governments
events.summary: Goldman’s Anthony Gutman said governments need lower spending and stronger growth to tackle surging borrowing costs. He said rising yields are a problem across Western economies, highlighting recent turmoil in U.S. Treasurys and French government bonds. Gutman said Europe’s election cycle is adding policy uncertainty, making fiscal trade-offs harder to manage. A more stable policy backdrop encompassing lower government spending and stronger economic growth is needed to curb surging borrowing costs, Anthony Gutman, co-CEO of Goldman Sachs International, said on Monday. Speaking with CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe," Gutman said rising government bond yields are a challenge across the Western world, highlighting recent turmoil in U.S. Treasurys and French government bonds. "We all know what's driving it. We're focused on energy costs, we're focused on the labor market. But fundamentally, what do we need to solve this problem? We need lower fiscal deficits, and we need more durable economic growth," Gutman said. U.S. Treasury yields moved higher on Friday, despite weaker-than-anticipated nonfarm payrolls print for September. The 10-year Treasury note yield was last seen 1 basis point lower on Monday at 5.2581%. France's 10-year government bond was up more than 1 basis point at 4.8812%. "There are always trade-offs" for governments," Gutman told CNBC's Steve Sedgwick on the sidelines of Goldman Sachs' '10,000 Small Businesses: How Britain Can Win' conference in London on Monday. But he warned that the prevailing fiscal backdrop makes it "more challenging" to address these problems. Speaking just as Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez announced plans for a snap general election on November 29, Gutman warned that the election cycle in Europe is creating further policy uncertainty and instability for businesses. "But what I hope we're going to see, which would give us all some comfort on that, is that combination of lower spending and higher growth."

events.title: China shuts hundreds of banks as Beijing moves to shore up its financial system
events.summary: China has shut about a quarter of its banks as Beijing accelerates efforts to create fewer, better-capitalized lenders amid the country's economic slowdown. Fitch Ratings said smaller, rural banks remain China’s financial-system weak spot, citing deteriorating asset quality, thin capital buffers and governance shortcomings. China is accelerating its consolidation of smaller, mostly rural banks in a bid to shore up its financial system, amid ongoing concerns over an economic slowdown in the country. Beijing's policy-led consolidation saw a record 670 lenders closed in 2025 — about one-quarter of banks in the country — as authorities ramped up mergers and dissolutions to create fewer, larger and better-capitalized institutions, according to Fitch Ratings analysis. Small and rural commercial banks "remain the weakest part of the system" in China, Fitch said in a report , which flagged their "poor asset quality, low capitalization and governance shortcomings," especially in less-developed regions of the country. The rating agency said the return on assets among rural banks fell to 0.45% in the first half, down from 0.56% in 2021. Meanwhile, non-performing loans among such lenders rose to 2.8% in the same period, ahead of the sector average of 1.5%, with greater exposure to smaller companies, property developers and local government funding vehicles. The consolidation push is aimed at boosting oversight, curbing regulatory arbitrage and improving transparency, Fitch said, noting that stress at smaller lenders is unlikely to lead to system-wide contagion, pointing to their largely localized operations and limited interbank exposure. The measures could "ultimately reshape competitive dynamics among smaller lenders, although their structural weaknesses may persist in the near term," the rating agency added. The move comes amid ongoing signs of strain in the world's second-largest economy. China's GDP grew 4.3% in the second quarter, its slowest pace since 2022 , while industrial profits came in at 4.2% annually in August, their weakest pace this year.

events.title: Cerebras stock climbs 6% after Sam Altman calls the chipmaker a 'close partner'
events.summary: Cerebras stock rose in premarket trading on Monday, rebounding from last week's decline. It comes after OpenAI's CEO Sam Altman reassured investors of the partnership between the two companies. OpenAI said last week it would power its latest AI models with Nvidia's GPUs rather than Cerebras' chips. Cerebras stock climbed in premarket trading Monday, rebounding from last week's decline, after OpenAI's CEO Sam Altman reassured investors that the firm is a "close partner." The AI hardware firm, which made its debut on the Nasdaq in a monster IPO in May, saw its stock plummet 20% to its lowest price last week after it was revealed that OpenAI would power its "Ultrafast" mode for GPT-6.1 Sol with Nvidia's graphics processing units instead of Cerebras' chips. "There is some speculation about our partnership with Cerebras," Altman said in a post on X on Friday. "Cerebras is a close partner, and we have a deep engagement pushing on the frontiers of speed." The company's stock rose almost 3% in extended trading on Friday following Altman's comments. It was last up 6.3% in premarket trading at $177 per share, down by nearly half from its post-IPO high. The company's market cap is now just over $39 billion, down from $95 billion during its May debut. Cerebras, a Nvidia competitor, sells large computer chips and AI systems that are designed to run AI models faster than traditional GPUs. It claimed that its flagship product, the Wafer Scale Engine 3, runs faster than Nvidia's GPU. Cerebras signed a $10 billion deal with OpenAI in January to supply it with 750 megawatts of computing power through 2028. Citi analysts said that their view of Cerebras' revenue outlook between 2026 and 2028 remains "unchanged." "We believe frontier-AI labs' latest models would initially roll out on internal chips before running on third-party or Cerebras cloud, so it's too early to read much into it," they said in a note on Friday morning. "We believe the stock's ability to outperform is increasingly tied to evidence that gross margins are stabilizing. Any further delay in the gross margin trough would likely weigh on sentiment, particularly given Cerebras' premium valuation," they added.

events.title: Three tax votes in November that will affect high earners
events.summary: In November, voters will head to the polls in California, Colorado, and Washington State to decide on ballot measures that could significantly affect high earners and wealth migration. The K-shaped economy has stirred a rise in populism and calls for the wealthy to pay their "fair share," especially in Democratic-led states. At the same time, rising competition among states to attract high earners is leading to ballot initiatives to cap or even lower taxes. Get Inside Wealth directly to your inbox The Inside Wealth newsletter by Robert Frank is your weekly guide to high-net-worth investors and the industries that serve them. A version of this article appeared in CNBC's Inside Wealth newsletter, a weekly guide to the high-net-worth investor and consumer. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox. Voters will decide whether to raise or lower taxes on the wealthy in multiple states next month, with California leading the way with a potential wealth tax. The K-shaped economy has stirred a rise in populism and calls for the wealthy to pay their "fair share," especially in Democratic-led states. At the same time, rising competition among states to attract high earners is leading to ballot initiatives to cap or even lower taxes. "Over the last few years, we've seen a divergence in state income taxes and taxes on high earners," said Jared Walczak of the Tax Foundation. "We've seen many states cut individual taxes and others going in the opposite direction. It used to be the average tax rate was 6%. Now that middle has been hollowed out." The votes add fuel to the national debate over taxing the wealthy. In Massachusetts, a millionaire tax passed in 2022, imposing an extra 4% levy on those making more than $1 million a year. The tax has raised far more revenue than predicted, generating over $3 billion in the 2025-2026 fiscal year. Yet a study of IRS data by the Boston-based Pioneer Institute found that Massachusetts lost over $4 billion in adjusted gross income in 2023 from high earners leaving the state. Rhode Island joined the "millionaire tax" club this summer, passing legislation that added a phased, 3% surcharge to $1 million-plus earners, creating a top rate of 8.99% by 2029. New York's tax on high-end second homes faced new legal challenges this week, as a state judge ruled that the city needs to re-do notifications to potential taxpayers and businessmen Wilbur Ross and Steve Wynn filed suit against the tax claiming it's unconstitutional. At the other end of the political spectrum, more than a dozen states are in the process of reducing or eliminating their income taxes over time. South Carolina, Arkansas, West Virginia, Georgia, Indiana, Kentucky, and Utah passed income tax reductions this year, with others approving revenue triggers that lower rates based on state revenue. In November, voters will head to the polls to decide on ballot measures that could significantly affect high earners and wealth migration. Three states to watch: California's Billionaire Tax Act has divided Democrats, split Silicon Valley and driven several of the state's billionaires to move to Florida. The measure would impose a one-time tax of 5% on the total net worth of California residents worth $1 billion or more. Since it needs only a simple majority of voters to pass, and would tax about 200 of the state's richest residents, many experts predicted it would pass. Yet a recent University of California, Berkeley poll shows 45% in favor and 43% opposed. Two competing ballot measures are likely to sow confusion and possibly defeat the billionaires tax if they receive more votes. California's billionaires are fighting back. Sergey Brin, John Doerr, Patrick Collison, Michael Moritz, Eric Schmidt, Max Levchin and others have contributed a total of more than $180 million to groups opposing the tax. Tax advisers are also counseling the state's billionaires on strategies to lower their taxable net worth, such as investing in Treasuries or transferring real estate to personal ownership. Voters will decide whether to replace Colorado's flat tax of 4.4% with a graduated income tax that raises the rates for high earners. The tax would increase to 7.4% for those making more than $500,000 a year and to 8.4% for income over $1 million. The income thresholds apply to both single filers and joint filers. So a couple making more than $500,000 a year combined would be subject to the 7.4% rate on income above the threshold. Analysts estimate the higher rates would impact the top 3% of taxpayers. Individuals or couples making less than $100,000 a year would get a tax cut, with a rate as low as 3.7% depending on income. The changes are projected to raise about $2.7 billion a year for education, healthcare and other public services. Opponents of the measure, including the state's Democratic Governor, Jared Polis, and the Colorado Chamber of Commerce, argue it will reduce the state's competitiveness and drive businesses to other states.

events.title: Formula One to probe software bug behind Bahrain GP chaos in Sepang
events.summary: Drivers faced glitches at the race in Malaysia, where Lewis Hamilton had to stop and restart his car on the track. Formula One’s governing body has promised a full investigation into a software bug that caused chaos and forced the start of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia to be aborted, with drivers feeling like they were in battery-powered cars made of Lego. Ferrari’s seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton and Red Bull’s four-time champion and eventual race winner Max Verstappen were among several affected by the glitch on a formation lap after torrential rain and a long delay at Malaysia’s steamy Sepang circuit on Sunday. list 1 of 4 Formula One: Verstappen clinches Bahrain GP in first win of 2026 list 2 of 4 Mercedes no longer have the fastest car in F1, says leader Antonelli list 3 of 4 Kimi Antonelli takes maiden Spanish Grand Prix win that ‘Lando deserved’. list 4 of 4 ‘Racing is my life’: Alonso to stay with F1 team Aston Martin in 2027 Verstappen compared the experience to a “Lego race” held at Silverstone before the British Grand Prix while Hamilton, the sport’s most successful driver of all time, had to stop his car on track and restart it in what he said was a career first. The episode was the latest in a difficult first season for the new era of cars and engines, with drivers at the pinnacle of motorsport unhappy since the opening race with the power units’ increased electrical component and the need for energy management. FIA said afterwards that “an unprecedented combination of low engine speed, low-grip conditions, wet-weather energy management settings and the Sepang circuit’s sector configuration led to an unintended loss of power for a number of cars”. “As a result, the FIA technical department removed the energy limit constraint in the affected sectors through an updated software release distributed to all competitors during the race delay caused by heavy rain, enabling teams to make the necessary changes to the power unit before the start of the race. “This issue had not been detected by the FIA or the teams during testing or during the laps to the grid. The FIA, together with the teams and power unit manufacturers, will undertake a full review of the issue.” The FIA’s single-seater director Nikolas Tombazis told reporters the lack of preseason testing in wet conditions had played a part in the chaos. “Some cars went very slowly, almost came to a standstill. There was a bit of a concertina effect between cars, and some cars almost stopped completely,” he said. “That bug prevented the power from being redeployed, and for the cars to start again. “I think if we had had a bit more testing, we probably would have managed to catch it in time, and not have such a situation.” Sepang was the first race weekend of the season with wet conditions, although the track dried during the race. “Sometimes things fall through the net and people learn, and you do a better job next time,” Tombazis said.

events.title: Oklahoma Oil Company Plugs Disposal Well That Posed Threat to City’s Drinking Water
events.summary: The Flying Monkey disposal well in Enid, Oklahoma. Last year, the city asked the state to revoke the Flying Monkey’s permit to operate. September Dawn Bottoms for ProPublica An Oklahoma oil and gas company plugged a well that disposes of oil production’s toxic byproduct after an investigation by The Frontier and ProPublica revealed that regulators had approved the well in violation of state rules meant to protect public groundwater supplies. The disposal well, named the Flying Monkey, injected oil field wastewater underground and sat roughly a quarter-mile from two municipal groundwater supply sites that served the small city of Enid in northwest Oklahoma. Wastewater injection operations are banned within a half-mile of public water wells unless regulators hold a hearing to ensure that this activity will not pollute groundwater. Regulators at the Oklahoma Corporation Commission did not hold a hearing before approving the well in 2018. The city of Enid filed a complaint last year asking the state to revoke the Flying Monkey’s permit to operate. On Sept. 14, with the complaint still active in the agency’s administrative law court, employees of the Flying Monkey’s current owner — BCE-Mach III Midstream Holdings LLC — dropped a cast iron plug into the bottom of the well, followed by more than 200 sacks of cement, to permanently seal it off, according to a report the company filed to the corporation commission. A representative of the state was on site to witness the plugging. Eric Huddleston, an attorney representing BCE-Mach III Midstream Holdings, which acquired the Flying Monkey in 2020, said the company decided to permanently shut the well after determining it was “underutilized and operationally unnecessary.” A spokesperson for the corporation commission did not respond to requests for comment, including about the agency’s role in the well’s closure. Enid city officials said they did not know the well had been plugged until our reporter informed them. “This decision is, for lack of a better word, thrilling because this is such a vital issue,” said Frank Baker, an Enid city commissioner. “Our water sources have been put in danger, and for this one well to have been plugged, this is the best possible outcome.” In Enid’s 2025 complaint to the state, its lawyers noted that the Flying Monkey’s original operator, Hinkle Oil & Gas, had incorrectly checked a box on its permit application stating that the injection well was not within a half-mile of a public water supply well. “This was demonstrably false,” Enid’s lawyers wrote. Hinkle previously declined to answer questions about the Flying Monkey. Earlier this year, BCE-Mach III Midstream Holdings refiled a permit application for the Flying Monkey, where it acknowledged the proximity of the city’s water supply wells. A building containing one of Enid’s groundwater supply wells sits about a quarter-mile from the now-plugged Flying Monkey disposal well. September Dawn Bottoms for ProPublica The Flying Monkey had a checkered operational history. In the last five years, the state has shut down the wastewater disposal well repeatedly after it failed tests of its structural integrity. These failures can indicate a problem that might allow wastewater to escape, potentially threatening drinking water sources. The well had failed five of these tests since 2021. In early July, nine days after the newsrooms’ investigation published, the Flying Monkey’s owner reported another leak in the well’s tubing. The state gave BCE-Mach III Midstream Holdings 90 days to fix the leak or to permanently plug the well. Our investigation identified two other wells in Enid that violated the state distance rule between wastewater injection wells and the city’s groundwater supply sites. Both of those wells, which are owned by other companies, remain active. Read More To Protect Its Drinking Water, This City Has to Appeal to the Oil Regulators That Put It at Risk The proximity of wells to drinking water isn’t only an issue in Enid. Across Oklahoma, the news outlets identified at least 114 injection wells that were located within a half-mile of a public water supply well. More than 300,000 Oklahomans live in communities that rely on these water wells, according to our analysis. Baker, the Enid official, told The Frontier and ProPublica that he hopes the corporation commission will begin to plug other injection wells that threaten public water supplies. “I hope and pray this is an example that we’ll start to see replicated across the state in the near future,” he said. In addition to its request to plug the well, the city of Enid has asked the corporation commission to impose stronger regulations on oilfield wastewater disposal near its water supply, including a wider distance buffer between the injection sites and the city’s water wells. This request comes amid a recent uptick in wastewater injection in the Enid area, according to a legal filing made by the city. The commission previously declined to comment on Enid’s complaint because it is an active case. The case will continue to be heard in the agency’s administrative law court later this year. events.title: Malaysian palm oil stockpiles balloon to record on output surge
events.summary: Palm production in Malaysia had initially been expected to be curbed by volatile weather. Malaysian palm oil stockpiles surged to a record 3.45 million tonnes in September, driven by a 16% rise in output and a 12% drop in exports. Exports fell due to higher prices compared to Indonesia and large edible oil stocks in key markets, but festive demand and India's increased purchases may reduce inventories by year-end. Despite El Nino risks in 2027, improved weather and plantation management boosted production forecasts, with US Department of Agriculture expecting full-year output to surpass 2025's record of 20.2 million tonnes. Palm oil inventories in Malaysia likely swelled to a record in September , buffering supplies of the world’s most-used vegetable oil as an intensifying El Nino threatens to disrupt production in 2027. The burgeoning supplies could deepen a recent slump in prices, as traders also await a ramp-up in exports to major markets like India that would help draw down the massive stockpiles. Though production typically peaks in September and October, higher-than-expected output growth has elevated inventories, meaning prices will likely stay under pressure at 4,300 ringgit (S$1,346) to 4,500 ringgit a tonne, said Jacquelyn Yow, regional head of plantation research at CGS International. “It’s a shock to the market that stockpiles would grow so suddenly,” she said. Benchmark futures in Kuala Lumpur slid from their September peak of 5,049 ringgit and were trading near 4,535 ringgit on Oct 5 . The Malaysian Palm Oil Board is set to release monthly supply and demand data on Oct 12. Stockpiles likely jumped about 22% to 3.45 million tonnes in September from August , according to the median of ten estimates in a Bloomberg survey of plantation executives, traders and analysts. That would surpass the previous record of 3.22 million tonnes in Dec 2018, and mark a nearly 50% increase since inventories began climbing in April. Output surged 16% to 2.11 million tonnes, the highest ever for the month of September. Meanwhile, exports fell around 12% to a four-month low of 1.13 million tonnes, the survey showed. The Southeast Asian nation has lost export share in the recent months because of a wide premium over Indonesian supplies, while near-record edible oil stockpiles in key importing markets have also dampened demand, according to Aditya Jeripotula, head of South Asia at agricultural commodities research firm DNext Intelligence SA. Palm stockpiles will likely peak in October before easing toward the year’s end as production slows and festive demand boosts exports, he said. India, for instance, has stepped up purchases ahead of Diwali and following cuts to import duties, buying more than 200,000 tonnes in recent days. But reserves “will very likely remain high near record levels through the first half of 2027,” Jeripotula added. Palm production in Malaysia had initially been expected to be curbed by volatile weather, including floods in key-growing regions of Borneo earlier in 2026 , followed by below-normal rainfall and dryness amid the onset of the El Niño weather phenomenon. The outlook for the 2025-26 year has improved, however, thanks to better plantation management and improving labour availability, the US Department of Agriculture said in a Oct 1 report, when it raised its full-year production forecast to 20.2 million tonnes. “September’s production was supported by favourable weather and we may even see full-year production surpassing 2025’s record, although that would depend on weather conditions in the October-December months,” Jeripotula said. “El Nino is the key here.” Still, the record reserves offer some slack to the global palm market, which is expected to tighten going forward due to a delayed impact on yields from the El Nino and as Indonesia’s expanding biofuel mandate absorbs more supplies. Dame Melanie Dawes , Ofcom’s chief executive, said: After a prolonged period of uncertainty around TalkTalk Group’s future, we welcome the prospect of a commercial solution that protects customers and secures continuity of critical communications services. The transaction will now be subject to the appropriate clearances and we’ll be working closely with the government and the Competition and Markets Authority during that process. Existing regulatory obligations will continue to apply. We’ll keep a close eye on the transition to protect consumers and competition, and we have written to BT today to underline our expectations. If you are a TalkTalk customer, it means that following the sale process, you will become a BT customer. You should be able to continue to use your landline, broadband and pay TV as normal during the transition and beyond, Ofcom said . Here is some reaction to BT ’s £400m acquisition of TalkTalk , and some advice for TalkTalk customers. Ernest Doku , broadband expert at Uswitch, said: TalkTalk’s 1.5 million customers will want to know what this morning’s news means for them. The short answer is: nothing changes today. BT has said TalkTalk will keep operating separately while regulators review the deal, so your broadband and landline carry on as normal, and there is nothing you need to do right now. BT should set out quickly and plainly what this means for contracts, prices and service in the future, so nobody is left guessing. In the meantime, keep paying as normal and leave your direct debit running, as missed payments could put your service at risk. Scammers thrive on moments like this, so if anyone contacts you out of the blue about the sale, hang up and get in touch with TalkTalk yourself through My Account on its website. If you or someone in your home relies on the landline or broadband for a care alarm or a medical reason, tell TalkTalk now so you’re registered for extra support such as priority fault repair. It’s still your provider for the time being, and it can only look after you properly if it knows who you are. If the new owner puts up your price beyond what was set out in your contract, or makes other significant changes to it, Ofcom’s rules mean you should be able to leave without an exit fee. For now, carry on as normal. If you’re out of contract, you’re free to look around as you always were, and it’s worth checking you’re still on the right deal. events.title: My family of 5 moved into a 3-bedroom duplex. I was dreading downsizing at first, but I'm glad we did.
events.summary: The author's family of five moved into a three-bedroom duplex. Courtesy of Melissa Noble Most of my previous homes have been bigger, two-story houses. However, my family of five just moved into a smaller three-bedroom duplex. I was dreading having less space at first, but there are unexpected benefits. I've always loved the idea of having a big family home . I grew up in a two-story house with six family members, and it was always loud, fun, and messy. Now that I'm a mother of three, I have a very different perspective on what it actually takes to run a busy family home. After living in multiple two-story houses in the last few years, I've realized that bigger isn't necessarily better in many ways. In August, our family of five downsized to a small three-bedroom duplex in Labrador on the Gold Coast, Australia. Before that, we'd been living with my parents , and prior to that, we lived in a double-story house in Bright, in country Victoria. Initially, I dreaded the idea of residing in what felt like a shoebox. How would we all cope? Would the kids drive each other nuts? How would they manage without a big yard to run around in? And most importantly, where on earth would I hide, aside from the shower? The first couple of weeks were an adjustment, as we got used to our smaller abode . But much to my surprise, I'm actually finding it to be a refreshing change, and there have been plenty of unexpected benefits. The inside is so much easier to clean Our previous homes took me at least three hours to clean each week. When you're busy running businesses and raising three children , that kind of time can feel like dead expenditure, a bit like paying rent. In contrast, it takes less than an hour to clean our new home. It's light and bright and somehow doesn't seem to accumulate dust in the same way the two-story properties did. Having a smaller space to maintain has saved me an enormous amount of time and energy. Instead of spending hours keeping on top of the housework , my husband and I have more time for things that actually matter to us, like making memories with our kids. The author spends less time on cleaning in her smaller home. Courtesy of Melissa Noble There's less yard work One of my favorite things about our home in country Victoria was the garden. It had these beautiful, mature trees that were spectacular to look at, but they also dropped a huge amount of foliage. As a result, my husband was forever outside raking up debris. Likewise, when we lived with my parents, he'd spend several hours a month mowing and maintaining their yard. Our new home is a different story. The back has a tiled courtyard, so there's no real maintenance required, and out front, there's a small yard. My husband or son can mow the grassed area in about 20 minutes. Again, this means we've gained more time to spend together as a family, rather than being tied down with the upkeep of a property. Less clutter, more functional With bigger homes , it's easy to fall into the trap of buying things to fill the space. Often, it's stuff you don't necessarily need, or at least that was my experience in the past. Before we downsized, we ditched a whole lot of our clutter. Toys the kids hadn't looked at in years went to the thrift shop. Old clothes were tossed or passed on to someone who could use them. In our new home, we've kept the furniture to a minimum, which has naturally reduced clutter. I feel like this has really helped with my mental health. Moving into a smaller space has also made us more conscious about the items we do own. We try to stick to items that are functional and serve a specific purpose in daily life. Cheaper bills It's still early days, and we haven't had to pay any bills yet, but we do expect to see some energy savings thanks to our move. The difference in our utility bills will really help our household budget over time. It's hard to compare like for like between our last two properties, as one was in a much cooler climate and needed heating at this time of year, and Mum and Dad's house had solar panels . We do expect our bills to be lower at our new home. Our water bills may also be cheaper, as there's less outdoor watering required. Small suits us, for the moment We know that our current home probably won't work as our kids grow older. I imagine that having three teenagers in a small duplex, haggling and loafing around, could test our patience in the long run. But for the moment, downsizing has been a refreshing change. There's something so liberating about simplifying things, living with less stuff, and having a smaller space to maintain. We're embracing our small-home chapter and appreciating the little things along the way. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: BT agrees rescue deal to buy broadband operator TalkTalk
events.summary: Published 5 October 2026, 07:37 BST The UK's biggest broadband provider, BT, has agreed to buy rival operator TalkTalk to save the company from collapse . The takeover would end of months of speculation over the future of TalkTalk and mean services for its millions of customers will continue as normal. BT chief executive Alison Kirkby said it provided "a safety net" for those who rely on TalkTalk. The administrator said it also provided certainty for TalkTalk's 900 staff. However, Virgin Media called the deal a "stitch up" which allows BT to "tighten its grip" over the market. The government has given itself the power to have the final say on the takeover, citing its importance to critical public services. TalkTalk has 1.5 million retail customers and one million wholesale customers across the UK. BT's Kirkby told the BBC's Today programme: "Two and a half million customers, including vulnerable households, and key emergency services might have lost their services if Talk Talk had failed, which it was on track to do. "So BT stepped in as we were the only viable option to take the business forward." TalkTalk began as a challenger to BT in the broadband market. It was listed on the London Stock Exchange, but was taken over by private equity in 2021. Since then, the firm has built up debt while losing customers, leaving it unable to pay some of those it owes money to. The Competition Markets Authority (CMA) will need to approve the takeover, which would give BT greater power over the broadband market. Tom Smith, a competition lawyer and former legal director at the CMA, said the regulator will be balancing that concern with other considerations. "When the CMA looks at it, it will look at what would have happened if the deal wasn't going through," he told the BBC. "If TalkTalk would have exited the market, for example, then really any deal is better than TalkTalk exiting, but then there might be alternative bidders as well that would have been less anticompetitive." However, the Department of Culture, Media, and Sport (DCMS) has given itself the power to make the final decision on the deal in the name of the public interest once the CMA has made its report. DCMS has given the CMA until 19 October to deliver its verdict. Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said: "Phone and broadband services are vital national infrastructure. "If TalkTalk services fail, there is a genuine risk to life and public services – including to hospitals, schools and emergency care. These are unprecedented circumstances that require action now." BT has said it will cost the firm £400m to buy TalkTalk. This includes the amount needed to buy TalkTalk from administration, fees, TalkTalk's £60m loss for this year, and BT effectively writing off the £100m TalkTalk owes BT's Openreach business. events.title: Brighter isn't better and more is less. The AI slowdown is nigh, no matter who says what
events.summary: There has been much chilly weather in the sunny meadowlands of AI futures. Fortunately, to use an indecently inappropriate adverb, the rest of the world isn’t really looking, being too busy chewing its nails over the very many other intimations of disaster. Sure, rebel swarms of attack agents breaking out of the labs isn’t a good look. OpenAI delaying its IPO and a new model launch likewise. All these things soak up whatever bandwidth the news media have to AI right now. Putting them in a bigger context, that of promises made and not kept, problems known but not fixed, the observable risk-reward ratios as models develop, we may at last start having a sense of what sort of crisis awaits. Actual crises are frequently triggered by crises in confidence, themselves caused when frameworks of assumption stop standing up to reality and wishful thinking. Thus, the assumption to date is that models will get more powerful and infrastructure more capable, in a way that justifies — demands — massive capex. The economics of giant infrastructure investment when you can’t buy what you need is a great bet in free markets that presupposes that freedom, and yeah, about that. A bigger problem is the idea that more powerful AI is always better. It frequently is, but that’s not good enough, When frontier models have to be kept in LLM jail for uncontrollable dishonesty, not so much. Here, the bigger context is that we’ve known that at heart LLM probability space is entirely relative. There is no ground truth there. Nobody has fixed hallucinations, and now we see the fascinating phenomenon of a machine that doesn’t understand truth but can deliberately lie. If more powerful models are better at that, scratch one assumption. Another huge assumption is that even at the current level of model reliability, agentic architectures are ready to be useful. Those who show all the caution of a chronic gambler on a winning "streak" are as ready to get the brakes slammed on as their opposites. The principal contender for the one true proof of concept that agentic AI is a dangerous fount of unexpected consequence is Meta’s new Muse. It is aimed at low-information credulous users and its star turn is, of course, shopping. The AI use case that’s five years away, and always has been. It’s Meta, so of course it soaks up all the information about you, your online activities and the people you talk to as much as it can. It will soon have ultracute animated Tamagotchi-style pets you can wear around your neck to improve your status as a Meta monitoring post. And we did say it was Meta, so has all the attention to security and careful design you may expect. Which is why it’s already been caught sending people’s physical addresses to strangers, and why when researcher Jonny at neuromatch.social went poking around its infrastructure — each instance runs permanently on its own Linux VM — they found just a ton of fun. Headline party tricks hard-coded. What looks like attempts to train off Claude. And yes, you can get it to run your own things on that VM deep within Meta, which Jonny points out is a botnet paradise waiting to happen. This banger of a bad ‘un is being given away to Meta users, who pretty much define a vulnerable target audience for tech that may not be totally trustworthy. Meta, of course, is dead against AI safety regulation. Place your bets on the headlines to follow. In any case, the upside of using agents as demoed in every keynote is either so trivial and trite — book me a restaurant! — or so catastrophic if it fails — organize my family vacation! — that consumer agents are a bust. It’s just that Meta may be bringing a lot of accelerant to that particular fire. There are other fires, of course, many known about since everything kicked off. Model collapse due to training on data contaminated with output? Still a thing, still no fix a "better" AI might provide. And that habit AI has of retailing everything and paying for nothing, choking off its own training data supply chain and a huge chunk of commerce and culture with it? Very much still a thing. Where AI does make consistent progress is in domain-specific tasks. Science, engineering, mathematics, and coding, if you match a model with enough reinforcement learning with humans who know how to manage them, there are startling results. You don’t get much innovation, not much newness, which is the true driver of progress. Better than humans is highly contextual. Computers have been better at chess for decades, but there isn’t a better chess. Horses run faster than humans, and that’s been useful for four millennia, but we got to peak horses quite some time ago. So the question is, have we reached peak AI, where the cost of future developments don’t match the risk they won’t work well enough to justify? If ChatGPT already writes a perfectly good business letter in a couple of seconds, there is no meaningful improvement to be had for users. Most AI is profoundly annoying, in ways that have nothing to do with the models and everything to do with perverted UX in an attempt to justify growth. That is both unsustainable and a tacit admission that AI hasn’t solved its use case problem. If we are at or near peak AI, is that the crisis that bursts that goddam bubble? Certainly a readjustment, as all bets on the continuous uptick curve are off. AI as it stands is useful enough to power a big industry sector, just in ways that are and remain at odds to how it is marketed and its future fantasies. Trust in AI Max may be shaken, but there's still room for lots of improvement. That slowdown that everyone who isn’t a miscreant is calling for may happen organically, if we escape the smoking-is-good-for-you mentality of the Metans and the Muskovites. That’s still a gamble we shouldn't be taking, but the odds may be better than we thought. ®

events.title: Pakistan installs fishing nets at security outposts to block drone attacks
events.summary: Strung several metres overhead, the nets are a low-cost solution in sensitive areas prone to deadly attacks by armed groups. Hangu, Pakistan – Police officer Fayyaz Khan and his colleagues ducked for cover as drones carrying explosives rained them down on their checkpost in northwest Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province this year. The April 16 attack was claimed by Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), commonly known as the Pakistan Taliban, and its fighters then opened fire from all sides of the Sarki Piyala police checkpost in Hangu district, about 30km (18 miles) from the border with Afghanistan and a hotbed of deadly attacks by armed groups, mainly the TTP. list 1 of 4 Suicide bombing in Pakistan’s Dera Ismail Khan kills at least 12 people list 2 of 4 Pakistan launches deadly air attacks on Afghanistan list 3 of 4 Pro-Imran Khan mass rally launched after Pakistan government talks fail list 4 of 4 Pakistan, India summon diplomats after two people killed in border incident The confrontation lasted roughly seven hours, killed the driver of an armoured vehicle and injured a constable, Khan, a 40-year-old police inspector, recalled. “There was a great deal of fear because we were in the middle of a battle. At that moment, we did not even know whether we would make it back home alive,” Khan told Al Jazeera. To defend against such attacks, the police in Hangu came up with an unlikely, low-cost solution – fishing nets strung several metres overhead between the checkpost’s rooftops and perimeter walls, forming a kind of aerial ceiling. Simple in construction and resembling what fishermen use for their work, the netting was first installed two months ago, according to the local police. Since then, Khan said, no drone attacks have taken place at Sarki Piyala. “If a drone comes over the checkpoint, there is a possibility that it could get caught in the net and be defused or stopped,” he said as his colleagues, strapped into bullet-resistant vests and holding guns in their hands, kept watch beneath a canopy of black mesh patched together with rope and wire. “Even if a drone does not get caught and explodes above the net, the damage is expected to be much less because most of the shrapnel and fragments would be dispersed in the air rather than falling directly onto the ground where the police personnel are positioned.” A standard checkpost can be covered with such nets for about 400,000 Pakistani rupees ($1,435), Hangu district police officer Tariq Habib told Al Jazeera. “The police have introduced the netting system at vulnerable police stations and checkposts to reduce the impact of drone and quadcopter attacks,” Habib said, adding that more nets were being installed at police stations across the district. He said the police in Hangu have asked for additional funding from the provincial government to expand the programme and their request is under review. A spokesman for the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa police said the nets have been installed at checkpoints and police posts in at least five other vulnerable districts: Kohat, Karak, Bannu, Lakki Marwat and Dera Ismail Khan. Even military outposts at some sites in the province have deployed the antidrone netting system. The fishing nets have been put up in response to a shift in the tactics of armed groups, which are pairing gunfire and mortars with drones and quadcopters. Pakistan has seen an increase in armed attacks in recent years, mainly targeting the police and the military, with many of them claimed by the TTP, which says it is fighting for a Taliban-style, religious-driven government in Pakistan. Pakistani officials have repeatedly accused Kabul’s Taliban government of providing the TTP a safe haven on its soil and have demanded that it prevent cross-border attacks into Pakistan. Kabul has denied the accusations and called the attacks Islamabad’s domestic security problem. In Hangu, the deadliest of such attacks happened on July 29 when attackers stormed a police outpost with quadcopters rigged with bombs before launching a ground ambush, killing at least 11 police officers and wounding 28. Fifteen attackers were also killed in the hours-long assault, claimed by the TTP. On September 20, another exchange of fire in Hangu killed six soldiers and eight attackers, according to the Pakistani army. That attack came two days after another armed group, called Ittehad-ul-Mujahideen Pakistan, killed 23 people, including 16 police officers, and bombed a mosque in coordinated attacks in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Kohat district. Police said they have recorded at least 16 attacks in Hangu this year, making it one of the most sensitive districts in the province. But police officer Zeeshan Khan said no drone or quadcopter attacks have occurred at Sarki Piyala and the nearby Baliamena checkposts since the fishing nets went up. He said the nets provide “an extra layer of security” to police personnel.

events.title: Coach services could be cut due to record diesel prices, operators warn
events.summary: Coach services could be cut due to record diesel prices, UK operators warn Rising fuel costs are pushing hundreds of firms out of business, threatening school transport, firms say Coach operators have said record diesel prices could force cuts to services including school transport, as hauliers warn rising fuel costs are pushing hundreds of firms out of business. The average price of diesel on UK forecourts hit a fresh record of more than £2 a litre last week, as the war in the Middle East continues to disrupt global fuel supplies. Alison Edwards, the director of policy at the Confederation of Passenger Transport (CPT), said the cost of fuel had “surged this year to unsustainable levels, pushing coach operators’ already tight margins to breaking point”. “It is time for urgent action,” she said. “Without intervention, soaring prices will mean difficult decisions on the availability of services, including home-to-school transport, and the viability of businesses.” Edwards said 85% of independent coach operators are family businesses, and called on the government to provide temporary support with the cost of diesel, adding that the industry “needs help”. Local bus operators in England have already received help with fuel costs via subsidies to help cover running costs. Coach companies, which say they carry out a similar role, have received no equivalent support. Richard Smith, the managing director of the Road Haulage Association (RHA), said the haulage sector was under similar strain. “Businesses in our sector operate on slim profit margins, typically about 2%, so the continuing high fuel costs are a huge challenge for us,” he said. He said hauliers were now paying an extra £350 a week for each truck compared with before the Iran war. “It’s just unsustainable,” he said. “If haulage, coach and van operators can’t pass these costs on, they struggle, and we’ve seen hundreds of transport businesses going bust already this year.” Hauliers are calling for a pause on planned fuel duty rises, and a rebate to help offset the cost of diesel. The RAC motoring organisation has called for the government to expand its 5p cut in fuel duty, which has already been extended until the end of the year . Rhys Hackling, the managing director of Direct Connect Logistics, said the impact on his own business had been “absolutely enormous”. The company runs 22 lorries out of Oxfordshire, Northamptonshire and Warrington, transporting goods ranging from supermarket products to live events equipment. “We are spending over £300 a week more than we were last year on fuel,” he said. “We normally spend about £50,000 a month on fuel … it’s now knocking on £65,000.” Many hauliers work on fixed contracts with customers, Hackling said, meaning rising fuel costs squeeze or wipe out their margins entirely. “If these events continue, then it’s going to put a lot of haulage firms out of business,” he said. Somebody somewhere is having to pay for this, whether it’s the haulage firm or whether it’s the consumer.” In a move offering some hope that fuel prices might ease, leaders of G7 nations said on Friday that they would release up to 100m barrels of their emergency diesel and crude oil stockpiles. The announcement was partly in response to Donald Trump suggesting he might introduce a ban on diesel exports after the rise in sales to overseas buyers pushed US prices to record highs. It appears to have averted the threat, which could have pushed diesel prices even higher in the UK, since Britain relies on the US for about a third of its diesel imports and does not refine enough to meet demand on its own. The benchmark Brent crude oil price declined by nearly 1% on Monday to just over $101 a barrel. The transport minister, Keir Mather, has said the UK’s fuel supply is “inherently resilient” and that people “shouldn’t be concerned about shortages”.

events.title: After 11 years on an H-1B visa, I still miss my family back home. Here’s why I stay in the US.
events.summary: Abhradeep Chatterjee and his wife moved to the US together 11 years ago; he's been on an H-1B since. Tim Evans for BI Abhradeep Chatterjee has lived in the US on an H-1B visa for 11 years — the uncertainty's been hard. He hasn't visited India to see family in over a decade. Despite it all, Chatterjee is choosing the US because of the opportunities for him and his family. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Abhradeep Chatterjee, 37, an Indian national who lives in Minnesota. The following has been edited for length and clarity. I was young and newly married when I came to the US from India in 2015. I didn't imagine I'd still be here 11 years later. I came for the opportunity to grow. The Indian multinational company I'd been working for, Tata Consultancy Services, sent me to New Jersey on an assignment. I continued building a career in the US on the H-1B visa, and the country has challenged me professionally in ways I couldn't have imagined when I arrived. But it's all been on a temporary visa . The uncertainty has been difficult. This is part of our ongoing coverage of how the Trump administration's H-1B visa changes affect workers. If you've been impacted and want to share your story, please fill out this short form for the reporter. My wife made sacrifices; our daughter gained opportunities My wife and I both wanted to come to the US. She moved on a dependent H-4 visa , which doesn't automatically come with work authorization. She had to wait until my employer filed my green card paperwork, which meant she couldn't work for nearly four years. Money wasn't our biggest issue — I felt guilty that she'd studied for a master's and wanted to work, but sacrificed her life to come to the US with me. Meanwhile, my career progressed from relocating with TCS to joining another company as a technical lead. In 2023, I joined the Japanese IT company, NTT Data, where I'm now an associate director. While I was able to transfer my H-1B visa between companies, it wasn't always a stress-free process. Because approvals aren't in your control, there's always a degree of uncertainty, which made it hard to fully relax. Chatterjee said the US has challenged him professionally. Tim Evans for BI Being exposed to different ways of thinking in America has made me more adaptable and empathetic. Our two-year-old daughter was born in the US, and I'm glad this has opened up opportunities for her to study at a good US university at a lower cost than if she were an international student. My wife and I have long imagined our future in the US. We've built friendships and community here. We've bought a home with a backyard where our daughter can play, and we have two dogs. When I see my daughter playing with friends outside, it feels like the exact kind of environment I hoped to provide for her. At the same time, there is a certain irony in that we've built a life that feels permanent while living with an immigration process that often feels anything but. Chatterjee is pursuing his dreams for his family. Tim Evans for BI Being separated from family in India has been costly The hardest part of my journey has been the distance from my family. I grew up with so many friends and relatives in India, but I haven't gone back since I moved to the US, so I've missed a lot. Because of my visa status , travel decisions come with planning and immigration considerations, including visa stamping. My parents are getting older, and there have been times when I've wished I could easily travel home. I've not been present for important moments, including an uncle's funeral and a cousin's wedding. My daughter's birth made me realize what my parents might be missing out on. Video calls can help, but they don't replace sitting with your parents in person. I'm hoping to get an employer-sponsored EB-3 green card. I have a 2018 priority date, signaling my place in line for approval, from a previous employer's petition, but my plan is for my current employer to sponsor my petition instead. I don't know how long the wait will be, but I'm expecting to wait several more years. I'm already getting a lot of white hair, so maybe all my hair will be white by the time I get a green card . Every time my wife and I have to renew our visas, we get nervous about what could happen. The uncertainty hasn't erased our hope My grandma used to say that everything comes with a cost. There are struggles, but the opportunities in the US are huge compared to what we had in India. My wife is now an accountant. I could, in theory, have the same job title at a company in India, but since a lot of companies, including mine, have a large US presence, I have more opportunities to work directly with clients and decision-makers here. Chatterjee and his wife have bought a home in Minnesota. Tim Evans for BI Over the years, I've occasionally searched my own name online, not as a vanity project but to see the positive impact of my work. There are many Abhradeep Chatterjees — I want to contribute enough professionally to leave a visible record in search results. The opportunities I have access to in the US are helping me leave a bigger mark. If something went wrong and I had to leave, I'd go back to India . My parents are there, and I had my childhood there. I don't want these years to be just about waiting. I've built a career, made friends, and learned. Uncertainty has been part of my life for a long time, but I've tried not to let it define my life. When I was young, I dreamed of being in the US and taking a photo with the Statue of Liberty. Now, my dream is for my family. My wife and I have worked hard to build a life here, and one of my greatest hopes is that our daughter will have the freedom and opportunity to pursue her dreams. That goal motivates many of the sacrifices we've made along the way. Business Insider confirmed he was employed by Tata Consultancy Services and NTT Data. Neither company responded to a request for comment. A USCIS spokesperson told Business Insider that employment-based immigration "must benefit the nation, American businesses, and American citizens," and that it is working to ensure visa programs "supplement, not supplant American workers." The Department of Labor declined to comment. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Russia ramps up attacks on Kyiv infrastructure as U.S. makes fresh push for peace talks
events.summary: Russia has pledged to intensify strikes on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities after a drone attack damaged the capital’s key Northern Bridge over the weekend. Moscow said the strikes were retaliation for Ukraine’s actions after Zelenskyy vowed to double down on attacks targeting Russian oil refineries. Zelenskyy also said the U.S. has proposed fresh trilateral peace talks by the end of October, with Ukraine responding positively to the initiative. Russia's Defense Ministry has pledged to further intensify military attacks on Kyiv and other major Ukrainian cities, following strikes on a second major bridge in Ukraine's capital over the weekend. The latest threat comes as Russian forces have ramped up attacks on Kyiv in recent weeks, targeting data centers , telecommunications facilities and energy infrastructure as it seeks to disrupt daily life in the capital and force power cuts ahead of winter . A Russian drone struck Kyiv's key Northern Bridge over the Dnipro River on Saturday, damaging the road surface and forcing traffic to be suspended. Two people were injured in the attack, according to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko. The attack came shortly after German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in Kyiv to pledge 1 billion euros ($1.1 billion) in military aid to Ukraine, and after Russian drones repeatedly targeted Kyiv's Southern Bridge earlier in the week. In an update posted via Telegram on Sunday, Russia's Defense Ministry confirmed the attack on the Northern Bridge, saying the bridge "supports the transfer of troops and the logistics of military cargo." The ministry also responded to comments from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy . In an interview with Reuters, Zelenskyy said in comments published Saturday that Ukraine would double down on attacking Russian oil refineries in retaliation to a new policy of airstrikes designed to force people to abandon Kyiv and other cities. Ukraine's president said Russian civilians would not be targeted in these strikes. Ukraine’s surprise robot offensive exposes a vulnerability in Putin’s war machine Putin orders army expansion as Zelenskyy warns Russia preparing to deploy 10,000 North Korean troops Russia ‘truly’ appreciates U.S. invite to G20 summit — but hasn’t decided if Putin will go Zelenskyy says Ukraine ready for ‘energy ceasefire,’ calls for trilateral meeting with Putin, Trump Putin floats ‘chance’ at peace with Ukraine as NATO chief warns Russia is becoming ‘increasingly reckless’ Russia preparing ‘massive strikes’ on Ukraine’s energy sites after deadliest attack of the year Russia's economy has defied the skeptics. Cracks are getting harder to hide 'Winter is coming’: Ukraine fears its toughest test since Russia’s full-scale invasion "In response to these threats, the Russian Defence Ministry recalls that the massive strikes are launched against Kiev and other Ukrainian regions specifically in retaliation for the actions of the Kiev regime's leader," Russia's Defense Ministry said Sunday via Telegram, according to a Google translation. Zelenskyy "bears full personal and political responsibility" for these intensified strikes, the ministry said. Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine more than four-and-a-half years ago, with fighting along the frontline virtually deadlocked as the conflict continues into a fifth winter. Zelenskyy said via social media on Sunday that the Trump administration has proposed a trilateral meeting at the technical level by the end of October, adding that Ukraine is open to the United Arab Emirates or another country proposed by the American side hosting the talks. "I know they will propose this to the Russian side as well, or may have already done so. We will wait for the response. We respond positively to negotiations," Zelenskyy said. CNBC has contacted a spokesperson for the White House and Russia's Embassy in London and is awaiting a response. U.S. President Donald Trump has previously urged Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian oil refineries, saying the attacks are "hurting the world" as fuel supply disruptions continue to prop up U.S. diesel prices .

events.title: Why Treasuries Are ‘Risky’ Again
events.summary: We all know that Treasury yields have been surging, alongside bond yields all around the world. So what explains the selloff and does it mean that bonds are becoming fundamentally riskier? What happens if investors can no longer hedge stocks with government debt? And how do expectations of the Federal Reserve's "reaction function" fit in? In this episode, we speak with Carolin Pflueger, associate professor at the University of Chicago and a resident scholar at the Chicago Fed, about her work on the bond market and central banks. We discuss why bonds have become more stock-like, what that means for yields, and the role of the Fed's credibility in making bonds “bond-like” again. (Source: Bloomberg)

events.title: LinkedIn pros have found a new key to getting opportunities: selfies
events.summary: Courtesy of Arielle Berlinsky and Tara Crymble LinkedIn creators are finding career success by posting work selfies and videos on the platform. AI's impact on LinkedIn is making authentic, personal posts more effective than polished content. LinkedIn launched a Next Gen Voices program to help young creators connect and grow their careers. Your next career opportunity could start with your front-facing camera. For some LinkedIn creators , selfies and unscripted videos are opening doors that career updates alone did not — from speaking invitations to a new job. Three LinkedIn professionals told Business Insider that what used to be awkward on a platform where your boss, colleagues, and potential employers are watching is becoming the new norm that those looking to stand out may need to adapt to. Arielle Berlinsky, the Director of Marketing at Movement Strategy, told Business Insider she started posting on LinkedIn while in a workplace where rules and expectations felt constraining, and LinkedIn became a space to share opinions, humor, and — eventually — her face. “Even if you're working for a small company, you have a certain box that you can be kept in or standards you have to uphold,” Berlinsky said, adding that she initially shared photos from work events, then began recording videos about experiences and lessons as they happened. "The one thing you carry with you everywhere is your face and your name and your personality because that's the heart of who you are," Berlinsky said. “I'm so much more than just my job and my title.” AI is reshaping tactics for how to stand out As AI makes polished posts easier to produce, some creators say personality can help people connect with the human behind the profile. Tara Crymble, an account manager at B2B influencer marketing agency Creatorbuzz , told Business Insider that showing her face and speaking on video helps convey something a text post can struggle to capture. “In this time of AI, it's so easy for people to get lost in this overly polished, filtered, corporate, or even robotic tone ,” Crymble said. “I think if you're posting your face or especially video content, you can add in your personality and your quirks into your content, and it just comes across as more genuine,” Crymble added. “And I think that layer of trust is more quickly built.” LinkedIn has been tightening its approach to AI content , introducing a “Seems like AI slop ” feedback option and tools to limit the distribution of generic AI-generated posts . Jack Appleby, a 37-year-old writer and creator consultant who dubbed himself an "elder millennial" in a conversation with Business Insider, said he is seeing personal photos gain traction and may be changing his tactics after initially building his 90,000 followers on LinkedIn almost exclusively through text posts. “I think the AI police are out in full force on LinkedIn, maybe more than any other social network,” Appleby said. “People are more concerned than ever whether something's made by someone real or made by AI,” Appleby added. “I think people want connection, and maybe it's time I let people get to know who I am as much as the way that I think." Gen Zers are emerging as the leading voices on LinkedIn Tara Crymble said that LinkedIn is evolving from an online resume to a social platform where people share slices of their own personal lives. Courtesy of Tara Crymble Crymble once used LinkedIn like a traditional résumé for job announcements. But last December, when she began sharing what she was doing and learning as a recent graduate , including her face and voice, Crymble said her following grew from roughly 1,000 to 6,000, and her posts have generated more than 250,000 impressions. “Not only was I getting opportunities such as speaking and media and opportunities to be in rooms that I wouldn't have originally had the chance to have, but I also received my current job,” Crymble said. “I found that out through my LinkedIn presence and connecting with the team.” Berlinsky said her posts have earned millions of impressions and helped her build a community of over 55,000 people. Berlinsky and Crymble both said they participate in LinkedIn's Next Gen Voices program, an invitation-only, 12-week cohort for Gen Z creators that offers opportunities to test features, provide feedback, and meet the LinkedIn team. "This may sound crass, but generally, if you know how to dress and present yourself , it's probably worth putting your face out there so people know who you are," Appleby said. "Most data I see, and people are often not comfortable hearing this, says it's often the most well-kept people or the most conventionally attractive people who get promotions in the workplace," Appleby added. Advice on how to get started Arielle Berlinsky said those just getting started should worry less about appearing perfect and think about authenticity instead. Courtesy of Arielle Berlinsky For those who are not social media natives like more Gen Zers, the young creators have tips on how to get unstuck on LinkedIn. "I've seen a lot of creators that fully embrace themselves, whether that be their interests or personality," said Crymble. "In a world of all this AI content, it shines through as relatable and is embraced back." Berlinsky recommends starting with a friend who can take photos of you doing something naturally, and practice speaking into the camera as though you're speaking to one person. “I'm going to show up and talk as if I'm talking to one person and not try to speak to everyone, not try to cater to everyone,” Berlinsky said, "Consistency matters more than sticking to a single format, so think about the memes and infographics that can also communicate personality." "Stop waiting for the ideal lighting or buy that thousand-dollar equipment," Berlinsky added. "The less you worry about filtering yourself, the less you worry about making it perfect, the more it will translate into success.” Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Silicon Valley founders' hottest funding source: the Bank of Best Friends
events.summary: iStock; Tyler Le/BI Katherine Naylor Pullman started Our Third Place, a networking group for women in media, as a part-time side project. It began four years ago with monthly, then weekly, dinners. Women in Chicago and Los Angeles reached out, wanting to host their own dinners. Now, Our Third Place is in 40 cities, and running it has blossomed into a full-time gig for Naylor Pullman, who left a previous job in brand partnerships. Our Third Place has grown to 1,800 members without big investors, and that's by design. "If someone were to throw us millions of dollars, they would then want millions of members," Naylor Pullman says. "I firmly believe you cannot scale community by the millions." She and the company's CEO, Ashley Preininger, are building by seed-strapping , a tactic where companies raise smaller investments and forgo the traditional venture capital cycle of Series A and Series B fundraising, and then grow the company through revenue. They're raising money now from family, friends, and members, because they can work within that smaller fundraising space, and keep costs for members lower when the company isn't beholden to massive investor returns. "We actually don't feel like we need a huge influx of cash to do what we need to do," Preininger says. Seed-strapping has become more appealing to founders as venture capital funding waned following the 2010s boom and the end of the zero-interest rate policy . The shift also comes amid the rise of the single-person startup , as more founders deploy AI agents to help with coding, accounting, marketing, and other tasks that once required expensive labor. The founders who spoke with me for this story tell me they're taking an alternate path to funding by choice, seeing that more money can come with more problems — more commitments, more expectations, and less control of their company. Amid "all the fundraising doom and gloom," says Caroline Lewis, managing partner at early-stage venture firm Nura Ventures, "the rules are being rewritten." "You can go back to business fundamentals of building a product that customers want to buy, then you can raise some capital and get some decent traction, and don't necessarily have to be beholden to the traditional venture train," Lewis says. For some founders, hopping off the venture capital treadmill allows them to build at the speed they want. Seed-strapping isn't new. Software company Zapier seed-strapped before the term was in the zeitgeist, raising just $1.3 million seed-strapping and eventually growing to hundreds of millions in annual revenue. But the tactic has gotten new attention as founders struggled to raise venture capital. The number of global venture deals has steadily fallen from more than 17,000 in the first quarter of 2022 to about 8,500 in the second quarter of 2026, according to data from Pitchbook. Deal value is hitting an all-time high, but that's largely fueled by big deals with OpenAI, Anthropic, and xAI. Since late 2024, AI startups have captured at least half of venture funding, with their stranglehold on the market climbing to 80% at the beginning of this year, according to Crunchbase. Anthropic , xAI , OpenAI , and Waymo accounted for nearly two-thirds of the money invested that quarter. The market is bifurcated between those companies that need lots of capital and can bring massive returns, and all the other good ideas that may need less compute power, less labor, and would bring smaller returns, says Charles Hudson, managing partner at venture firm Precursor Ventures. Big venture funds look for areas where they can make large investments and look for massive returns. "The biggest challenge is: how do you finance these companies through that little middle period?" He says. "There's lots of money to get started. If you're building something big, there's lots of money to shoot for the moon." But for companies that raise a seed round of a few million, and may need another few million down the line, there could be fewer investors in that sweet spot. "Who's going to provide you that money?" The number of global venture deals has dropped from more than 17,000 in the first quarter of 2022 to about 8,500 in the second quarter of 2026. According to Carta, 41% of the US-based companies that raised a seed round in 2022 didn't fundraise beyond that. Another 21% continued to fundraise, but did not pursue a Series A round. These companies have also maintained lower headcounts than those that did raise a Series A round or beyond, sticking with median staff numbers of between six and eight people, compared to 22 at firms that raised more money. About half of startups that raised seed money in 2018 moved to a Series A within three years, according to data provided by Carta. But among those that raised a seed round in 2022, fewer than a third of new startups made the leap to a Series A by 2025. "The overall trend is that graduation rates have decreased," Hamza Shad, insights manager at Carta, tells me in an email. "This suggests that seed-strapping — whether willingly or unwillingly — has become more common." Lauren Dines worked in venture for five years, but left to found and work full-time on Breaknine, an AI startup that handles personalized outreach, late last year. "While I was in venture, I saw a lot of companies where I was like, this is a good idea, it's just not venture scalable." By steering away from the venture route and shunning expectations of massive growth, she can potentially accelerate the typical venture timeline, exiting in three to five years instead of seven to 10. It's potentially less risky than seeking to raise tens of millions of dollars and get returns in the hundreds of millions. Dines says her goal is to grow her business, and then make a strategic decision about how to move forward. "It was never my dream to have a venture-backed business." Dines thought about: "What do I need, and how can I best get there?" when it comes to her own needs and life. "This is probably the most efficient path to getting there." Women have also struggled to raise venture capital, with all-female leadership teams taking home just 6.5% of venture deals in 2024. But women founders and investors make up nearly half of all angel investors . Boot-strapping and seed-strapping are ways around the funding blocks. That's part of the thought process behind how Shannon Davenport, who founded Esker Beauty, has built her company. She boot-strapped it for about four years, then went looking for venture capital. But Davenport says she found that the VCs had a thesis for how her business should fit the market that didn't align with what she knew about her products and customers. She raised smaller investments in a seed stage, and now, says her company is approaching profitability, targeting the end of the year. "My most important valued asset is my time," Davenport says. And chasing venture money ate away at the time she could spend doing the product work that she's passionate abou
