events.title: Lao man deported by the US to Eswatini is released after more than a year in prison
events.summary: A Lao man deported by the United States to Eswatini under the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown has been released after more than a year in prison CAPE TOWN, South Africa -- A Laotian citizen deported by the United States to Eswatini under the Trump administration's immigration crackdown was released from a maximum-security prison in the African nation on Sunday after being held there for more than a year, his lawyer said. Phone Chomsavanh was among five immigrants deported to Eswatini — where he has no ties — in July 2025 in the early days of the Trump administration's secretive and highly contentious third-country deportation program. Chomsavanh's U.S.-based lawyer, Tin Thanh Nguyen, said in a statement announcing his release that he had only been informed that he was being deported to Eswatini shortly before a military cargo plane carrying him and other deportees landed there more than 14 months ago. Chomsavanh was now being deported to Laos, Nguyen said. Chomsavanh and the four other immigrants he was deported to Eswatini with were convicted of serious crimes in the U.S., but had served their sentences by the time they were sent to the Matsapha Correctional Complex near Eswatini's administrative capital, Mbabane. “He had already served his time. Instead they put him on a plane without telling him where it was headed and left him in a prison in a country he had never heard of, where nobody ever accused him of anything," Nguyen said. “He sat there for more than a year. No notice, no hearing, no chance to object. That is not due process by any definition.” He said in separate messages to The Associated Press that Chomsavanh had left Eswatini and landed in Johannesburg en route to Laos. An Eswatini government spokesperson didn’t immediately acknowledge Chomsavanh’s release. Chomsavanh was born in a refugee camp in Thailand after his parents fled Laos, and his family moved to the United States when he was 7, his lawyer said. Chomsavanh is one of around 500 immigrants who have been deported from the United States to African countries that aren't their home nations since the third-country program began last year, according to advocacy groups Human Rights First and Refugees International, which have been monitoring the deportations. Around a dozen African countries have accepted third-country deportees from the U.S., some in exchange for millions of dollars in payments. Eswatini, which is Africa's last absolute monarchy and is ruled by a king, was paid $5.1 million by the Trump administration to take deportees, according to the agreement between the countries. Eswatini has received around 30 deportees so far. Suspect in FlyDubai incident was previously identified as security risk: Officials Father, son federally charged in connection to death of Ole Miss student District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' The program, which results in immigrants being held in countries they have no ties to and where they haven't been charged with any crime, has been fiercely criticized by rights groups and lawyers. It has been the subject of legal challenges in the U.S. and in some of the countries where immigrants have been sent. The Trump administration has defended the policy as a way to quickly remove immigrants who have final deportation orders from the U.S. when their home countries might not immediately take them back. Last month, a U.S. appeals court upheld a judge's ruling to halt the program, because it didn’t give immigrants facing removal from the U.S. time to challenge their deportation to a third country if they fear persecution or torture there. The U.S. Supreme Court ruled last week to temporarily allow U.S. President Donald Trump's administration to continue swiftly removing immigrants to third countries, though it will hear arguments in the case in December. The program has largely been carried out in secrecy, with little transparency over how many immigrants have been deported to third countries, and where and in what conditions they are being held. events.title: Holiday cottage company insisted on a death certificate to amend our break
events.summary: Sykes Holiday Cottages showed no empathy and insisted on paperwork we didn’t have so soon after my husband’s death W e booked a break with Sykes Holiday Cottages for 11 of us to celebrate my mum’s 80th birthday last February. The cost was £2,400, paid for by my 87-year-old dad, but it was my husband who made the booking. In January, my husband was diagnosed with aggressive lymphoma, and he died 10 days before the trip. My parents and some other members of the party still planned to take the holiday, and my dad informed Sykes of the death, since my husband was their point of contact. Sykes declared that the booking could not be honoured in my late husband’s name and that they would need a copy of his death certificate to move it into my name. We did not have one since an inquest into the death had been ordered. Sykes said a copy of my marriage certificate would suffice. I submitted this, only to be told that “an official document recognised by the state that confirms the passing of the deceased” was required. We provided a screenshot of the inquest listing from the coroner’s court website but were advised that this was not sufficient evidence. My GP wrote a letter confirming the death, but Sykes did not reply, and by then we were all too distressed to continue. Later, Sykes sent numerous emails to my late husband’s email address asking whether he had enjoyed the stay. We never received a refund, and I have not felt emotionally strong enough to do anything further before now. I could hardly believe what I was reading as I trawled through Sykes’s correspondence. Its response, on being informed of your husband’s untimely death, was to send him an email asking for information. When Sykes received the requested marriage certificate, the company simultaneously stated in an email that this provided sufficient proof for the booking to be transferred to your name, and that the booking could not be transferred without an official confirmation of death. The GP letter confirming the death merely elicited an email saying Sykes would be in touch. By then, the trip was two days away. Sykes still did not amend the booking name, nor did it acknowledge the link to the coroner’s inquest listing. The next you heard from them was the first of several emails addressed to your late husband hoping that he had enjoyed the holiday. When you asked them to stop using his email address, Sykes apologised for the “inconvenience”. Four days later, when you had to complain about another such email to him, you were told unapologetically that feedback forms are sent automatically. By then, Sykes had been informed multiple times over a fortnight that your husband had died. Sykes, I discover, does not have an official bereavement policy which, given the size of the business, is poor enough. But empathy does not require an official mandate and you received none. Its onerous name change requirements are more suitable for a visa application than checking into a Cumbrian cottage. It refunded the £2,400 pronto when I got in touch and added £150 in “goodwill”. I think that’s a paltry sum for the distress it caused, but you have accepted it so you can put the ordeal behind you. A spokesperson said: “We have contacted the family directly to apologise and resolve the matter, and are reviewing our processes to ensure situations like this are always handled with the care and sensitivity they deserve.” Hats off to first-class customer service Our spirits need some good news, so here are some tales of how customer service ought to be. “We bought a secondhand Scandibørn bed from a third-party seller and found four screws were missing,” writes CC . “They were so specialist that no shop even knew what they were called. We contacted Scandibørn with low expectations of help, but they immediately offered to send us the missing screws for free. Exemplary customer service, which has earned a customer for life.” MS , meanwhile, raises his revamped hat to Tilley. “Thirty years ago I bought a Tilley hat, which became a constant companion on walks and holidays. It was beginning to show its age and, since the label promised a lifetime guarantee, I contacted Tilley. I was asked to submit photographs and was promptly invited to choose from three designs. The replacement was dispatched within days, with a handling charge of £20. Sadly, this one will outlast me.” We welcome letters but cannot answer individually. events.title: Djokovic defeats top seed Zverev to reach China Open semifinals
events.summary: Novak Djokovic to face Daniil Medvedev in the semifinals in Beijing after the Russian defeats Francisco Cerundolo. Novak Djokovic has brushed aside ongoing injury-related struggles and produced a trademark comeback to defeat top seed Alexander Zverev 4-6, 6-4, 6-4 for a place in the China Open semifinals, extending his unbeaten record in the tournament. Playing the ATP 500 event in Beijing for the first time since 2015, the six-time champion was pushed to the limit by reigning French Open and US Open champion Zverev, who delivered 19 aces in the match on Sunday. list 1 of 4 Sabalenka, Rybakina handed shock defeats at China Open tennis list 2 of 4 World No 1 Sinner withdraws from Shanghai Masters as knee injury lingers list 3 of 4 ‘So far so good’: Novak Djokovic ready for tennis comeback at China Open list 4 of 4 Asian Games: Alex Eala out of gold medal contention after semifinal loss Meeting for the first time in nearly 16 months, Djokovic struggled to contain the German’s power in the early stages as the 29-year-old Zverev claimed the opening set, but the Serb gradually worked his way into the match and refused to let his opponent pull away. “I had a terrible start – two double faults at the beginning. It was quite cold, and honestly, I didn’t feel warmed up, but my fault,” Djokovic said. “I gave him an early break, and then it was hard to come back in the first set.” The contest was briefly interrupted by a moment of controversy when Zverev argued that the electronic advertising signage had gone dark during a rally and requested a video review after losing the point. Replays showed a section of the signage had switched off although not as Zverev was missing the forehand. The chair umpire ordered the point to be replayed, prompting a frustrated exchange from Djokovic. The turning point came late in the second set when Djokovic broke at 5-4 to level the match, shifting the momentum in his favour after a tightly contested battle. With little separating the pair in the third, the Serbian struck again at 5-4 on the Zverev serve, securing the decisive break to seal the victory in two hours and 35 minutes. “I was trying to be aggressive and come to the net and change up the pace, not giving the same pattern,” Djokovic said. “I am just glad that I held my nerves, played good shots at important moments, 5-4 in the second and third.” The pair had not met since Roland Garros in 2025, where Djokovic won in four sets, and Sunday’s encounter again highlighted the Serb’s ability to deliver under pressure despite a season disrupted by physical issues. With the victory, Djokovic moved a step closer to a seventh China Open title and an elusive first trophy of the year while denying Zverev another opportunity to strengthen his bid for the world number one ranking. Djokovic will face Daniil Medvedev in the semifinals after the Russian defeated Francisco Cerundolo 7-6(4), 6-3 earlier. Rybakina withdraws from Wuhan after China Open exit World number one Elena Rybakina withdrew from this month’s Wuhan Open due to a foot injury, tournament organisers said on Sunday, a day after the Kazakh suffered a shock defeat in her opening match at the China Open. Rybakina, who lost to world number 118 Alina Charaeva in Beijing, said she would take time away from competition to recover. “I’m very sorry to the fans who were looking forward to seeing me play,” Rybakina said in a story posted on the tournament’s Instagram account. “I’ll take some time to rest and recover. Thank you for your understanding and continued support.” The 27-year-old has been managing a lingering lower leg and foot problem that also forced her to retire from her Cincinnati quarterfinal against Iga Swiatek in August. Despite the setback, Rybakina recovered in time for the US Open, where she claimed her third Grand Slam title , rose to world number one and became the first player to qualify for the season-ending WTA Finals. Rybakina is next expected to compete this month in the Ningbo Open in China, where she will try to defend her title. The Wuhan Open is scheduled to take place from October 12 to 18.

events.title: Russia hospitalizes almost 200 people after researcher's death from plague: Reports
events.summary: Russia’s public health watchdog said the employee at the center of the case was diagnosed with “pneumonia of unknown etiology.” Expanded testing did not detect microorganisms linked to the employee’s work and authorities said the sanitary and epidemiological situation in the region remains stable, according to local media reports. Nearly 200 people have been placed under medical observation in Russia's Irkutsk region in eastern Siberia over suspected exposure to plague, according to local media reports. The report said 189 people were being monitored following the illness of an employee at an anti-plague research institute in Irkutsk. Alexei Tsydenov, head of the nearby Republic of Buryatia, said the woman had died from an unspecified form of plague. Russia's public health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor said Sunday that the employee had been diagnosed with "pneumonia of unknown etiology" and that the sanitary and epidemiological situation in the Irkutsk region and the cities of Irkutsk and Shelekhov remained stable. The agency said expanded testing had not detected microorganisms linked to the employee's work. The update follows local media reports on Friday that a 27-year-old employee at an anti-plague institute had fallen ill with suspected pneumonic plague after returning from a work trip to Buryatia, where an outbreak had been reported near the border with Mongolia, citing Russian Telegram channel Mash. The White House is monitoring reports of the suspected case and related quarantines in Russia, Axios reported Sunday, citing a Trump administration official. The official said the administration was "aware, monitoring the outbreak, and assessing options," the report said. The Russian and Moscow ministries of health, the World Health Organization and the U.S. State Department did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment.

events.title: Middle East oil exports surpass pre-war levels despite tensions, data shows
events.summary: IRGC commander says oil flows through US-supervised route in Hormuz are ‘negligible’. Crude oil exports from the Middle East have risen above pre-war levels on four of the seven days in the last week of September, provisional data from ship-tracking firm Kpler showed. However, senior Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) commander Ali Fadavi said in a televised interview on Sunday night that only three to four million barrels of oil per day (bpd) are now moving through the route, dismissing the amount as “negligible” when compared with pre-war traffic. list 1 of 3 Iran says Hormuz to remain closed until US meets conditions list 2 of 3 US withdraws B-1 bomber aircraft from UK’s Fairford base amid Iran fears list 3 of 3 Why is fighting intensifying in Yemen’s Taiz governorate? Fadavi said, for the first time, no US vessels were present in the Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz, the Sea of Oman or even the northern Indian Ocean and US warships are “100 percent vulnerable” to IRGC attacks. Kpler data showed crude exports from the region exceeded pre-war levels on September 24 and between September 27 and 29, rising to 19.5-22.5 million bpd. Around that time, Iran claimed success in attacking ships – including US Navy vessels – near the Strait of Hormuz, saying the strikes had forced Washington to move its warships further from the Iranian coast. Before the US-Israel war on Iran began, exports averaged 18 million bpd between March 2025 and February 2026. According to Kpler data, the overall tally for crude, oil products, chemicals and non-gas liquids averaged 22.4 million bpd in the seven days to September 30. On October 1, the seven-day moving average for crude exports was at 18.5 million bpd. This includes transits via the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, exports from terminals and ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman. The number of liquefied natural gas cargoes exiting the Strait of Hormuz also rose in September to its highest monthly level since February. The figures exclude any vessels that might have crossed the strait with their automatic identification system transponders turned off to avoid detection. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency reported at least one attack a day in the Strait of Hormuz or in the Gulf of Aden since October 2. On Sunday, Iran’s top negotiator and parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said the Strait of Hormuz would remain closed until the United States accepts Tehran’s seven-day plan to reopen the waterway.

events.title: Saudi Aramco cuts Asia crude prices to six-year low amid recovery as oil flows rebound
events.summary: Saudi Aramco has cut prices for its flagship crude grade sold to Asian buyers to a six-year low, as the world’s largest oil exporter competes for market share amid a recovery in oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. The state-owned Saudi oil company will sell Arab Light crude to Asian customers at a discount of $5 a barrel below the regional benchmark for November, widening the discount from $2 a barrel in October, according to a Bloomberg survey. Traders and refiners polled by Bloomberg had expected Aramco to raise prices by $5 a barrel for November. The price reduction signals that Saudi Arabia may be seeking to boost sales to Asia as oil flows from the Middle East recover after months of disruption linked to the Iran war. Aramco raised its November crude prices for Europe by $3 a barrel, while leaving prices for the US unchanged from October, Bloomberg reported. Although attacks on vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz continue, the volume of oil passing through the waterway has increased over the past few months. Saudi Arabia sold almost 100 million barrels of oil to Asian buyers in mid-September, helping to avert a looming supply crunch. The kingdom has also restored much of the crude flow through its East-West pipeline after suffering damage in an attack. The recovery has helped increase oil exports from the Middle East, with JPMorgan estimating last week that shipments had reached 98 per cent of prewar levels, Bloomberg reported. The pipeline allows Saudi Arabia to transport crude from its eastern oilfields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, providing an alternative export route that bypasses the strait. Aramco’s official selling prices apply to crude supplied under long-term contracts to refiners, who would typically collect their shipments from Ras Tanura on Saudi Arabia's Gulf coast. Ras Tanura hosts one of the world’s largest oil export terminals and a major refining facility. The port handles a significant share of Saudi crude exports, with cargoes typically heading to markets in Europe and Asia, including China, Japan and South Korea. But continued risks to shipping through the strait have prompted many customers to avoid the route. Aramco has asked Asian refiners to submit nominations for the volumes they intend to collect in November from ports inside the Arabian Gulf, as well as from Yanbu on the Red Sea and Sidi Kerir on Egypt's Mediterranean coast, Bloomberg reported.

events.title: Who were the top teen athletes at the Asian Games?
events.summary: China’s Zhang Zhanshuo, 19, finished with seven gold medals while compatriot Yu Zidi won three record-breaking golds. Teenage athletes have headlined some of the biggest Asian Games triumphs, leading their countries to historic gold medals, breaking records and cementing their legacy as formidable forces in the field. Far from being intimidated by competitors double or triple their age, these schoolchildren remained cool and unfazed as they cruised to gold at their Asian Games debut. list 1 of 4 How a comedy of errors ‘ruined everything’ for athletes at the Asian Games list 2 of 4 China swimmer makes Asian Games history as Thai sprinter wins track 100m list 3 of 4 Malaysia’s Ng, Sivasangari book 2028 Olympics berth with Asian Games gold list 4 of 4 Asian Games: Rumesh Pathirage wins javelin gold, Arshad Nadeem is fourth Many are already familiar with the pressure and expectations of the world stage and have dominated their sport all season. Al Jazeera Sport looks at some of the stars who left their mark in Japan: At just 13, Yu was named female Most Valuable Player (MVP), as she bagged three gold medals and broke as many Asian Games records in a fairytale debut. The schoolgirl stormed to victory in the women’s 200m butterfly, 200m and 400m individual medley (IM) and had a comfortable lead over her competitors. Her time of two minutes and 6.10 seconds (2:06.10) in the 200m IM stands as a world junior record and second-fastest time ever. “I don’t think I am what people describe as a prodigy,” she said after being crowned MVP. “I will continue to train hard, push myself and work alongside young athletes across Asia to inspire more young people to love and take part in sports, especially swimming.” Zhang held up seven fingers after his 400m freestyle win to count out his gold medals at the Games – the most at this edition, and more than what 27 of the 45 participating nations had in their medal tally at the conclusion of the event. He set Games records in the 400m and 800m freestyle, an Asian record in the 200m, and helped power China to gold and Asian records in the men’s 4x100m and 4x200m freestyle relays. But the 19-year-old has bigger victories in sight. “The Asian Games is not the goal. I’m still aiming for the Olympics and competing with the best,” he said. The teenager’s haul helped China sign off from swimming with 30 golds out of 41 medal events in the pool, with chief rival Japan a distant second with seven titles. Ohashi broke the world record in the men’s 200m breaststroke (2:04.83) in front of a home crowd to become the first swimmer under the 2:05 mark. The gold added to his title in the 100m breaststroke shared with China’s Dong Zhihao, bronze in the 50m breaststroke, and silver in the mixed and men’s 4x100m medley relays. The teenager said he was surprised and honoured that Olympic champion Leon Marchand knew who he was, after the Frenchman described the 17-year-old as a “scary” prospect ahead of the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. “I respect him because I know just how strong he is. But if I want to win, he’s someone I know I’ll have to beat.” Ohashi’s world record performance came just a week after the teenager recovered from COVID-19. Yan was already javelin world number one and Asian record holder when she stepped onto the field for her Games debut – her first and only throw of 70.46 metres was enough for gold and a Games record. It was the sixth-best of all time and well ahead of Olympic champion and home hero Haruka Kitaguchi’s 62.70m. Yan is closing in on the world record of 72.28m set by Barbora Spotakova in 2008. In May, she hurled a world-leading, record-breaking 71.74m to open an unprecedented season. Chen stormed to a new Games record in the women’s 100m en route to her first gold as she announced herself as the new sprint queen in Asia. “I have no limits,” was her response when asked how much faster she hopes to run. She followed up her podium finish with a silver in the 200m and gold in the women’s and mixed 4x100m relays. Goto narrowly missed gold in the men’s 400m hurdles, but his 47.93s was enough for a world under-18 best time, Asian under-20 best time, and a new personal best. The teen star has run sub-50 seconds eight times this season alone, an impressive feat for a 17-year-old. His Asian Games silver added to the World Under-20 one he bagged in August. Mohod scripted history for India when she became the first Indian to win an individual recurve archery gold at the Games. The 17-year-old helped India to gold in the women’s team recurve, and partnered with Dhiraj Bommadevara for mixed team silver. Mohod’s gold was no stroke of luck; she defeated South Korea’s reigning world champion and Olympic medallist Kang Chaeyoung in the quarterfinals before dominating China’s Zhu Jingyi in the semifinals. “Ever since I’ve made it to the national team, I’ve been visualising this moment.

events.title: Samoa PM apologises after Nazi salute video emerges
events.summary: Pacific island nation’s leader says 2007 video showing him saying ‘Heil Hitler’ does not reflect his beliefs. Samoa’s Prime Minister La’auli Leuatea Schmidt has apologised after previously unseen video showed him leading a Nazi salute and saying “Heil Hitler” at a family gathering. Schmidt issued the apology on Monday after the Samoa Observer, a local newspaper, published the seven-second clip the previous day. The footage was recorded at a Schmidt family reunion on the island of Savai‘i in July 2007, when he was an MP and deputy speaker of parliament. In the video, Schmidt is holding a microphone as he leads a “hip hip” exchange with the group before telling those present to raise their right hands and say “Heil Hitler”. About a dozen people visible in the footage appear to follow him. Radio New Zealand said it had independently verified the footage through its correspondent in Samoa. Schmidt said on Monday that the words and gesture were inappropriate regardless of what was intended at the gathering and apologised for the offence they could cause. “I reject Nazism, antisemitism, racism and all forms of political extremism,” he said, adding that the episode did not represent his beliefs or the values of Samoa’s government and people. The apology followed criticism from academics contacted by the Samoa Observer. Richard Evans, a historian of Nazi Germany, told the Samoa Observer by email that the footage was “shocking and disturbing”. The paper also quoted University of Canterbury academic Anne-Marie Brady as saying Schmidt should explain and apologise. Schmidt, who became prime minister in 2025, has made strong public expressions of support for Israel. He wore a Jewish prayer shawl at his swearing-in, where a shofar, a horn used in Jewish religious ceremonies, was sounded. He has also pledged to open a Samoan embassy in Jerusalem before the end of 2026, a step taken by only a handful of countries because of the city’s disputed status and Palestinian claims to East Jerusalem as the capital of a future state. In his Monday statement, Schmidt said he considered the controversy addressed and would focus on the country’s economic and social challenges.

events.title: Ben Affleck says he had a ‘heart attack’ when he first saw what AI could do — then he used it in his movie
events.summary: Ben Affleck said his company's AI tools are designed to support, not replace, people working in film. Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty Images Ben Affleck said his first close look at AI gave him a "heart attack." He then built a company that spent eight months shooting footage to train AI tools for film crews. Affleck said he used AI on his upcoming film, "Animals," but won't say exactly how. Ben Affleck said he wants AI to support filmmakers and artists in the creative process. Speaking at the Bloomberg Screentime event in Los Angeles over the weekend, Affleck said his company's AI tools are meant to help creatives work more efficiently, not make them obsolete. Affleck said his interest in AI grew after he started a visual-effects company, and he was able to use his celebrity status to get a closer look at the early work coming out of Google and OpenAI. "At first, I kind of had a heart attack. I called Matt Damon , and I was like, dude, we have to do as many movies in the next few years because we're finished," Affleck said. He said he began wondering how AI could be used "in an ethical way" to help people make movies without shutting others out. His solution, he said, was to create his own dataset so the technology could work "hand in glove" with artists. So, Affleck said he "raised the money" and spent eight months shooting a large collection of footage, which he used to further train existing AI models for specific filmmaking tasks. He said AI models first learn basic concepts, such as colors, from huge amounts of footage. But to understand the finer points of filmmaking, the models need more professionally shot material. "In order to obtain that information, I was concerned that most of the models being used had been trained on my peers' — people I know — work and I was uncomfortable with that," Affleck said. "I thought, that's not really a viable business." Instead, Affleck said, his company takes open models built on publicly available footage and trains them for cinematic work. Filmmakers can then further train the tools on their own productions as they work, retaining the proprietary nature of their footage and the learning that comes from it, he said. Affleck added that the AI is not meant to "replace people" nor "eliminate" them. "I don't believe that there will ever be 'Just type it in and make a movie that people want to see,'" Affleck said. "But the whole effort behind it was to do something ethical, to do something that did not displace people, but that allowed people in this economy and this world to benefit from this technology." In July, Netflix paid $587 million for Affleck's company, InterPositive. Affleck said he also used the AI tool "for lots of things" on his upcoming film, "Animals," mostly during post-production, though he declined to say exactly how. "Animals" is set to be released on Netflix on October 9. "I'm a little bit hesitant to point out what they are or even talk about it because, like, in my business, we're trying to foster the illusion of reality, right?" Affleck said, comparing it to a magician explaining how a trick works. AI remains deeply divisive in Hollywood. Some figures, including James Cameron and Martin Scorsese, have supported its use as a creative tool, while others, such as Guillermo del Toro and Christopher Nolan, have questioned its potential impact on jobs and artistic control. events.title: SGX and partners roll out youth stock programme to lower barriers and equip young investors
events.summary: The Youth Stock Ambassadors Programme will give selected young investors capital market education, practical exposure and opportunities to engage with the ecosystem. SINGAPORE – A new initiative was launched on Oct 5 to get more young investors interested in the Singapore stock market. Called the Youth Stock Ambassadors Programme, the scheme will give selected young investors capital market education, practical exposure and opportunities to engage with the ecosystem. It was launched by the Singapore Exchange, Securities Association of Singapore and Securities Investors Association Singapore (SIAS). It comes as the SGX kicked off its scheme on Oct 5 to make investing in higher-priced stocks more affordable for investors, with the reduction of board lot sizes for an initial 11 selected stocks. The three organisations said in a statement: “Together, these initiatives lower the barriers to entry for investing, arm younger investors with more information on the Singapore stock market, and provide them the opportunity to access higher-value Singapore stocks with smaller amounts of initial capital.” The new programme will be a youth-led platform that is open to students in tertiary institutions. The students should have an interest in capital markets and investing. The Securities Association of Singapore and SIAS will start by engaging the SIAS Youth Chapter to gather feedback and create the programme together. Young investors who are selected as Youth Stock Ambassadors will receive capital market education and training, opportunities to engage with listed companies, as well as internships and mentorship. These youth will also develop analytical, research and content creation skills. “The programme aims to build a community of informed investors who can help inspire and support the next generation on their investment journeys,” the three organisations said. Members of the Securities Association of Singapore will also work closely with SIAS to increase overall engagement with young investors, not just through the new programme. Securities Association of Singapore chairman Wilson He said: “The reduction in board lot sizes is a positive step towards making Singapore equities more accessible, but it is only part of the equation. “It must be complemented by investor education, access to quality research, mentorship, internship opportunities and practical market exposure.” He added that the new scheme aims to empower young investors with the knowledge, confidence and support needed to become informed, long-term participants in Singapore’s capital markets. He noted that the association’s member brokerages are also committed to supporting the reduced board lot roll-out through their own investor education and outreach initiatives. SGX group head of global financial markets Ng Yao Loong said that building the next generation of investors goes beyond making Singapore equities more accessible. “The Youth Stock Ambassadors Programme provides opportunities for young investors to engage with listed companies and market practitioners, helping them build informed investing habits and a longer-term perspective,” he added. Meanwhile, SIAS vice-president Ang Hao Yao noted that an issue among young investors is that they may be overwhelmed by the amount of available information. They also need to build a strong foundation in investment principles and knowledge. “For many, the amount needed to get started on investing in Singapore stocks can be a real barrier. With the launch of reduced board lot sizes, it lowers the entry point by making the Singapore market more approachable and creates an opportunity to build sound investing habits earlier,” he said. Tay Jingxuan, an executive committee member at the Singapore Institute of Technology’s Investment and Commerce Club, said that the lot size reduction is a timely opportunity for students and young adults to begin their investment journey early. “While many young individuals recognise the importance of early investing, capital constraints often pose a significant barrier,” she added. “For many students, setting aside a few thousand dollars to start building positions in blue-chip stocks can be difficult, given our limited savings and inconsistent part-time income.” She added that the board lot size reduction means that young investors may feel less intimidated when they want to invest, as they no longer have to commit a large portion of their personal capital with limited investing experience. Phoon Mei Gi, president of the Nanyang Technological University Investment Interactive Club, also said that it gives young investors like her more flexibility. “For example, I could set aside around $150 every month to slowly build a position in a higher-priced stock that I previously did not consider because the minimum board lot was too expensive. Instead of waiting until I’ve saved up a much larger amount, I can start smaller and invest more consistently,” she said.

events.title: From hotel suites to virtual reality, museums turn to licensing deals as costs rise
events.summary: Natural History Museum and British Museum among cultural institutions leveraging collections and exhibitions They are often free to visit but museums are bolstering their finances by putting their stamp on everything from upmarket hotel suites to trendy jumpsuits and virtual reality experiences. Forget buying a T-shirt. If you can afford the “from £724” price tag, you can spend the night in the Natural History Museum family suite at the Park Plaza London Riverbank hotel, which has an interior inspired by the museum’s founder, Sir Richard Owen, complete with Tyrannosaurus rex bunk beds. Deals such as this are becoming more commonplace as cultural institutions look to leverage their renowned collections and trusted brands in the face of funding cuts and rising costs. Data shows that overall UK sales of licensed merchandise and services grew 7% to $19.2bn (£14.5bn) last year, according to the industry trade body Licensing International. A breakdown of the UK market figures shows that the “art property” category, which includes museums, grew by more than 8%, while “attractions and promotions” (which includes immersive experiences at museums and art galleries) soared by 53%. “Our licensing programme continues to grow consistently at about 15% year on year,” said Louisa Skevington, the licensing manager at the Natural History Museum, who added that “experiences” were becoming an increasingly important part of that. “It’s about finding creative ways to bring the museum and its stories to people wherever they are, while continuing to grow the reach and impact of the programme.” The Natural History Museum’s previous deals include a Farrow & Ball paint range inspired by Werner’s Nomenclature of Colours and a collection with the fashion brand Lucy & Yak featuring dinosaur-print jumpsuits and dungarees, aimed at millennials and gen Z. More recently it worked with the virtual reality experience company Sandbox on the prehistoric adventure Age of Dinosaurs. The importance of licensing means a growing number of museums, galleries and heritage organisations are exhibiting at this week’s Brand Licensing Europe conference in London. New attenders include the National Gallery, the National Trust for Scotland, the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford and Tate Enterprises. They join the British Museum , the Natural History Museum, the Victoria and Albert Museum and the Imperial War Museum. The competition is stiff, however, as the agenda includes talks on the “Bluey effect” and the new Harry Potter TV series. The huge demand for Bayeux tapestry tickets “demonstrates the appetite for major cultural moments, and the opportunity to build on that interest beyond a visit to the museum”, says Craig Bendle, the manager of product licensing at the British Museum. Indeed, the Bayeux tapestry merchandise created by its separate retail team, which includes a collaboration with the London department store Liberty, made it into Vogue . Bendle reports growing interest from brands that want to create something “genuinely distinctive”, with the museum’s collection of more than 8m objects an “extraordinary source of inspiration”, he says. The V&A is also looking for novel ways to draw on its 2.8m objects. It launched 63 product ranges in 2025, which demonstrates the “growing role licensing plays in taking the V&A beyond our museum walls”, said Jen Maude-Roxby, its head of licensing and business development. That programme includes William Morris-inspired phone cases with the tech accessories brand CASETiFY, and pictures for the art store of Samsung’s “the Frame” TV, which displays artworks when the TV is off, transforming the blank monitor into a picture.

events.title: ‘I didn’t know what to do’: collapse of providers of high-end digs leaves students in shock
events.summary: Cost of living crisis and drop in international students hits market for purpose-built accommodation “I t was dead in the middle of summer, it was a shock,” says Nathalie Sriwiboonrattan. The fourth-year game design student at Abertay University was at home with her family thousands of miles away in Thailand when she discovered the owner of her Scottish studio flat had abruptly gone bust. “I was like, my hands are tied. I’m not in the country. I don’t know what to do,” she says. Sriwiboonrattan was forced to act quickly to secure new housing for the academic year, which has just begun, paying £850 to have her possessions moved. Her sudden upheaval was emblematic of the wider crisis in student housing. While UK universities face a financial crisis , providers of accommodation are grappling with falling international student numbers , a cost of living squeeze and higher borrowing and build costs, exacerbated by the Iran war, affecting upgrades at older properties. A string of tower blocks known as purpose-built student accommodation (PBSA), targeted at more affluent students, have run into financial difficulty. It had been touted as the ultimate student living: smart city centre blocks with gyms, cinemas and rooftop terraces have sprung up across the UK. A world away from the traditional image of dirty and dingy shared digs , the flats have offered a spacious alternative for their relatively affluent residents – often international students. Now, some sit half empty, and several schemes have gone bust . Sriwiboonrattan was among nearly 70 students in Dundee who were left scrambling to find accommodation in late July after the collapse of the owner of Marketgait Apartments, a 116-room city centre block that had a concierge and a shared games lounge with a pool table. Despite the boom in housing developed by financial institutions in recent years, many students heading off to university this term faced a different dilemma. Rents at the tower blocks have grown much faster than maintenance loans for British students, leaving PSBAs financially out of reach. Meanwhile, the cost of living crisis has put financial pressure on students seeking university-owned or managed accommodation, while rising rents have hit those wanting to live in shared private rentals. Underlining the scale of the shortage of affordable housing, the students’ union in Bristol included an emergency support number for the housing charity Shelter in an email to new students. At PSBAs, the national average rent, excluding London, is £191 a week including bills, according to the website StuRents. At the top end, en suite rooms in Manchester command a weekly rent of £170 to £320 , whereas in London, en suite rooms are £250 to £650 a week , and studio apartments in Bloomsbury cost between £550 and £800 plus. “I wasn’t able to get into PBSA because it is very expensive in Birmingham,” says Soham Chougale, 23, a student at University College Birmingham. “I am an international student, so my working hours are capped at 20 hours [a week in term time], which means I can’t afford to live in PBSA,” says Chougale, the education officer at UCB Guild of Students . He lived in university-owned dorms for the first two years of his aviation management degree and now shares a two-bedroom privately rented flat with a friend. On campus, he paid £660 rent including bills a month during the first year, which rose by 10% in his second year; now he pays £700 rent a month, excluding bills. While living on campus “gave me the best feeling of community” and “I still have those friends that I met on the first day”, the wifi was patchy, some facilities were broken and there was a mouse infestation, he recounts. “PBSA can be quite pricey,” says Matthew Pointon, a real estate analyst at Capital Economics, but adds: “Normally professionally managed buildings are better in terms of quality.” In London, which attracts the richest students, there is still demand for upmarket accommodation, but outside the capital, there is an oversupply in some cities, such as Coventry, Leeds and Nottingham. This week, university staff began strikes in Dundee, Edinburgh and Nottingham over budget cuts, with the industrial action threatening to wipe out a term of teaching for many students. In Nottingham, demand has fallen from a pandemic peak of 46,295 beds in 2022-23 to 42,290 beds in 2025-26, while 7,700 more PSBA beds came on to the market, the student housing charity Unipol calculated. The number of students arriving from China has stagnated, and those from the new growth countries India, Pakistan and Nigeria are much more cost-conscious than the pre-Covid students from China , says Martin Blakey, an adviser on student living and the former chief executive of Unipol.

events.title: The 2029 tipping point: Western populations are about to start shrinking, piling pressure on public finances
events.summary: Europe's population will peak in 2029 according to forecasts, while the U.S.'s lies further ahead but is heavily dependent on immigration. Moody's says the fiscal pressures from aging emerge long before populations actually start shrinking. AI and increased productivity can only partially offset the long-term challenge of an aging workforce, Chemla said. As Western populations age, fewer workers and higher costs will strain public finances, credit rating agency Moody's has warned. Europe is at the sharp end of the demographic shift. The European Union's population is projected to peak as soon as 2029, "after which a sustained long-term decline will begin," according to the European Commission. The U.S. Census Bureau does not expect the American population to peak until 2080 under its main projection , or until 2043 under its low-immigration scenario. Excluding immigration impact, the population decline has already started. But Moody's says the fiscal pressures from aging emerge long before populations actually start shrinking. Today, G7 economies have about three working-age people for every person over 65. That ratio is expected to fall to around two by 2050, putting further pressure on growth and public finances, including healthcare systems, according to Moody's. Aging populations affect economies through slower economic growth, greater pressure on public finances from pension and care costs, changing consumer demand, and shifts in real interest rates and sovereign yields, Olivier Chemla, vice president of credit strategy and standards at Moody's, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Friday. In a report published last week, Moody's forecasts that the world's aging populations will have fundamental impacts on the global economy and lead to difficult policy decisions. While population growth has long been a tailwind for growth and creditworthiness, falling fertility rates and unprecedented speed of changing age structures are now changing that picture, Moody's writes. "Fewer workers will limit productive capacity, while fewer households and consumers will weaken demand. As a result, countries will have to rely more on productivity to sustain growth," the report states. "This is a partial mitigant because you can certainly replace and enhance the supply side of the economy in factories and in services, but at the same time, robots do not consume – at least not yet – and so on the demand side, you will still be having that gap, which will slow growth," he added. And it's not only Europe and the U.S., but emerging economies are aging rapidly, too. China's share of people aged 65 and over has doubled from 7% to 14% over the past two decades, with Brazil, Thailand and Turkiye on similar trajectories. These countries will face the costs of aging at much lower income levels than the advanced economies that aged before them, the report says, noting that in Europe, the same shift took several decades.

events.title: Mid-East oil exports exceeded pre-Iran war levels: Kpler data
events.summary: Crude oil exports reached pre-war levels in September. Middle East oil exports, excluding Iran, surpassed pre-Iran war levels last week despite attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, with shipments rising above the 18 million barrels per day average. Around 40% of oil now bypasses the Strait of Hormuz, mainly flowing through Saudi and UAE pipelines, including routes via the Red Sea to avoid Iran’s blockade attempts. Saudi Arabia and the UAE benefit from pipeline routes that bypass Hormuz; Saudi’s East–West pipeline resumed on Sept 22 after attacks, supporting export recovery despite ongoing regional tensions. SINGAPORE – Middle East oil exports, excluding Iran, surpassed their pre-war levels last week, despite attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, according to data from the maritime tracking firm Kpler. For the first time since the US and Israel launched their offensive against Iran at the end of February , the weekly average of shipments rose for several days above the pre-conflict average of 18 million barrels per day. Crude oil exports reached pre-war levels in September, with at least 16.5 million barrels leaving the region, excluding Iran, Kpler said on Sept 30 . “Forty per cent now bypass Hormuz, and most crude crossing the strait changes tankers offshore,” Kpler said, adding that most of the oil flowed through Saudi and United Arab Emirates pipelines. These figures include flows via the Red Sea, a route increasingly used to bypass the blockade Iran is attempting to impose on Hormuz – where around a fifth of the world’s petroleum supplies crossed before the conflict. Iran still claims control over the strait, and ships without its authorisation risk coming under attack, but more and more are making it out, and alternative routes meant to bypass the waterway are operating at full capacity. Despite the rebound, experts stressed that the situation was far from normal, and Iran remains deprived of a large share of its own exports by a US counterblockade of its ports. Saudi Arabia is benefiting from the reactivation of its East-West pipeline, which links the kingdom’s main oil fields in the east to its Yanbu terminal on the Red Sea, allowing it to bypass Hormuz. Shut down on Sept 11 after being hit by strikes launched from Iraq, the pipeline resumed operations on Sept 22 , Amena Bakr, an analyst at Kpler, said last week. The United Arab Emirates is also able to bypass Hormuz thanks to its pipeline linking Abu Dhabi’s fields to Fujairah, a terminal just outside the strait on the Gulf of Oman. Around 3.10am GMT (11.10am Singapore time) on Oct 5 , Brent North Sea crude for December delivery fell 0.79% to US$101.44 a barrel. Its US counterpart, West Texas Intermediate for November delivery, dropped 1.2% to US$90.02. AFP

events.title: SGX board lot reduction kicks in for 11 stocks, including the three S’pore banks
events.summary: The initial 11 stocks included in the board lot size reduction exercise accounted for 35% of trading activity on SGX in the first six months of 2026. SINGAPORE – Investors will now find it more affordable to buy the pricier stocks on the Singapore Exchange, as the board lot size reduction for an initial 11 stocks kicked in on Oct 5. These stocks are: DBS, Great Eastern Holdings, Haw Par Corporation, Jardine Cycle & Carriage, Jardine Matheson Holdings, Keppel, OCBC, Prudential, SGX, UOB and Venture Corporation. They accounted for 35% of trading activity on SGX in the first six months of 2026. For stocks that are priced between $10 and $100 a share, the minimum trading quantity has been cut from 100 units to 10 units. And if a stock trades on the bourse with a price above $100, the minimum trading size will be just one unit. Besides stocks, the changes will also cover stapled securities, real estate investment trusts, business trusts, company warrants – excluding special purpose acquisition company warrants – as well as depository receipts and depository shares. SGX said the board lot size reductions will remain even if the stocks fall below the $10 or $100 thresholds. The Straits Times Index was trading slightly higher by 0.15% during the morning trading session of Oct 5. It hit 5,643.21 at around 11.40am, just before the noon break. DBS, one of the stocks on SGX’s initial list for board lot reduction, saw prices rise by 0.43% to trade at $77.53 just before noon. However, OCBC and UOB both saw prices fall slightly. OCBC was trading down 0.32% at $31.54, while UOB was trading 1.16% lower at $42.61. SGX had said the board lot revision is expected to lower barriers to market participation and improve affordability for retail investors. The bourse will also conduct a review every quarter to see if additional instruments can qualify for the reduced board lot size. The next review will take place in January 2027. It will take into consideration daily closing prices from July 2026 to December 2026. SGX noted that any changes to the board lot size will be announced within the first five trading days after the end of each calendar quarter. Sue-Ann Tan is a business correspondent at The Straits Times, covering capital markets and sustainable finance.

events.title: Russian lab worker dies of suspected plague in Siberia; US monitoring case
events.summary: A Russian agency links the lab worker’s death to ‘pneumonia of unknown’ origin. An employee of a Russian plague research institute in the remote Siberian region of Irkutsk has died of a suspected pneumonic plague infection, regional officials have said, even as dozens of others have been placed under quarantine. Alexei Tsydenov, the governor of the Buryatia region, said in a post on his Telegram channel on Saturday that a woman in the neighbouring Irkutsk region had “died, maybe of the plague”. list 1 of 3 Russia’s nuclear plants are ageing. Who will pay to dismantle them? list 2 of 3 Russia hits Kyiv bridge as Germany’s Merz visits Ukraine’s capital list 3 of 3 Ukraine ready for US-backed talks with Russia: Zelenskyy Tsydenov, however, tried to reassure the local population by insisting that Russian authorities had confirmed the woman had not travelled to Buryatia. Russia’s official TASS news agency separately reported on Sunday that the country’s consumer watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, said in a statement that an employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East had been diagnosed with “pneumonia of unknown aetiology”. The watchdog also said it had expanded testing of samples from the patient and found no microorganisms associated with her professional activities. Media reports say authorities in Siberia’s Irkutsk have placed nearly 200 people under medical observation. The US Department of State, in a statement to Al Jazeera, said Washington was “monitoring the situation closely with the CDC [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention] and our other interagency partners”. “We encourage Russian authorities to share accurate information quickly and openly,” the State Department official said in the statement. Pneumonic plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, usually found in small mammals and their fleas. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), the plague is highly infectious and can be fatal if not treated early. Local media named the woman who died as 28-year-old laboratory technician Darya Shipilova.

events.title: British government ‘complacent about food as a national security matter’
events.summary: Experts say country does not have plan to feed people in a crisis and is unprepared for future shortages Britain does not have a plan for how to feed people in a crisis and is unprepared for potential future food shortages, according to a warning from more than 150 experts delivered to Andy Burnham. The climate crisis, geopolitical shocks, cyber-attacks and energy outages are among the threats to food chain security, according to the open letter, which claims the government is “complacent about food as a national security matter”. Academics, business leaders, community groups and food partnerships are urging the new government to treat food as a national security issue and work to make the UK’s food system more resilient, in a era when food supplies “can be weaponised”, they caution. The signatories warn that the “just-in-time” delivery system built up over recent decades “is not fit for today’s or tomorrow’s challenges”, as little stock is held along the food supply chain and the UK does not have any national food storage. Ministers wound up the strategic food stockpile that had been in place since the second world war in the 1990s. “The food system is exposed to shocks and threats from geopolitics, climate heating, ransomware, energy outages, software malfunction and disinformation,” according to the letter. The experts go on to warn: “These shocks will fall upon a system that is highly wasteful, import-dependent, environmentally unsustainable, and driven by the pursuit of private profit rather than resilience, with millions of people unable to afford a decent, healthy diet.” The letter calls on ministers to do the following. Establish a new system of local food resilience committees under the Civil Contingencies Act 2004. Audit the UK’s reliance on a few very large food companies and food imports. Realign national food production around nutritional needs. Create national, regional, local and community food storage schemes. Support the decentralisation of the UK’s food supply. The warning comes weeks after the National Audit Office, the public spending watchdog, issued a rebuke to ministers , accusing them of failing to do enough to help households and businesses plan for possible emergencies. The government’s own research has shown Britons are less prepared for potential future catastrophic events than citizens of several other European countries, while the UK is more reliant on food imports than some of its neighbours. The environment secretary, Angela Eagle, recently recommended that UK households build up stores of enough food and water to survive a few days without power or water, amid warnings that the El Niño weather phenomenon could bring a wet, stormy winter to the UK. The letter claims the government is not paying enough attention to what such a store should look like, and is failing to consider that many lower-income households may not be able to afford to build up a stockpile. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning One of the signatories, Prof Tim Lang of the Centre for Food Policy, City St George’s, University of London, said: “We need a system shift: grow more food; more regionalism, diversity and storage at multiple levels, not just households; and public engagement in civil food defence. Central government must provide more strategic leadership while encouraging actions at different levels. Communities and households cannot resolve faultlines in the UK’s food system.” Prof Paul Behrens of the Oxford Martin School, University of Oxford, who also signed the letter, said: “Food resilience, healthy diet and environmental benefits all point in the same direction: grow more of the vegetables, fruit and pulses people actually need, closer to home.” The Cabinet Office is to launch a campaign telling households to stock up on tinned foods alongside preparations for future emergencies. The government’s Prepare website outlines steps it says people should take, which include assembling items at home that could include tinned meat, fruit or vegetables that do not need cooking. Eagle has said she would oversee farming improvements and a reservoir-building programme that should help Britain face extreme weather.

events.title: Thai bourse plans dual-class share structure to boost listings
events.summary: The move is designed to ease the concern of founders about diluting their control and end a lean patch in new listings. Thailand plans to introduce a dual-class share structure by 2027 to encourage more companies, especially family-owned, to list without losing control. The new structure aims to increase market liquidity and align Bangkok with other regional financial centres like Hong Kong. The Stock Exchange of Thailand expects a boost in IPOs in 2027, pending resolution of global economic concerns like the Middle East conflict and fuel costs. BANGKOK – Thailand plans to establish a dual-class share structure to entice more companies to list on the local exchange, a move designed to ease the concern of founders about diluting their control and end a lean patch in new listings. The proposed move, expected to be implemented in 2027, also aims to satisfy institutional investors who want greater access to the nation’s top companies, according to Kitipong Urapeepatanapong, chairman of Stock Exchange of Thailand (SET). The changes to Thailand’s public company law will enable listed firms to issue different classes of shares with unequal voting rights, he said. A dual-class share structure would also put Bangkok in the same league as markets like Hong Kong, broaden its pool of listed companies while deepening market liquidity amid competition from regional financial centres. “From my discussions with a number of family-owned businesses, many don’t want to list, or when they do, they sell only a small amount of shares because they want to protect themselves from a takeover,” he said in an interview. Thai companies have raised about 700 million baht (S$26.7 million) through initial public offerings so far in 2026 , down 95% from 2025 and on track for the lowest annual total since the exchange began providing data in 2003. “Thai companies have delayed their IPOs as the conflict in the Middle East and high fuel costs weigh on the economic outlook,” SET president Asadej Kongsiri said recently. “We have a strong IPO pipeline. If the war ends later this year, we expect 2027 to be a very busy year for IPOs.” Companies classified as family-owned business represented 705 of the 843 companies listed on the Thai stock exchange as at July. The family companies had a combined market capitalisation of 10.93 trillion baht, accounting for 54% of the total market value of Thai-listed companies. Some Thai companies offer only a small portion of their shares to the public, list on foreign exchanges that offer dual-share structures or avoid going public altogether, Kitipong said. “We need to provide this option similar to other regional rivals if we want to attract family-owned businesses in Thailand to list,” he said. “It would also help increase liquidity, which has been a major complaint among international funds.” Foreign investors say that some of the nation’s prime listed companies do not have enough free float for them to buy and trade shares, Kitipong said. The stock exchange has been working with the Finance Ministry, Securities and Exchange Commission and other agencies on the dual-class share amendment, which is expected to be passed by the Parliament in 2026 , Kitipong said. events.title: US coastguard suspends search for six on board crashed medical jet
events.summary: Debris found off Nantucket island after the air ambulance disappeared while flying from Bermuda to Boston. The United States coastguard has suspended its search for six people on board a medical transport jet that crashed while flying from Bermuda to Boston. “Suspending a search is not an easy decision,” Rear Admiral Matthew Lake, commander of the ⁠coastguard’s Northeast District, said in a statement on Sunday. list 1 of 2 Brazil’s presidential race: Three key takeaways from the first round list 2 of 2 Nicaragua says it will withdraw from Central American Parliament The search was called off after teams spent about 66 hours covering 4,445 miles (7,150km) by air and sea and confirmed that debris found off the shore of Massachusetts’s Nantucket Island came from the aircraft. The Gulfstream G100 carried two pilots, two medical staff, a patient and a relative, Clarence Togeretz, director of flight operations at Canada-based Latitude Air Ambulance, told Canada’s public broadcaster CBC. The four crew members were Canadian, and the two passengers were Bermudian, according to authorities. In a statement on Sunday, Latitude Air Ambulance said, “Given the information shared by authorities and the conclusion of ⁠the search-and-rescue phase, we must now face the heartbreaking reality that the four members of our Latitude team, our patient and the patient’s family escort, who were ⁠aboard Heartbeat 104, are presumed to have died.” Attention has turned to what happened in the jet’s final minutes, when flight-tracking data showed a steep descent and air traffic controllers struggled to re-establish contact. Authorities have not determined what caused the aircraft to come down. The aircraft had flown to Bermuda to collect the patient and was heading to Boston Logan International airport. The US Federal Aviation Administration alerted the coastguard at about 2am on Saturday (06:00 GMT) after contact with the jet was lost. Lake said at a Sunday news conference that the water around the debris was about 80 to 90 feet (24-27 metres) deep. He offered condolences to the families of those on board and thanked the agencies involved in the operation. Latitude Air Ambulance specialises in medical evacuation and repatriation flights, carrying patients home from other countries. The company says its missions are normally staffed by two pilots and medical personnel.

events.title: Opening the taps on diesel reserves is a risky gamble for Europe
events.summary: US President Donald Trump has bounced Europe into a risky gamble. On Friday, under threat of a US ban on diesel exports, the Group of Seven major economies agreed to release emergency petroleum stocks. Mr Trump may be looking just to elections in a month, but London, Paris and Berlin risk burning their remaining reserves. Opening the taps is meant to alleviate the crisis in diesel caused by the US-Iran war. The G7 countries collectively will provide 100 million barrels over four months, split between crude and refined products, and front-loaded with diesel. In return, they have all agreed not to impose restrictions on oil exports – for now. The Gulf shuttle scheme, guarded by US ships and aviation, appears to have succeeded in restoring crude oil flows to near prewar levels. This comes at a heavy cost in death and injury of mariners, damage to vessels, and hiring and guarding the vessels. Escorting refined product shipments is harder: they are more varied, travel in smaller ships and are usually more flammable than crude. Before the war, the Arab countries within the Gulf exported about 5.5 million barrels daily of refined products, particularly diesel, jet fuel and heavy fuel oil. That plunged to below 2 million barrels per day when the US began its attack, and has recovered to 3 million bpd or so. Iran added another 900,000 bpd of net exports of refined products and natural gas liquids. This has now fallen to near-zero by sea, and perhaps minor amounts going overland by lorry or rail. Europe and Japan hold large stocks of petroleum products, especially diesel and petrol, while the US’s strategic petroleum reserve is almost entirely crude oil. The US has marketed about 130 million barrels, taking its crude stocks down to the lowest levels since the early 1980s. It looks doubtful that it can provide much more without causing permanent damage to the artificial salt caverns that hold the oil. Though this drawdown has helped keep crude prices hovering at relatively moderate levels, that is not the locus of the current crisis – Brent crude closed the week at $102 per barrel, while wholesale diesel in New York is going for $200. If half the proposed release consists of diesel, it amounts to about 400,000 bpd over four months, replacing about a third of the exports lost this year. That would be helpful, but far from a full or permanent solution. There is also the oddity that European stocks are not owned by their governments, unlike in the US. Instead, oil companies are mandated to hold more than normal commercial levels. Approval for a release does not necessarily mean that all that diesel comes on the market. Despite the tight conditions, commercial product stocks at the crucial Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp hub actually rose last month, and are not down much since May, unlike in the US where they have plummeted. Hard hit from a diesel ban The proposed prohibition of American diesel exports would have hit Europe hard. The UK and EU import about 270,000 bpd of diesel from the US, a third of their total imports, though this jumped to 420,000 bpd during the worst of the crunch this summer. It would have hurt other nations too, and would quickly have rebounded on the US as refiners would have cut back runs. The US still imports significant amounts of petrol – a politically more visible and sensitive fuel – and might well have faced retaliatory bans. Should the Europeans have resisted the demand, or called Mr Trump’s bluff? On the one hand, they worried about a difficult winter. If he had just forbidden sales specifically to Europe, the fuel would have been shuffled around through other countries to end up there anyway. So, to have a real impact, he would have had to impose a blanket ban. Strategic stocks are made to be used in emergencies. While the US had already emptied much of the SPR in 2022 and hardly refilled it since, European stocks are well above legal minimum levels, and have been rebuilt since 2022. Solidarity between the G7 and the members of the International Energy Agency is fundamental for collective management of energy shocks. On the other hand, the European countries did not start this war, they are not combatants, and they do not control it. If they burn through their reserves over the next four months, they had better be sure a resolution to the crisis is coming soon. The hazy thinking coming out of the White House and the Pentagon about war aims and strategy does not inspire such confidence. Polls suggest the Republicans will suffer a drubbing in November’s midterm elections. After that, Mr Trump will find it hard to advance any of his domestic agenda. Many expect he will back down in Iran, perhaps after launching one final thunderclap so he can go home claiming a victory. That itself runs the risk that Tehran miscalculates, and decides to respond in kind rather than absorbing the blow. But it is at least as likely that, unable to achieve much at home, he will escalate. In turn, if the Iranians had not realised it already, all the headlines inform them that refineries are an Achilles heel. The Ukrainian campaign against Russia tells the same tale. Refineries in Israel and in all the Gulf states except Oman were damaged earlier this year. Saudi refineries in Jazan and Yanbu have been attacked from Yemen over the past month, and on Saturday, there were reports of a fire and smoke at a refinery in Riyadh. Europe wants to avoid the worst cases of a US diesel export ban on the one hand, and running short in the middle of a flare-up of the conflict in midwinter. The way it structures its strategic stocks gives it a way out. It can appear to have conceded to Mr Trump’s demands for a big release. But if its companies do not actually want to sell much of their stocks, that is not the governments’ fault, and will not become apparent for some weeks anyway. By then, the US elections will be over and the next moves by Washington and Tehran may be clearer.

events.title: The Live Conversation: Education Beyond the Checklist
events.summary: The International Schools Festival puts the spotlight on new approaches to education and how best to go about the application process Over 1,700 parents, students and educators attended the International Schools Festival – Hong Kong Island 2026. Held at Hong Kong Ocean Park Marriott Hotel on September 19, it featured 46 schools and education advisers, and offered families guidance on admissions, curricula, university applications and future education planning. Across five parent talks and 10 school-led information sessions, speakers returned to one central message: education should not be driven by fear or the pursuit of a perfect résumé. Whether choosing a primary school or planning for university, families should focus on well-being, curiosity and adaptability. A new approach to admissions At the morning panel session entitled, “Rethinking the Admissions Journey,” school leaders challenged the idea that primary admissions should be treated as a test children must be trained to pass. Instead of rehearsed answers, they said schools want to see curiosity, confidence, emotional readiness and a child’s natural ability to communicate and engage with others. At English Schools Foundation’s (ESF) Kennedy School, principal Brenda Cook said they do not look for one fixed type of applicant profile.

events.title: ‘Unwelcome and unsafe’: Why Japanese companies are retreating from China at a historic rate
events.summary: The number of Japanese companies operating in China fell to the lowest level on record: report. The exodus is likely to intensify amid the diplomatic feud between Asia's top two economies. Tariff risks, growing labour and manufacturing costs, and cutthroat local competition also weighed on profit margins. Japanese companies are leaving China in record numbers, as a slowing Chinese economy and a diplomatic freeze force businesses to reassess their presence in the world's second-largest economy. The number of Japanese companies operating in China fell to a historic low, standing at 10,118 as of June, according to Teikoku Databank , a corporate credit research firm in Japan. That's down 22% from the previous survey held in June 2024 and about 30% below the 2012 peak, and the lowest since Teikoku began tracking the data in 2010. Japanese firms, which were already planning to reduce their footprint in China, are considering withdrawing from the market with greater urgency since China-Japan ties went into a tailspin, said Jeremy Chan, an analyst at political consultancy firm Eurasia Group. The exodus is likely to intensify as the diplomatic feud between Asia's top two economies forces Japanese companies — already grappling with shrinking profitability strained by tariff risks, growing labor and manufacturing costs, cutthroat local competition — to shrink or shut their operation in China, Teikoku said in its report last week. Some firms have reduced dependence on China without fully decoupling from it, it added. China-Japan relations have come under heavy strain since Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi told parliament in November last year that Japan could get militarily involved in the event of a Chinese invasion of Taiwan. Beijing has responded by curbing exports of critical minerals to Japanese companies and urged citizens to refrain from traveling to Japan. Factors such as U.S. tariffs and a growing public resistance to Chinese goods and a growing Indian market have also further incentivised Japanese businesses' push to diversify away from Beijing, said Martin Schulz, chief policy economist at Fujitsu Research Institute. "Investment in China is weathering the perfect storm," he said. In the past two years, a record number of 4,137 Japanese companies fully withdrew from China, according to Teikoku's data. Only 1,221 entered over the same period, through subsidiaries, factories or representative offices, the fewest on record outside the Covid-19 pandemic. Japanese firms have grown increasingly reliant on the U.S. market while shifting away from China, what was once a key market, said Jesper Koll, expert director at Monex Group. Topix-listed companies saw the share of profits derived in China dwindle to less than 15% so far this year, down from 23% in 2020, while those from the U.S. rose to 35% compared with 25% over the same period, according to Koll's estimates. Washington is "openly courting" Japanese players to aid its re-industrialization efforts while Beijing has shifted towards a "made in and made by China" model, Koll said. Cases of Japanese nationals being detained by Beijing this year have further added to businesses' concerns about sending personnel to China, analysts say. Several Japanese nationals, including executives at top Japanese firms, were reportedly detained in August over alleged violations of dual-use goods export restrictions. "Japanese firms and their employees increasingly feel unwelcome and unsafe in China," Chan said. An April report from Japan External Trade Organization showed that companies are increasingly reluctant to expand their business in China. On Tuesday, a day after the Teikoku report, Chinese vice premier He Lifeng said China "always welcomes" Japanese enterprises to develop business and share market opportunities in the country. He told a delegation from the Japanese Association for the Promotion of International Trade to "keep to the right course on historical issues … and play a greater role in advancing China-Japan economic and trade cooperation." Automakers, parts suppliers and export-oriented manufacturers are the most likely to scale back in China, said Kei Koga, a professor at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore. Companies that have localized and can compete with Chinese rivals, particularly medical and precision equipment makers, are more likely to stay, he added.
