events.title: Far East Orchard crosses $3 billion AUM target with higher stakes in business trust managers
events.summary: Alan Tang, group chief executive of Far East Orchard, noted that the accretive acquisition is a significant step towards scaling a fully integrated lodging platform. Far East Orchard is acquiring an additional 42% stake in Far East Hospitality Trust managers, raising its ownership to 75% and increasing its core assets under management to S$3.9 billion. This acquisition accelerates Far East Orchard’s "FEOR30" roadmap and supports a new core AUM target of at least S$5 billion by FY2030. The S$28.3 million cash deal strengthens recurring income, enhances growth flexibility, and expands capital-efficient channels alongside its private fund platform. SINGAPORE – Far East Orchard is acquiring an additional 42% stake in the managers of Far East Hospitality Trust (FEHT) , a transaction that will propel its core assets under management (AUM) past its $3 billion goal to $3.9 billion, four years earlier than targeted. Far East Orchard said on the morning of Oct 5 that the $28.3 million deal will raise its ownership in the managers from its current 33% to 75%. The remaining 25% will continue to be held by the seller, FEO Asset Management, a wholly owned subsidiary of Far East Organization Centre. The acquisition involves shares in both FEO Hospitality Asset Management, the manager of Far East Hospitality Real Estate Investment Trust ( FEH- Reit ), and FEO Hospitality Trust Management, the trustee-manager of Far East Hospitality Business Trust (FEH-BT). FEHT is a hospitality stapled group with a market capitalisation of $1.25 billion. It comprises FEH- Reit and FEH-BT and holds a portfolio of 13 properties, comprising 12 properties in Singapore and a hotel in Japan. Far East Orchard said in its statement that the deal with its associates is a strategic move to accelerate Far East Orchard’s “FEOR30” business road map . By gaining effective control of the FEHT managers, Far East Orchard’s core AUM will scale by about 86%, jumping from $2.1 billion to $3.9 billion. This exceeds the company’s previously announced core AUM target of $3 billion, and supports a new core AUM target of “at least $5 billion” by financial year 2030, Far East Orchard said. “By strengthening our alignment with FEHT, we are expanding our recurring income base and broadening the channels through which we can grow in a capital-efficient manner, including capital recycling and capital-light AUM growth alongside our existing private fund platform,” he said. “This gives us greater flexibility to grow faster, build more resilient earnings, and capture value and maximise returns across the full asset lifecycle.” The $28.3 million consideration will be paid entirely in cash, funded by Far East Orchard’s internal resources. As part of the transaction’s conditions, FEO Hospitality Asset Management will distribute a dividend in specie of roughly 165.2 million FEHT stapled securities to its shareholders.

events.title: Brazil’s presidential race: Three key takeaways from the first round
events.summary: Flavio Bolsonaro beat polling expectations as Brazil’s right gained ground, setting up October 25 run-off with Lula. Brazil’s closely watched presidential election is heading to a second round between leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, prolonging a deeply polarised race with major implications for the country and the wider region. Brazil’s electoral court confirmed on Sunday that the two candidates will advance to a run-off on October 25 after neither won the majority needed to secure the presidency outright, with Bolsonaro leading at 56 million votes to Lula’s almost 53 million. list 1 of 4 Brazil’s Lula and Bolsonaro close campaigns ahead of critical election list 2 of 4 Will Brazil’s Lula halt the right-wing wave sweeping Latin America? list 3 of 4 Polls close in Brazil’s polarised election pitting Lula against Bolsonaro list 4 of 4 Lula and Bolsonaro vote in Brazil’s polarised presidential election Lula, 80, is seeking a fourth, non-consecutive term after a political career spanning nearly five decades. Bolsonaro, 45, is the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro and is trying to return his father’s right-wing movement to power, even as the former president serves a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election. The election comes at a pivotal time for Latin America’s largest economy. Brazilians are grappling with concerns over crime and the cost of living, while the country faces an increasingly tense relationship with the United States. The vote is also being closely watched across a region that has shifted sharply to the right in a series of recent elections. While a second round was widely expected, the first-round result did not play out quite as pollsters had predicted. Here are some of the key takeaways from the election so far. Brazil is heading for another Lula-Bolsonaro run-off With nearly 99 percent of votes reported, Bolsonaro had about 47 percent of valid votes, compared with 44.9 percent for Lula. Neither reached the 50 percent threshold needed to win in the first round. That sets up another Lula-Bolsonaro showdown, four years after Lula narrowly defeated former President Jair Bolsonaro. This time, he will face the former president’s eldest son. The race could be extremely close, as polling ahead of Sunday’s vote suggested Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro were roughly tied in a potential run-off. That puts voters who backed one of the other 10 candidates in the first round at the centre of the fight for the presidency over the next three weeks. Ronaldo Caiado and Renan Santos, who together received about 5.3 million votes, have previously said they will not endorse either candidate in the run-off. Flavio Bolsonaro did better than polls suggested Most polls leading up to election day predicted the race would be pushed into the second round, but had Lula finishing the first round ahead of Bolsonaro. Instead, Bolsonaro emerged with a lead of two percentage points, raising questions about why the final polls underestimated his support. On Sunday, Bolsonaro said the results showed that Brazilians want change. Analysts told the Reuters news agency that Bolsonaro may have benefitted from “protest votes” from people who may have preferred another candidate but saw defeating Lula as the priority. Many had been expected to shift their support to Bolsonaro only in a second round, meaning this could have consequences for his support in three weeks. “The protest vote foreshadows what is to come in the run-off,” political analyst Rafael Favetti told Reuters. “While this should benefit Flavio Bolsonaro now, his growth potential in the second round drops precisely because that support has already been front-loaded.” After the results came in, Lula said the votes were “unexpected” but that he would come back stronger in the run-off. “I admit, I was convinced I would win in the first round. The game is about to start. We are in extra time. In extra time, we will win over the Brazilian people,” the 80-year-old said. The right had a strong night in Congress, too Bolsonaro’s surprising performance in the first round was part of a broader show of strength for Brazil’s right. Right-wing parties, led by Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party (PL), were performing strongly in both houses of Congress, with the PL on track to emerge as the largest force in the Chamber of Deputies and making gains in the Senate. This included victories for other members of the Bolsonaro family , including former First Lady Michelle Bolsonaro, Flavio’s stepmother, who won a Senate seat in the Federal District, her first elected office. His brother, Carlos Bolsonaro, was elected to the Senate in Santa Catarina. The results show that the political movement built around former President Jair Bolsonaro – known as “bolsonarista” – remains a powerful electoral force, even with the former president barred from running himself.

events.title: AkzoNobel to sell South-east Asia paints business to Nippon Paint for US$1.35 billion
events.summary: Dulux paint maker AkzoNobel earlier divested its decorative paints operations in India and Pakistan for US$1.6 billion and €50 million respectively. AkzoNobel agreed to sell its Southeast Asian decorative paints business to Nippon Paint for US$1.35 billion, covering operations in eight countries. The deal is expected to close by mid-2027, except Indonesia's sale, which will close in late 2026, with net cash proceeds around US$1 billion. AkzoNobel aims to focus on its merger with US coatings maker Axalta and has no current plans to sell more assets, while Nippon Paint remains interested in larger acquisitions. AkzoNobel said on Oct 5 it has agreed to sell its South-east Asian decorative paints business to Nippon Paint for US$1.35 billion (S$1.72 billion), completing a review of its Asian decorative paints portfolio. The sale covers decorative paints operations in Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Singapore, Papua New Guinea and Australia, the Dutch paints maker said, adding that it expects net cash proceeds of about US$1 billion after tax and payments to minority partners. The Dulux paint maker earlier divested its decorative paints operations in India and Pakistan for US$1.6 billion and €50 million (S$71.8 million), respectively. “The successful completion of our Asia portfolio review is part of an ongoing strategy to focus our portfolio on areas where we can achieve differentiating scale and strengthen our position,” AkzoNobel chief executive Greg Poux-Guillaume said in a statement. The Indonesia deal is expected to close separately in late 2026, while the remaining transactions are expected to close around mid-2027. AkzoNobel said it will now focus on the successful closing of its merger with US coatings maker Axalta, which was announced in November 2025 . Nippon Paint submitted multiple proposals to acquire AkzoNobel’s decorative paints business, the Dutch company said in July, valuing it at about €7.5 billion. That approach followed the withdrawal of a €12.5 billion bid for the entire company that Nippon Paint had pursued jointly with US-based paint maker Sherwin-Williams in June. The Financial Times, which earlier reported the South-east Asia deal, said Nippon remains interested in a larger deal for the decorative paint business, but that integration of the South-east Asia business could occupy the company for some time and AkzoNobel does not have plans to sell further assets from the business. events.title: How India became dangerously addicted to Chinese imports
events.summary: Xi and Modi have vowed to address growing trade imbalances Take a walk into an Indian toy shop and as well as picking up a new favourite plaything for a child, you might just get an insight into how the nation is battling for a better economic relationship with its all-powerful neighbour China. Six years ago, in an attempt to push local manufacturing and keep substandard toys out of its market, India raised tariffs on imported toys from 20% to 60% and eventually to 70%. Retailers were up in arms and said that domestic firms could never match the foreign-made stuff. But the combination of higher customs duties and quality control standards worked. Indian imports of toys fell by a third from nearly $300m (£227m) in 2020 to $100m this year, while exports rose from around $129m to $200m in the same period. Moreover, the country was able to drastically reduce its dependence on China, which held a 70% share of the local toy market. The sector stands out as a rare exception in India's otherwise unsuccessful attempts to rebalance an increasingly lopsided trading relationship with its larger neighbour, which some experts say, is now among the most asymmetric in the world. Even as diplomatic ties between the two countries completely broke down following the Galwan Valley clashes in 2020 and Delhi announced a slew of anti-dumping duties and a ban on Chinese apps such as Tik Tok, its trade deficit with Beijing has only ballooned - from $44bn in 2020 to an eye-popping $112bn this year. "India's economic dependence on China continued to deepen while political, security, and investment ties were at their lowest point," Kevin Zongzhe Li, a Washington-based Fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute's Centre for China Analysis, told the BBC. More worryingly, exports to China remained below pre-pandemic level even as imports doubled in this period. "China now supplies over 30% of India's industrial imports, and India depends on it for more than 100 critical products. And the imbalance is worsening," says Ajay Srivastava of the Delhi-based Global Trade and Research Initiative (GTRI). If the rapid pace of imports continues, bilateral deficit could jump to $134bn, giving Beijing even more leverage over Indian industry, according to Srivastava. Anti-China sentiment hit a fever pitch post border skirmishes in 2020, but relations have now thawed On the sidelines of the Brics summit in Delhi in September, amid a deepening thaw between the Asian giants, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping vowed to address , external these "structural trade imbalances and supply chain issues". But given how deeply entrenched Chinese imports have become to India's industrial economy, this will be a formidable task for Delhi, experts told the BBC. That's primarily because India depends on China to not merely consume end-products, but increasingly to produce industrial goods. To be true, India has reduced its reliance on imports of finished goods such as smartphones and solar equipment, and now produces more than a quarter of the world's iPhones. "Yet, production remains largely assembly-based and depends heavily on imported components, particularly from China," says Srivastava. It's the same story with industrial machinery, battery inputs, chemicals, solar cells, and manufacturing equipment. Electrical machinery and electronics alone account for 36% of imports, followed by machinery and mechanical appliances at 21.7%, while organic chemicals and plastics also have a significant share, according to the Observer Research Foundation (ORF) think tank. "Their interruption would not merely affect consumption; it would disrupt production itself," according to Soumya Bhowmik, a Fellow at ORF's Centre for New Economic Diplomacy, who argues that this reflects India's difficulty in substituting Chinese inputs with local production. Besides a growing reliance on inputs and raw material, Chinese imports to India are also being propelled by other macroeconomic trends. China has huge excess capacity in sectors from steel to solar panels and electric vehicles, while its slowing economy cannot absorb the output. Manufacturers are therefore increasingly turning to overseas markets, selling goods cheaply. China's trade surplus is expected to top $1tn for a second straight year. A lot of these goods are coming to Indian shores because it is rapidly expanding manufacturing across segments of the economy, but also as "Western markets impose tariffs and other restrictions", says Srivastava. India has reduced smartphone imports but depends heavily on China for components On the other hand, lack of access to the Chinese market remains a major challenge for Indian companies. "Indian products face a variety of tariff and non-tariff hurdles in China that make it difficult to scale exports," says Li.

events.summary: Bankruptcies among Japanese companies more than 100 years old are running at a record pace in 2026, according to Teikoku Databank. Rising costs, labor shortages, a shrinking domestic market and succession challenges are testing Japan’s long-established businesses, experts told CNBC. The challenges are pushing some long-established companies to reassess their businesses, growth strategies and ownership structures. Founded in 1858, Japanese sesame oil maker Kadoya Sesame Mills has witnessed the country transform over generations — surviving world wars and Japan's asset bubble. Now, more than two decades after listing on the Jasdaq Securities Exchange in 2004, Kadoya is set to go private through a tender offer backed by Japanese private equity firm Integral. The move comes as the company navigates rising raw-material costs and heightened geopolitical risks. Japan's long-established businesses are being tested by factors ranging from a shrinking domestic market and labor shortages to succession challenges, experts told CNBC. Bankruptcies among Japanese businesses with more than 100 years of history are occurring at a record pace, reaching 112 in the first eight months of 2026, according to Teikoku Databank. Japan's century-old companies have achieved enduring prosperity through a long-term perspective fostered by family ownership, strong roots in local communities and a business approach that stays within their means, said Shigeto Nagai, head of Japan economics at Oxford Economics. Their long histories and years of capital accumulation have also left them with sound balance sheets and stable profit margins. "However, they are increasingly concerned that they cannot foresee a future of sustained high profits over the long term and fear they will gradually fall into decline," Nagai said. Rising costs and labor shortages have become major challenges for Japanese companies in the post-pandemic business environment, said Harumi Taguchi, principal economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence. "Although inflation has made it easier for companies to pass on costs than during the deflationary period, many still cannot fully reflect higher expenses in sales prices," Taguchi pointed out. Higher costs are particularly difficult for smaller and domestically focused Japanese businesses to absorb given their weaker sales bases, she said. Pricing power is therefore a key factor in determining which companies can adapt. Bankruptcies linked to higher prices jumped 23.8% to 556 in the first half of 2026, while labor-shortage bankruptcies climbed 12.4% to 227, according to Teikoku Databank. Sube Shoten, a tofu maker founded in 1877 during Japan's Meiji era, reportedly ceased operations in May and began preparing to file for bankruptcy as low profit margins and a recent surge in raw-material costs clouded its business outlook. Another major challenge is intensifying domestic competition and labor shortages as Japan's birth rate declines and its population ages, Nagai said. Expanding overseas is another challenge as the domestic market, historically a stable source of revenue, continues to shrink. But there is no "one-size-fits-all" prescription, Nagai added. Succession is another growing challenge. Bankruptcies linked to a lack of successors rose 16.9% to 312 from a year earlier in the first half of 2026, according to Teikoku Databank. A weaker yen, corporate governance reforms, activist pressure and succession challenges among founder-owned businesses are pushing owners and boards to reassess their options, alongside broader pressures including inflation, tariffs, labor costs and interest rates, said Paul Aversano, managing director and global practice leader of Alvarez & Marsal's Global Transaction Advisory Group. "It is that combination, rather than any single issue, that is shaping decisions," he said.

events.title: Property downturn worsens with less than 50pc of auctions leading to a sale
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Auction clearance rate sinks to three-month low, Sydney and Melbourne property a 'drag' on results The traditional spring selling boom is off to a poor start. ( ABC News: Kate Ainsworth ) Property sales for the spring season are off to a weak start. It comes off the back of two long weekends in major capital cities and the RBA lifting the cash rate again last week. Some economists predict capital city property prices could fall 10-15 per cent from peak to trough. Australia's auction clearance rate has slumped to a three-month low, while new data shows the number of unsold homes has surged by more than 20 per cent in the past year. Less than half the auctions that occurred across the country last week resulted in a successful sale. The preliminary clearance rate in the past week fell to 48.2 per cent, its lowest since late June (47.4 per cent) and the second-lowest preliminary reading for the year so far. It has also been hovering at or below the 50 per cent mark for several months, coinciding with a steep decline in property prices and weak sentiment in the housing market. In the past week, 1,223 auctions were held in the nation's capital cities. So there were 12.8 per cent fewer auctions than the previous week. It was also a significant 47.5 per cent drop from a year ago, according to new data from property research firm Cotality. Less than half the homes that hit the market and went to auction sold in the last week, Cotality data shows. ( Supplied: Cotality ) Sharp fall in number of auctions held Cotality's research director Tim Lawless said the weak result came off the back of long weekends in some states and the Reserve Bank's decision to lift interest rates for a fourth time this year. It also comes after changes in this year's federal budget that sent shock waves through the property sector , including heavily restricted negative gearing, and in many cases higher capital gains tax for sellers. Preliminary clearance rates across the major capitals last week compared with previous years. ( Supplied: Cotality ) Sydney and Melbourne "have been a drag on the national result", Mr Lawless said. In Sydney, 304 auctions were held in the past week, down 61 per cent to the week before. It was also a 38.5 per cent drop compared to a year ago. There were 670 auctions held in Melbourne. That was a 136 per cent jump compared to the previous week when the city was having the AFL grand final long weekend. But in the past 12 months, the number of auctions held in Melbourne has dropped 45.6 per cent, the largest decline of any capital city. Tim Lawless says clearance rates have hit a three-month low. ( ABC News: Jessica Ross ) Property taking up to six months to sell Another real estate analysis firm, SQM Research, also released new data, showing some homes were sitting unsold on the market for as long as six months. Homes that sat unsold for more than 180 days were clogging the market, with 10.5 per cent more older listings compared to a year ago. Old housing stock is clogging the market. ( Supplied: SQM Research ) Spring's traditional selling boom has ground to a halt so far this season, with the number of unsold homes across the country totalling 276,000, a 21.6 per cent annual increase. "The bulk of the increase is property that has been on the market for one to six months and hasn't sold," SQM Research director Louis Christopher said. "In Sydney, fewer vendors are listing than a year ago, yet total stock is up almost a fifth. That's a demand problem, not a supply surge." The housing market is slumping and experts warn more falls are to come. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) Brisbane and Adelaide have had the largest increase in the number of properties available for sale, up 43.5 and 39.5 per cent respectively, according to SQM's data. Melbourne, meanwhile, had 30.3 per cent more homes up for sale than it did a year ago. Perth's figure was up 21.3 per cent, while Canberra's was up 17.8 per cent. SQM's figures also showed there were 4,872 distressed sales across Australia in September, which was a 29 per cent jump compared to the same period last year. It follows the ABC reporting last week that Australian housing values had dropped for a sixth straight month, with many economists warning there will be further price falls ahead. Mr Lawless said Australian households were "deeply pessimistic" about the cost-of-living crisis, interest recent hikes and the budget's changes to property taxes creating "less favourable conditions".

events.title: Marc Elias’ Democracy Docket sees Trump 2.0 success
events.summary: The News One of the Democratic Party’s most prolific lawyers also is becoming one of its most prolific posters. Marc Elias has argued dozens of cases around mail-in balloting and election access across the country and in front of the Supreme Court over the last decade. But he has also moonlighted as an election law content creator and advisor for Democracy Docket, a digital media company he founded in 2020 to focus on redistricting, gerrymandering, and voting access. What began as a hobby to help explain complex redistricting cases more effectively has grown into a serious media operation. Last month, Democracy Docket surpassed 500,000 free email subscribers, the company first told Semafor, including 70,000 subscribers paying $10 a month or $120 per year. The company also has a YouTube channel with more than 800,000 subscribers, a following that has grown significantly in recent months (the account has added half a million subscribers on the platform since January 2025). “In this era where so many political disputes, so many public controversies really wind up in court, and oftentimes the court arguments frame the public debate — I think lawyers have an obligation to speak directly and plainly in language that everyone, non-lawyers and lawyers alike, can understand,” he said. “That is something I’ve tried to do, particularly in the area of voting and elections, but really more broadly, in the area of democracy.” Elias told Semafor that he founded the outlet for a fairly prosaic reason: He’d maxed out the number of people he could send emails to on a private email listserv that he’d previously used to send election and redistricting law updates to a few hundred Democratic policymakers, executives, and officials across the country. The timing turned out to be convenient: COVID-19 lockdowns prompted a wave of court cases around mail-in balloting, an issue which Elias knew well and was, at times, directly involved in. Democracy Docket began posting public legal documents before many news outlets, gaining email subscribers and direct online traffic through Twitter and Facebook. Elias told Semafor that his readership is a mix of DC insiders, #Resistance liberals who watch Elias’ interviews on MS NOW, and legal and political professionals interested in keeping up with the ins and outs of election laws and voting access issues. While Elias told Semafor he dedicates just a few days a month to the management side, he acknowledged Democracy Docket has become a profitable enterprise. Asked how much money the company brought in each year, Elias declined to elaborate but said that the vast majority of the company’s revenue came from basic subscriptions, with a small but growing VIP tier of supporters paying $500 a year. Those projections would likely put the company in the ballpark of $9 million to $11 million in annual revenue. Max’s view Democracy Docket is part of a wave of new digital news outlets founded in the Trump era that have surged during the Republican president’s second term. While liberal and left-of-center audiences channeled their interest (and horror) with Trump during his first term by tuning into MSNBC, CNN, The New York Times, and The Washington Post, this go around, shares of those audiences have seemed to abandon traditional outlets for more ideological new media outlets positioned against traditional media. Outlets like Zeteo, The Bulwark, Crooked Media, and More Perfect Union have added millions of readers, listeners, and YouTube subscribers, even as cable news viewership continues to slide. Some of the movement appears to be ideological: Elias told me that some of the best days of membership for the site have come in the wake of blow-ups at major news outlets like CBS News, which he argues shows viewers were upset with what they saw as media owners’ capitulation to Donald Trump. But perhaps more interesting, Democracy Docket’s real innovation is in the continued erosion of the wall between real political players and the media that cover them. The proximity between Elias’ legal work and journalistic output is likely a bit too close for those who prefer a more traditional separation of church and state, though Elias insists that he’s fairly hands-off when it comes to the newsroom’s coverage. He said that he has occasionally disagreed with Democracy Docket’s stories and opinions. “Sometimes you’ll see they report it one way and then I write an opinion piece and I don’t correct them in my opinion piece, I just like say ‘this is what I think about the case, and if you want to know what I think the outcome of the case is, you know, become a premium member,’” he said. Notable Older outlets like the Guardian and The Atlantic have similarly benefited from increased left-of-center interest by explicitly positioning themselves as checks on the current administration — and even on some of their less-aggressive peers.

events.title: CEO’s podcast sparks tensions atop The Atlantic
events.summary: The Scoop Atlantic CEO Nicholas Thompson was talking about the media business on Vox’s podcast last month when host Peter Kafka asked him: How was the magazine’s editor-in-chief, Jeffrey Goldberg, feeling about the growing success of Thompson’s personal podcast? “We make a lot of money on the stuff I do,” he said. “Jeff likes when we make money.” Thompson’s response ricocheted around The Atlantic’s newsroom. Thompson’s podcast, , has emerged as a source of tension between the magazine’s business and editorial teams. Journalists have complained that the lucrative and high-profile show is not subject to The Atlantic’s editorial rules, input, or oversight — yet a casual listener could easily take it for an Atlantic editorial product. Thompson’s show is made by the magazine’s business side, and — like any number of contemporary podcasts — features interviews with technologists and business leaders, interspersed with sponsored content. When the podcast launched in 2024, the newsroom raised no objections; The Atlantic has featured a robust paid content arm for years through its creative marketing studio and custom events business. But as the show’s profile has risen in recent months, the podcast has caused increasing consternation internally. Thompson, despite his commercial role, is a well-known former tech reporter and former editor-in-chief of Wired. Last year, when he published a well-received memoir of his family and time as an elite long-distance runner, The Atlantic ran an excerpt . On , he has booked and interviewed top-tier guests, including OpenAI founder Sam Altman — leading staff to complain that the CEO’s bookings are, intentionally or not, undercutting the newsroom’s own efforts. According to four people familiar with the situation, the podcast has been a particular source of friction between Thompson and Goldberg. Goldberg, who also has a close relationship with Atlantic owner Laurene Powell Jobs, does not report to the CEO and instead reports directly to the Atlantic’s board of directors. (Goldberg had formally reported to Thompson’s predecessor, Bob Cohn.) Dissolving Lines The traditional separation between news outlets’ editorial and business halves has been facing pressure from both sides of that line. Axel Springer CEO Mathias Dopfner’s podcast has drawn world leaders, cultural figures, and executives. Axios CEO Jim VandeHei regularly writes columns and occasionally breaks news on the company’s site, in addition to steering its business. The growth of independent media in the Substack era has also created a generation of journalists who run both the business and editorial arms of their own small media outlets. In this media environment, Thompson’s sponsored podcast is hardly an outlier. But it’s the latest instance in which Thompson’s attempts to nudge the newsroom on the business side have run up against a more skeptical and traditionalist editorial staff. Deepening the tension are differing views about the substance of the AI story. Thompson inked a content-licensing deal between The Atlantic and OpenAI in 2024, angering newsroom staffers, some of whom view the frontier AI labs as having stolen journalists’ work for training. The publication’s editorial union publicly expressed skepticism of the deal and the publication’s policies around AI. The magazine’s tech editor published an op-ed saying publishers like The Atlantic were making a “ devil’s bargain .” In an August 2024 letter first reported by Semafor, editorial staff said OpenAI was hallucinating Atlantic stories and linking to aggregation of the publication’s reporting. And while The Atlantic has published largely skeptical coverage of major AI companies and their products’ impact on society, Thompson’s tone, in his podcasts and LinkedIn posts, has been more optimistic. The View From The Atlantic The Atlantic declined to comment. But one senior company source stressed that there are clear disclaimers demarcating content made by the business side of the company, even if the content itself can feel journalistic in tone — perhaps unsurprising in the case of , as Thompson is a former journalist. Max’s view The Atlantic is one of the clear media success stories of the second Trump term, fueled by Signalgate and other critical reporting and commentary on the Trump administration, a successful events business, and shrewd moves to capitalize on the public stumbles of its DC neighbor, The Washington Post. The 168-year-old magazine’s breakout journalism, its digital success, and a bit of good timing have given both Goldberg and Thompson plenty to brag about on the media podcast circuit. But strains at the top of the organization over its brand and direction reflect many premium news outlets’ dilemmas about survival and profit in a post-traffic, AI-ascendant media age. Marketers have infinite options for buying ads, meaning publishers no longer have the leverage they did when they controlled much of their own distribution. Meanwhile, independent journalists are developing direct relationships with advertisers and marketers, creating more fluidity between the editorial and business sides of their brands. Still, the old boundaries existed for a reason. Fragmentation has allowed many powerful figures to get their message across by circumventing traditional media outlets whose questions many CEOs and politicians don’t want to answer. It’s not surprising that Altman was willing to sit down with The Atlantic’s CEO on a sponsored business-side podcast, but not with the magazine’s tech journalists. Room for Disagreement Readers and audiences understand that when someone runs or owns a news outlet, they have the right to make it publish their opinions and thoughts, Kafka told Thompson. “It’s not against the law, but it’s also a little creepy.”

events.title: AI nonprofit will spend $10 million on journalism
events.summary: The Scoop A Silicon Valley nonprofit close to the AI safety movement is pledging $10 million by the end of 2027 to fund mainstream and independent coverage of artificial intelligence. The Tarbell Center for AI Journalism plans to announce that it is launching an institutional grantmaking fund, which executive director Cillian Crosson said will provide grants to newsrooms and other ambitious AI reporting projects. The first recipient of the grant is , NPR’s new video podcast from former hosts Kevin Roose and Casey Newton, which is receiving a $480,000 grant from the organization. Tarbell is also separately backing NPR’s “Power and Influence” desk, giving the public media outlet $250,000 to help expand its coverage of how AI intersects with politics, money, and power. “We think that having resources at newsrooms is an important part of ensuring strong coverage,” Crosson told Semafor. The new fund will “increase our support but it also allows us to more easily support a more diverse range of perspectives.” The organization, which is backed by groups including the deep-pocketed nonprofit Coefficient Giving , said it plans to fund investigative teams, AI verticals at national outlets, and other large-scale initiatives in new and legacy media. In particular, the organization is focused on expanding reporting and on frontier companies and the ways that AI companies and aligned political action groups are influencing American politics and tech regulations. It’s a significant expansion from the organization’s previous commitments, which have totaled $400,000 over four years. Tarbell’s previous grants focused on backing early-career journalists inside established newsrooms, offering media organizations reporting grants ranging from $1,000 to $20,000 to work on individual stories on AI. With increased monetary backing, the organization said it planned to issue grants between $50,000 and $500,000, but could make multimillion-dollar grants for the right projects. Funding and AI safety In recent years, Tarbell fellows have fanned out across several major news outlets, breaking stories that have often exposed reckless or aggressive actions by AI companies and frontier labs. Though Tarbell offers funding with no formal strings attached, it has drawn criticism from some in the AI industry and on the political right who see it as fueling what they view as exaggerated safety concerns. The subjects of some of Tarbell’s journalism, including OpenAI, have complained about the reporting and financial support from some organizations aligned with effective altruism, a loose philosophical movement whose concerns include an AI-driven apocalypse. As Semafor previously reported , cash-strapped news organizations have balanced concerns about optics of outside groups funding journalism with the much-needed financial support and aggressive journalists who have broken legitimate stories about AI and safety concerns. Semafor has not found instances where Tarbell interfered directly in any stories, and the organization is quick to point out that not all of the projects it backs are AI skeptics or strong AI safety proponents. In a telephone interview last week, Crosson reminded Semafor that the organization has two editorial firewalls: One between itself and its backers, and another between Tarbell and the media organizations it supports. It discloses its donors over $10,000, its fellows maintain complete autonomy over their reporting, and the organization asks news outlets it partners with to disclose when it has provided funding to support a journalist or project. In an interview with Semafor, Roose noted that Newton had worked with Tarbell at Platformer in recent years, and found the organization to be a strong supporter of independent journalism, and did not interfere or insert itself into any editorial content. “Their funding has been very useful in helping us get started,” Roose said. “It was a way for us to de-risk going out on our own. We’re feeling quite good about it and we’re grateful.”

events.title: Trump tells South Korea to sign on to Alaska LNG deal or 'I'll just charge them more'
events.summary: Trump said if South Korea does not sign on to the $50 billion Alaska LNG project he will charge them more or "double it up," without specifying what would be doubled. South Korea has said it is still assessing the Alaska project, with participation dependent on commercial viability and compliance with domestic legal procedures. Trump also announced an $8.4 billion oil recovery project that South Korean local media reported was not part of the countries’ agreement, citing Seoul’s industry ministry. U.S. President Donald Trump said he "didn't jump the gun" in announcing South Korea's participation in a $50 billion Alaska LNG project, warning Seoul could pay "double" if it does not sign on soon. His remarks come amid a discrepancy between Washington and Seoul over South Korea's planned energy and infrastructure investments in the U.S., with Trump announcing projects that Seoul has said are not yet finalized. "If they don't want to do it, that's OK with me. I'll just charge them more," Trump told reporters Friday, according to the White House. "Tell them if they don't sign shortly, I'm going to double it up." Trump did not specify what would be doubled. South Korean local media, though, raised the possibility that he was referring to higher tariffs on the country. When asked whether he had prematurely announced South Korea's involvement in the Alaska LNG project, Trump said he "didn't jump the gun." Trump's remarks come after South Korea said it was still assessing the Alaska LNG project, with any participation dependent on its commercial viability and compliance with domestic legal procedures. Separately, Trump said on Truth Social Friday that South Korea's investment deal "keeps getting BETTER," announcing an additional $8.4 billion enhanced oil recovery project. Enhanced oil recovery uses techniques such as carbon dioxide injection to increase the amount of crude oil produced from an oil field. South Korean local media further reported that the oil recovery project was not included in the agreements reached between Seoul and Washington, citing the country's industry ministry. The ministry was seeking to verify Trump's announcement and had contacted the U.S. through trade channels for clarification, according to the report.

events.title: Saudi Arabia unexpectedly cuts November oil prices to Asia to lowest in 6 years
events.summary: The largest Middle Eastern crude exporter set the November Arab Light crude oil official selling price to Asia at US$5 a barrel below the average of Oman and Dubai prices, down US$3 from the previous month. Saudi Arabia unexpectedly cut its oil prices for sale to Asia in November to their lowest in six years, while raising them for north-west Europe and the Mediterranean, a pricing document showed on Oct 5. The largest Middle Eastern crude exporter set the November Arab Light crude oil official selling price (OSP) to Asia at US$5 a barrel, below the average of Oman and Dubai prices, down US$3 from the previous month. The discount for November is the widest since June 2020, Reuters data showed. This was against expectations of a US$3 a barrel hike for its November OSP in a Reuters survey in line with gains seen in the Middle Eastern benchmarks. State oil company Saudi Aramco cut the November OSPs of heavier grades, Arab Medium and Arab Heavy, sold to Asia by US$5 a barrel. Aramco has been looking at offering discounts for oil loaded off Oman to compensate buyers for record freight rates, sources familiar with the matter said last week, as it sought to protect its market share after disruptions from the US-Israeli war against Iran affected exports. The OSP cuts appeared to be aimed at compensating buyers for the elevated freight costs, said three Asian refining sources who spoke on condition of anonymity. The cost of booking a very large crude carrier capable of hauling two million barrels of oil from the Gulf to China on a time charter basis was US$1.2 million (S$1.53 million) a day on Oct 2, according to LSEG data. It was about US$80,000 a day a year ago. One of the sources also said the lower OSPs could offset the waiting time and longer voyage for Saudi oil exported from the Egyptian port of Sidi Kerir, where cargo loadings have been delayed. Since September, Saudi Aramco has sold millions of barrels of crude through ship-to-ship transfers outside the Strait of Hormuz, pushing oil flows through the strategic waterway to pre-conflict levels. The kingdom also resumed loading at the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea after a brief suspension as a drone attack shut its key East-West oil pipeline. Separately, Saudi Aramco raised the November OSPs for north-west Europe by US$3 a barrel across all grades. Aramco kept prices unchanged for buyers in the United States. REUTERS

events.title: The job interview question you don't have to answer
events.summary: Prepare all you like, but there is often still one job interview question that leaves you feeling uncomfortable. While employers in the UK are within their rights to ask you how much you get paid in your current role, applicants are not obliged to tell them. Recruiters have been encouraged to stop posing questions about salary history and, in the EU, new rules will prevent them doing so. But in the UK, there is still a chance of it coming up, so how best should you answer? Sometimes it feels like interviewers, and interviewees, tip-toe around the subject of money. But Louise Rudd, a senior adviser at the workplace advice and conciliation service Acas, says there are no regulations that prevent employers from asking interviewees about their current salary, or their salary expectations. She says employers, if they do want to know, should ask each applicant the same questions to ensure they are treated fairly. A few years ago, a campaign was launched urging employers to stop asking new recruits how much they were paid in their previous jobs. It had its own hashtag - #EndSalaryHistory. The Fawcett Society, which campaigns for women and gender equality, said that asking the question risked maintaining historic unfair differences in pay due to gender, race and disability inequality. Rather than offering a salary based on skills, experience and performance, it meant employers rewarded an individual's perceived worth and negotiating skills instead, the society said. The Recruitment and Employment Confederation supported the move, urging recruiters not to ask. Employers in the EU will be banned from asking about salary history in new rules being rolled out across the bloc. But that's not featured in Cabinet Office plans in the UK, which instead concentrates on telling employers to publish salary information in job adverts . When you're going for a new job, you can reveal your current salary if you are happy to. Some people asked by BBC News out and about in London suggested they would reply with an inflated salary - so they get paid more in the next job. However, the risks of lying in an interview can far outweigh the possible reward. There are no requirements for you to disclose your salary if you don't want to. Rudd says some people might prefer to give their salary expectations, or outline their understanding of the salary range for the role. Recruitment firms often say applicants could instead focus on their skills and experience, so those are used as a measure of what they should be paid, not their salary history. Shazia Ejaz, director of campaigns at the Recruitment and Employment Confederation, says jobseekers should approach questions about pay with "realism but also confidence". "Candidates can focus on showcasing the value they bring, the benefits that matter most to them and to go to the interview knowing the market rate for the role," she says. "Jobseekers who have done their homework on salaries and can explain the contribution they will make are in the strongest position to secure the right package." What was your worst job interview? events.title: Air Force removes all bombers from British base and redeploys them to the U.S. after a planned terror attack linked to Iran was foiled
events.summary: The U.S. Air Force has brought home its bombers stationed at a U.S.-run military air base in England used to strike Iran following an investigation into a planned terror attack at the RAF Fairford base. The bombers were redeployed to their home bases in the United States, according to a Pentagon official who was not authorized to discuss sensitive military movements and spoke Sunday on condition of anonymity. Aviation watchers such as the Military Air Tracking Alliance have observed dozens of B-52 and B-1 bombers operating out of RAF Fairford since the opening days of the Iran war. Observers noticed a host of B-1 bombers fly out of the base on Sunday. The move comes as President Donald Trump weighs options for his war on Iran — including new strikes — despite his initial promises to Americans that the campaign would  last a matter of weeks . “We have decisions that I’ll make about Iran. Iran’s been decimated. So the only question is — it’ll either be the easy way, or the hard way,” Trump told reporters on Saturday as he left the White House for a rally in Ohio. A dual British-Iranian national was arrested in central London last week on suspicion of plotting a terror attack, following a security incident at RAF Fairford in late September. In total, six people have been taken into custody and then  released on bail  during the investigation. British authorities have  linked the incident to Tehran . Iran has denied involvement, but it has previously said it considers any base used to attack its territory  a legitimate target . U.K. officials say proxies linked to Iran have been behind a string of arson and other attacks in Britain and other countries, many of them targeting the Jewish community and intended to sow fear. They have previously warned that Tehran could expand its targets in the U.K. if conflicts in the Middle East continue. RAF Fairford, located 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of London, has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East. The U.S. military still  maintains a sizable presence  in the Middle East. On Thursday, a U.S. official said the recently deployed USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier, as well as the USS Malkin Island amphibious readiness group — a group of ships that together carry over 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines — are heading for the region. The official said the move could result in three carriers in the region as early as the end of October. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Japan’s population is shrinking at an accelerating rate, but the nationalist prime minister is making it harder for foreigners to live there
events.summary: New census data over the past week showed Japan’s population shrank more quickly than in the prior tally. Also last week, the government rolled out tougher rules for foreign nationals who want to live in Japan. While foreigners make up just 3.4% of Japan’s population, the share has increased to a record high and a political backlash has been building—even as the country also grapples with rapidly aging demographics and the need to find new workers to sustain economic growth. On Tuesday, the latest five-year population survey detailed how stark Japan’s situation is. As of October 2025, the total population, including foreign residents, was 22.9 million, down 2.5% from five years earlier. The prior census in 2020 showed a dip of 0.7%. The number of Japanese nationals revealed an even steeper decline of 3.5% to 119.1 million, following a 1.4% drop in the 2020 count. Meanwhile, foreign residents jumped 40% to a record high of 3.84 million, and permanent residents climbed 17% to 947,125. Like other wealthy economies in Asia, Japan’s birth rate has been below the replacement level of 2.1 children per woman for decades, and the population has been in steady decline since around 2008. At the same time, Japan is aging, and the percentage of people age 65 and older rose to 29.4% in 2025 from 28.5% in 2020. In fact, adult diapers have been outselling baby diapers since 2011. The country is scrambling to find ways to encourage people to have more kids. For example, Tokyo’s metropolitan government launched a dating app to bring more couples together. Tokyo also started a four-day workweek and partial leave policy for city workers to help those who are parents balance childcare and work. By contrast, policies have turned more hostile when it comes to foreigners. On Thursday, the Japanese government increased fees for permanent residency to $1,271 from $64 — a 2,000% jump that marks the largest increase in the country’s history. The cost for a five-year residence permit shot up to $475 from $38. Japan also imposed more detailed requirements on income for permanent residents, who must now earn a minimum of $36,428 per year. And for the first time, applicants for permanent residency will be evaluated based on their Japanese language skills as well as their grasp of rules and customs. On top of that, the government can revoke permanent residency for not meeting pension contribution obligations, failing to pay health insurance and taxes, and violating immigration law or the penal code. The changes come as Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has ushered in a more nationalist, right-wing stance. On the global stage, that has meant taking a harder line against rivals like China and North Korea, while also bulking up Japan’s military. Domestically, the pivot has translated to a crackdown on immigration and even tourism, drawing criticism that Takaichi is encouraging xenophobia. In July, the government hiked some tourist visa prices by more than 400%.  In a post on X ahead of the government’s new residency rules, Takaichi said many permanent residents could not maintain independent livelihoods. “The government recognizes that, with the increasing number of foreign residents, there are citizens who feel anxiety and a sense of unfairness, and is addressing this by making ‘foreign policy’ more ‘orderly’ so that both citizens and foreigners can live safely and securely,” she wrote. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Money stolen by scammers hijacking UK social media accounts rises 400%
events.summary: Many cases involve criminals using other people’s identities to sell fake event tickets to friends and family The total amount stolen by criminals who hack into people’s emails and social media accounts and then pretend to be them has risen by more than 400% in a year, official UK data shows. In many cases, the scammers are hijacking people’s accounts in order to use their identity to sell fake event tickets – such as to sold-out gigs – to unsuspecting friends and family. The total reported amount stolen via email and social media account hacking reached £6.3m in the 2025-26 financial year, compared with £1.2m in 2024-25, according to the Report Fraud service run by the City of London police, which holds national responsibility for economic crime. However, the true total may be much higher as many scam victims do not report the crime, often because they feel embarrassed, and sometimes because the individual amount of money involved was relatively small. The Guardian previously featured the case of a music fan whose Instagram account was targeted by hackers, who used her identity to advertise tickets to an Oasis gig and stole £1,400 from her friends. She said the hackers impersonated her so well that her friends and family genuinely thought they were speaking to her. Others have been scammed by fraudulent WhatsApp and text messages in which a criminal pretends to be their child or a relative who is in an emergency situation and urgently needs cash. This has been dubbed the “Hi mum” scam . Data from Santander has shown that among customers of the bank, fraudsters pretending to be someone’s son were the most successful at extracting cash, followed by daughters. Ch Supt Amanda Wolf, head of Report Fraud operations, said: “For most people, being hacked isn’t just a cyber issue – it’s personal. It can leave victims locked out of important accounts, worried about what information has been accessed, and concerned that criminals may use their identity to target others.” She added that what starts with one compromised account “can quickly impact family, friends and colleagues as fraudsters exploit trusted relationships to commit further fraud”. Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters Report Fraud is launching an awareness campaign urging the public to protect their online accounts from hackers by switching to passkeys where they are available. A passkey uses an individual’s device and biometrics to authenticate them and cannot be hacked like a password.

events.summary: More than 150 million Brazilians voted Sunday in a pivotal presidential election for Latin America’s largest economy, after a campaign dominated by tensions between Brasília and Washington. events.summary: China closed a record 670 banks last year, or nearly one in four lenders, as Beijing pushes to de-risk amid slowing economic growth. After a massive credit expansion drove growth, “the financial system’s problems now constrain that growth ,” a Rhodium Group expert told ChinaTalk. events.title: Supreme Court Justice Alito said he's 'thought about' retirement as Senate control hangs in balance
events.summary: Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito told CBS News he has "thought about" retiring after the high court's last term but decided against it. Alito, 76, is the second-oldest justice on the bench, and speculation had swirled that he would retire while Republicans control the Senate and the White House. The possibility that Democrats might flip the Senate after November's election could jeopardize a potential Supreme Court nomination by President Donald Trump. Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito has "thought about" retiring after the high court's last term but decided against it, believing he could still make "a valuable contribution," he said in an interview with CBS News . Alito, 76, is the second-oldest justice on the bench, and speculation had swirled that he would retire while Republicans control the Senate and the White House — when the chances of swiftly confirming a GOP-backed candidate to the bench would be high. The possibility that the Senate could flip to Democrats after November's midterm election may make confirmation of any potential nominee of President Donald Trump more difficult or impossible if Democrats control the Senate. "I've been bemused by the retirement speculation; it's not too pleasant to look up and see the vultures circling," Alito said in a separate interview with "Fox News Sunday." "I don't have a calculation for it ... I think it would be foolhardy to make a calculation [that] I'm going to serve for a certain number of additional years." Alito's status as one of the court's most conservative justices has sparked the speculation that he would retire ahead of the midterms — a decision the justice ultimately has not made. Should Democrats take control of the Senate, they would effectively have veto power over a Supreme Court nomination. Justice Clarence Thomas, 78 — the court's oldest justice and a member of its conservative bloc — has also been on retirement watch. Inside the China espionage case that ensnared former Fed advisor John Rogers AI's coming roadblock in regulation: Antitrust hawks Trump holds up to $1 billion in bonds tied to institutions he can affect Rep. James Comer expands House investigation into prediction market insider trading The politics and timing of Supreme Court vacancies have been closely watched since Justice Antonin Scalia died in 2016. Then-Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell refused to take up President Barack Obama's nomination of Merrick Garland to the Supreme Court until after the 2016 presidential election, allowing Trump the time to nominate and confirm Justice Neil Gorsuch. Then, after Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg died in 2020, McConnell moved quickly to confirm Trump's nominee, Amy Coney Barrett , just over a week before the 2020 presidential election. The Court is now controlled by a 6-3 conservative majority. Democrats currently hold an edge in national House polling and in the CBS News Battleground Tracker model, which estimates a narrow Democratic majority after the midterm election, which looms just 30 days away. The Senate is also now in play, with Republicans locked in unexpectedly tight races across the country amid voter ire over prices and the economy. Democrats need to net at least four seats while defending all the seats they currently have to win a Senate majority.

events.title: All U.S. bombers leave UK air base on concerns of suspected terror plots; more tankers struck near Iran in the Middle East
events.summary: The U.S. withdrew all of its B-1 bombers stationed at a UK air base that is used by American military forces to strike Iran after an investigation discovered a planned terror attack. At least two vessels were struck over the weekend in waters near Oman and Iran, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre reported. Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said the Strait of Hormuz would not reopen unless Iran met its conditions for ending the war with the U.S. The U.S. Air Force withdrew all of its B-1 bombers stationed at an air base in southern England that is used by American military forces to strike Iran after an investigation discovered a planned terror attack, The Associated Press reported Sunday. The bombers were redeployed back to their home bases in the United States, AP reported, citing a Pentagon official who was not authorized to discuss sensitive military movements and spoke on condition of anonymity. Aviation watchers such as the Military Air Tracking Alliance and others have observed dozens of B-52 and B-1 bombers operating out of RAF Fairford since the opening days of the Iran war, AP said. These observers saw many B-1 bombers take off from the base on Sunday. A dual British-Iranian national was arrested in central London last week on suspicion of plotting a terror attack, following a security incident at RAF Fairford in late September. In total, authorities took six individuals into custody and later released them on bail during the investigation. British authorities have linked the terror plot to Tehran, although Iran has denied involvement. RAF Fairford is located 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of London and has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East. More tankers struck in the Middle East At least two vessels were struck over the weekend in waters near Oman and Iran , the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre reported, as Tehran reiterated its position on Sunday that the Strait of Hormuz would not reopen unless its conditions for ending the war with the U.S. are met. On Saturday, the UKMTO, a British maritime security alert service, said it received a report of a crude oil tanker being hit by an unknown projectile four nautical miles east of Oman. It said another tanker was reported as being similarly struck Sunday in the Strait of Hormuz, causing damage to its engine room. Attacks on shipping in the strait, through which about a fifth of the world's oil supplies moved before the start of the U.S. and Israel-led war on Feb. 28, have been happening on a regular basis for weeks. "The Strait of Hormuz will not open until Iran's seven conditions based on the Islamabad Memorandum are met, and Iran will not regulate its national security with tweets from American officials," Iranian state media agency Nour News quoted Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf as saying Sunday. President Donald Trump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian signed an interim deal in June, known as the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, that resulted in a brief hiatus in fighting. Tehran's conditions for allowing ships to proceed freely through the Strait of Hormuz include a halt to U.S. "acts of aggression," an end to the U.S. naval blockade of its ports and economic warfare, and the release of Iranian assets. A key demand of the U.S. has been that Iran dismantle its nuclear weapons program. Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia's energy infrastructure reportedly came under renewed attacks. Reuters reported Saturday that Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said they had targeted a facility owned by Saudi Arabian oil giant Aramco in the capital Riyadh with ballistic missiles and drones. The group said the attack was in retaliation for Saudi attacks on Yemen's Sanaa and other provinces. A large plume of smoke and fire rose above the facility, Reuters quoted a witness as saying. Saudi authorities have not commented on the reported attack. Aramco did not immediately respond to CNBC's emailed request for comment. If confirmed, it would be the latest escalation in what has effectively become a second front in the Iran war. Some investors say they expect full-scale fighting to resume in the Middle East. "The situation is fluid and volatile. To me, as we are developing and looking at the situation, it's not a question of if, but when the conflict resumes full force," Bader Al-Saif, founding president of Al-Saif Consulting, told CNBC's Access Middle East show on Friday. The ongoing attacks and prospect of a further escalation have driven energy prices higher in recent weeks, raising inflation expectations globally and putting upward pressure on government borrowing costs . Reports that the U.S. is sending a third aircraft carrier strike group to the Middle East, along with an amphibious force carrying 2,000 Marines, pushed crude oil prices higher on Thursday.

events.title: Tom Cruise suffers one of the worst movie debuts of his career. Reviews were so bad Warner Bros. ran ‘decide for yourself’ ads
events.summary: On the cusp of the studio’s merger with Paramount , Warner Bros.’  “Digger”  flopped in its opening weekend, handing Tom Cruise one of the worst debuts of his career and serving as a bitter final note for Warner Bros. as a standalone studio. No. 1 in North American theaters instead went to Amazon MGM’s  “Verity,” extending the streak for Colleen Hoover adaptations at the box office. It debuted with $32.6 million. The film, directed by Michael Showalter, stars Dakota Johnson as a writer hired to ghostwrite a book series by an incapacitated author (Anne Hathaway). But all eyes were on how “Digger,” one of the year’s biggest gambles, would perform. Alejandro G. Iñárritu’s critically panned satire grossed a paltry $8 million domestically. Cruise is typically a big draw overseas, but international sales, $12 million from 74 markets, were also weak. After reviews so bad that Warner Bros. opted to run “decide for yourself” ads, estimates for “Digger” had been revised down over the past week. It’s a painfully rough start for a movie that cost at least $125 million to make. Reports have pegged the production budget closer to $150 million. The marketing spend is estimated at another $100 million. “Digger” had been positioned as a potential awards-season heavyweight, dated almost exactly the same as Warner Bros.’  “One Battle After Another”  was last year. “Digger” is a similarly politically charged release that handed a large budget to a top filmmaker working from an original story. But this big swing by Warner Bros. Motion Picture Group co-chairs Michael De Luca and Pam Abdy won’t pay off as well as “One Battle After Another.” It grossed $213.2 million worldwide and, more importantly,  won best picture at the Academy Awards. ‘Digger’ flops at a moment of Hollywood transformation The disappointing opening comes just as Paramount Skydance is closing its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery . After U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín on Wednesday  approved the $110 billion deal , Paramount said it would close the merger on Tuesday. In a flush year for Hollywood, Warner Bros. has failed to get one film to $100 million domestically, though its December release, “Dune: Part III,” will easily cross that. De Luca and Abdy are expected to depart Warner Bros. this week. Mass layoffs are anticipated to follow. “‘Digger’ collapsed this weekend and the new management of the combined Paramount and Warner Bros., David Ellison and Josh Greenstein and Dana Goldberg, will soon decide what kind of movies they want from WB,” wrote David A. Gross, a film consultant who publishes a newsletter on box office figures. “Paramount does not have a recent history of making big, auteur-driven films like this — that strategy appears to be over and out.” Critics (51% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes) slammed “Digger” as a strained climate change farce, though Cruise’s over-the-top performance was received more warmly. Audiences agreed, giving it a “C+” CinemaScore. Cruise has spent most of the last decade starring in “Mission: Impossible” movies and “Top Gun: Maverick,” both franchises that have allowed him to remain a top action hero into his 60s. The 64-year-old’s last major box-office disappointment was 2017’s “The Mummy,” which grossed $409.2 million worldwide on a $195 million budget. To help sell “Digger,” Cruise pulled out all the stops. He even granted his first lengthy magazine interview in years. ‘Avengers: Endgame’ retakes all-time crown Last weekend’s top film,  “Avengers Endgame: Encore,” slid to seventh place with $4.4 million domestically and $14.4 million overseas. But the Marvel re-release’s second week allowed “Endgame” to just nudge ahead of “Avatar” to reclaim the title of highest grossing film ever, not accounting for inflation. The two films have traded spots in recent years with re-releases. “Endgame” now tallies $2.9255 billion, while “Avatar” has $2.9237 billion. The rest of the top-sellers in cinemas over the weekend were holdovers: Zach Cregger’s video game adaptation  “Resident Evil”  for Sony Pictures; Lance Oppenheim’s A24 drama  “Primetime,”  with Robert Pattinson as “To Catch a Predator” host Chris Hansen; and Paramount’s  “Heart of the Beast,”  starring Brad Pitt as a retired veteran who treks through the Alaskan wilderness with his combat dog after a plane crash. In its third week, “Resident Evil” came in second with $12.5 million. “Heart of the Beast” followed with $11 million. And “Primetime” collected $8 million in its second weekend. Top 10 movies by domestic box office With final domestic figures being released Monday, this list factors in the estimated ticket sales for Friday through Sunday at U.S. and Canadian theaters, according to Rentrak: 1. “Verity,” $32.6 million. 2. “Resident Evil,” $12.5 million. 3. “Heart of the Beast,” $11 million. 4. “Primetime,” $8 million. 5. “Digger,” $8 million. 6. “Forgotten Island,” $7.2 million. 7. “Avengers: Endgame: Encore,” $4.4 million. 8. “Drishyam: The Conclusion,” $2.7 million. 9. “Practical Magic 2,” $2.7 million. 10. “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” $2.5 million. events.title: Sam Altman said 'the world should accept some bad things happening' for the benefits of AI
events.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told Decoded by POLITICO that he does not accept "the really catastrophic risks" of AI. Heather Diehl/Getty Images OpenAI's Sam Altman diverged from Anthropic's views, saying that we should embrace AI despite risks. Altman agrees with tougher AI regulations, but advocates for a "lighter touch." He believes people will do "orders of magnitude more good stuff than bad stuff" with AI. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said there was a fundamental difference in worldview between his company and rival Anthropic on artificial intelligence regulation, arguing in an exclusive interview with Decoded by POLITICO that the technology's benefits justify accepting some risks — and that AI should remain broadly accessible to the public. "I think there's a lot of daylight," Altman told Decoded co-author and POLITICO senior tech reporter Brendan Bordelon. Asked specifically where he diverges from Anthropic and its CEO Dario Amodei, Altman said, "we believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency." Anthropic has long been viewed as the strongest proponent of AI regulations within the industry, a stance that until recently was at odds with the lighter touch approach favored by OpenAI. But the policy differences between the two leading AI firms have narrowed in recent months, with OpenAI coming out in favor of tougher rules as it grapples with high-profile hacking incidents and rogue behavior by its models. Altman agreed with Amodei's call last month to slow the development of the most advanced AI models. His company has followed Anthropic in endorsing new state laws that impose stricter safety requirements than what the ChatGPT maker had previously supported — a shift from its prior state strategy . And OpenAI lobbyists recently endorsed a bipartisan House proposal that would require top AI companies to embed outside safety evaluators. Despite the convergence, Altman tried to distinguish his firm's regulatory stance from Anthropic's. "I disagree, but I understand the perspective of people who are like, 'This technology is going to get so powerful, and it's so dangerous, that a single lab in San Francisco should have it and make sure nothing bad happens, and kind of figure out how to dole out the benefits,'" said Altman. But he called it "a completely unacceptable tradeoff" that runs counter to the "lighter touch regulatory stance" backed by OpenAI. "I wouldn't take a trade of saying like, 'We'll make sure there's no major hacks, there's no kind of like misuse of this technology, there's zero scams, there's zero all the other bad things that will happen," said Altman. "Because I think people will do tremendously — orders of magnitude more — good stuff than bad stuff." The OpenAI CEO later added that he does not accept "the really catastrophic risks," including the potential for "a serious loss of control to AI." The interview, appearing in Monday's debut edition of Decoded and its accompanying daily podcast, also delved into President Donald Trump's new AI accord with top tech firms and his attempted rebrand of AI to "super intelligence;" the rash of autonomous hacking incidents carried out by OpenAI models and whether the company should face legal liability; Altman's thoughts on AI industry money flowing into U.S. politics; the influence of effective altruists inside OpenAI; and his views on key political power players including French President Emmanuel Macron to California Gov. events.title: Tories to pledge to scrap Environment Agency and Natural England
events.summary: Shadow chancellor will also promise to scrap affordable homes regulations as part of strategy to refocus on growth The Conservatives will announce a bonfire of regulations including abolishing affordable homes and community funding rules as well as scrapping Natural England and the Environment Agency . The shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, will say the party intends to “streamline regulations” that protect nature and oblige developers to include affordable homes and community services such as GP surgeries, to speed up infrastructure and housebuilding. The announcements on Monday are a signal that the party intends to refocus on the economy, an area where it has made relatively little progress in the polls. Tory strategists believe there is a major opening to make gains against Reform and Labour, given the limited focus on growth from Andy Burnham and the chancellor, John Healey, at the Labour conference last week. The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch , published a new tract on Sunday called The Right Way, which she said would be the bedrock that underpinned the party’s policy development before the next election. Polls have the party still trailing third behind Labour and Reform UK. Introducing the document – inspired by Margaret Thatcher’s The Right Approach from 1976 – Badenoch said the Conservatives still expected to win the next election and needed to “hit the ground running … We will need to be ready from day one, having already shown people what kind of government we are going to be.” “Keir Starmer didn’t have a plan. That’s why he’s gone,” she said. “Andy Burnham doesn’t have one either and that is why I know the announcements he is making will all come to naught. We have to be different, different from Labour, and different from the party we were two years ago.” In a slew of announcements at the Conservative party conference on Monday, the Tories will pledge measures that they claim would cut the price of a new home by £50,0000, including scrapping net zero regulations on housebuilding, such as the Future Homes Standard, which requires all new homes in England to be zero-carbon ready. The party will promise to replace section 106 agreements and the community infrastructure levy that oblige developers to build a proportion of affordable housing and support school and health service demands locally. Instead, there will be a “one stop” levy on developers, Griffith will say. The party has also pledged to abolish Natural England and the Environment Agency, “moving to a more streamlined regulatory landscape to protect our environment”. Griffith will say in his first speech as shadow chancellor that the Tories would continue to back the expansion of Heathrow airport and leave the Aarhus convention, which makes it easier for community groups to oppose developments. Conservative shadow Treasury ministers will be tasked with finding new ways of simplifying tax for individuals and businesses, Griffith will say, calling the tax code “a cat’s cradle of complexity”. Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning In his speech, he will say: “No one else is coming to save our economy. Only we can inject reality, tell the hard truths and make this a country we are proud to hand on to the next generation. “Our task just got bigger. We face a prime minister that wants to return Britain to an imagined past. A socialist fever dream of the 1970s. Cheaper homes, lower taxes and less red tape. This will be the most ambitious deregulation project in a generation. We will be more prepared than ever before. We will set out our plans line by line. Every bill, every regulation, every chapter.” Griffith will say that the government must speed up the building of a Heathrow third runway in whatever way it can. “I refuse to accept for a single moment that the country of Brunel and Bazalgette, of the vaccine taskforce and the Mulberry harbours , has to sit around waiting until the 2040s to get a third runway built,” he will say. Burnham has recently expressed personal scepticism about the Heathrow third runway, saying he would take differing views seriously. The new shadow housing secretary, Katie Lam, will say the scrapping of housing regulations and of enforcement bodies would mean “anti-growth ideologues can never again hold our country hostage”. The party said Natural England and the Environment Agency were preventing too many homes being built and adding unnecessary costs to building. Both bodies would be scrapped, with their necessary functions brought directly into Defra.
