events.title: C-Suite Member Spotlight: 140 Years of Everyday Moments
events.summary: As DFI Retail Group marks its 140th anniversary, Group Chief Executive Scott Price says the company’s future will depend on fulfilling the needs of our customers, investing in innovation and continuing to earn trust in the everyday moments that define modern retail. A morning stop for breakfast before work. A coffee picked up between meetings. A grocery stop on the way home. A stop for health and beauty products. A weekend trip to choose furniture for a growing family. A rewards offer that helps make the weekly shop go further. These are ordinary moments in Hong Kong life. Yet for DFI Retail Group, they represent the foundation of a business that has grown with the city for 140 years. Founded in Hong Kong in 1886, DFI has evolved from a local enterprise into one of Asia’s leading retail groups, serving millions of customers every week through brands spanning food, convenience, health and beauty, home furnishings and loyalty rewards. For Scott Price, Group Chief Executive of DFI Retail Group, the anniversary is not only a milestone in the company’s history. It is also a reminder of the role retailers play in daily life, often in ways that consumers rarely stop to consider. “Retail is woven into people’s lives in ways that often go unnoticed,” Price says. “It is there in the everyday decisions people make for themselves and their families. When retailers do their job well, they make life a little easier, a little healthier and a little more convenient.” DFI is marking its 140th anniversary under the theme “140 Years of Everyday Moments”, a phrase Price says reflects both the Group’s history and its continuing purpose. While anniversaries are often viewed as opportunities to look back, DFI is using the milestone to recognise the customers, team members and communities that have shaped the business, and to focus on how retail must continue adapting to changing expectations. Price explains that few industries are as closely connected to the routines of everyday life as retail. Across DFI’s portfolio, customers encounter its brands at different moments and for different needs. From supermarkets such as Market Place to Mannings and Guardian for health, wellness and self-care products, to 7-11 for a snack or collectible, and to IKEA for homewares, Price says its brands are connected by a common purpose: Serving Asia sustainably for generations with everyday moments. That role has become more important as lifestyles have changed. Consumers today are busier, more digitally connected and more discerning. They expect retailers to provide not only the right products, but also convenience, value, reliability and a seamless experience across physical and digital channels. In a city such as Hong Kong, where time, space and household budgets are constant considerations, retail is expected to work harder for customers. “Customers consistently value businesses that understand their needs and earn their trust,” Price says. “That has remained true even as the way people shop has changed dramatically.” Adapting Through Generations of Change Reflecting on DFI’s 140-year history, it has unfolded alongside Hong Kong’s transformation from a trading port into a global financial and commercial centre. During that period, the retail industry has been reshaped by urbanisation, rising living standards, changing family structures, technological innovation and the emergence of digital commerce. Shopping habits have shifted from traditional high-street transactions to omnichannel experiences, loyalty ecosystems and data-driven personalisation. For retailers, the challenge is no longer simply to operate stores. It is to understand customers across multiple touchpoints and respond quickly to changing needs. “Over more than four decades in Asia, I’ve seen enormous change in how people shop and interact with brands,” Price says. “But customers consistently value businesses that understand their needs and earn their trust.” Price explains that maintaining that trust requires continuous investment. As such, the Group is strengthening its capabilities in technology, talent, supply chain and customer engagement, while remaining focused on the fundamentals of quality, service and value. The company is also operating in a market where expectations of retailers are broadening. Customers increasingly want businesses to act responsibly, support healthier lifestyles and contribute positively to the communities in which they operate. For Price, these demands are not separate from the future of retail. They are central to it. Retailers that succeed over the long term, he believes, will be those able to combine operational excellence with a deeper understanding of people’s lives – how they shop, what they value, how they make choices and what kind of support they expect from trusted brands. In such a competitive and fast-changing sector, trust has become one of retail’s most important assets, Price says.

events.title: Court tosses 10-year manslaughter sentence due to an AI-generated video of the victim ‘created from the imaginings’ of his sister
events.summary: An Arizona man’s  10-year manslaughter sentence  has been tossed in a case where a video generated by artificial intelligence portrayed the deceased victim addressing a judge before the punishment was imposed. In a decision released Wednesday, the Arizona Court of Appeals concluded Gabriel Paul Horcasitas must be resentenced in the 2021 shooting death of Christopher Pelkey because the AI video wasn’t reliable. The court found the video crossed the line, saying it didn’t reflect actual events and presented statements made in the footage as coming directly from the victim. “Indeed, rather than document an event or recording a particular moment, the AI video presents a depiction of the victim and his thoughts created from the imaginings of the victim’s sister,” the three-judge panel wrote. Jessica Gattuso, an attorney who represented victims in the case, and Kristen Reller, Horcasitas’ lawyer, declined to comment Thursday on the decision. Reller had argued Superior Court Judge Todd Lang violated due process protections by relying on AI evidence. Gattuso and prosecutors told the appeals court that the lower-court judge didn’t err, saying the footage was an accurate representation of Pelkey’s character. In what’s believed to be a first in U.S. courts, Pelkey’s family used AI to create a video of his likeness to give him a voice. Pelkey’s sister, Stacey Wales, raised the idea of her brother speaking for himself after struggling to figure out what he would say. Wales expected an appeal on the sentence and was disappointed the AI video was cited as the reason, saying her only goal was to humanize her brother for the judge. “It feels unfair because there is a convicted murderer sitting in prison that has blankets and walls of protection around their rights. Where are the rights for the victim?” Wales said. A victim appeals lawyer has told the family that using AI again could result in another appeal. “We will continue to let his voice be heard in whatever allowable medium we can convey that through the court system,” Wales said. The AI-generated victim impact statement was played during a May 2025 sentencing hearing after nine of Pelkey’s family members and friends stood before the judge describing how emotionally devastated they were by his killing. Authorities say Horcasitas, 55, fatally shot Pelkey, 37, during a November 2021 road rage encounter at a stoplight in Chandler, a suburb of Phoenix. Pelkey, who was unarmed, was shot after getting out of his truck and walking toward Horcasitas’ vehicle. Horcasitas was convicted of manslaughter in Pelkey’s death and endangerment for a gunshot that struck another vehicle at the intersection during the encounter. The AI rendering of Pelkey said he wished he could still be with his friends and family, voiced a belief in forgiveness and said it was a shame Horcasitas had encountered him because “in another life, we probably could have been friends.” The video didn’t request a specific prison sentence. Horcasitas’ appellate lawyer argued her client had no meaningful opportunity to rebut material in the AI-generated video. It’s not clear if attorneys or the court were aware in advance that an AI-generated video would be used. But attorneys representing Pelkey’s family said in court records that Arizona law does not require victims to disclose statements they plan to make in court to prosecutors, defense attorneys or the judge — and that victims can exercise their rights by speaking before the court or submitting statements that are written or recorded on audio or video. In a statement Thursday, the Maricopa County Attorney’s Office said its prosecutors knew the victim’s family would address the court during sentencing but weren’t aware of the nature of it. While the use of AI within the court system is expanding, it’s typically been reserved for administrative tasks, legal research and case preparation. In Arizona, it’s helped  inform the public of rulings in significant cases . But using AI to generate victim impact statements marks a new tool for sharing information with the court outside the evidentiary phases. Reller told the appeals court that the video doesn’t disclose who wrote the words used by the AI version of Pelkey and wasn’t backed up with evidence establishing that its contents accurately reflected Pelkey’s views. It also had an “undue emotional weight” and conveyed an authenticity that wouldn’t have been there had a family member read the same words aloud, Reller said. Horcasitas’ lawyer contended the judge weighed the statements made in the AI-generated video when deciding on a sentence, but prosecutors argued Lang didn’t consider the footage when issuing the punishment. Shortly before delivering the sentence, the judge commented that he “loved that AI” but didn’t say from the bench whether the video factored into his decision. Lang said he felt Pelkey’s “obvious forgiveness of Mr. Horcasitas reflects the character I heard about today.” The family’s lawyers say the judge was already inundated with relevant information from Pelkey’s family and friends before the AI video was played — and that nothing in the video was inflammatory. Horcasitas’ attorney didn’t object to the AI video. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Trump reiterates pledge to send $5,000 checks, and hands out smaller payments, as midterm elections loom
events.summary: President Donald Trump is touting two federal cash-payment programs already underway while renewing a much larger $5,000 check promise contingent on Republicans retaining Congress. The cash offers come as Republicans head into the final stretch of a midterm campaign dominated by concerns about prices and the economy. Trump has previously claimed Americans would receive checks that never materialized, and some polling shows voters are skeptical. With Election Day less than a month away, President Donald Trump is touting two federal cash-payment programs already underway while renewing a much larger $5,000 check promise contingent on Republicans retaining Congress. On Friday, Trump announced one-time $90 payments to 20.8 million Medicare beneficiaries. A day later, he revived an earlier promise to give every adult U.S. citizen $5,000 — but only if Republicans retain control of Congress in November. "If Republicans win the House of Representatives and the Senate in the 2026 Midterm Elections, I'm going to give all Adult Citizens in the United States of America, $5,000," Trump said in a Truth Social video post Saturday. The president made a similar pledge at the Republican National Committee's first midterm convention in Dallas last month. Trump hasn't provided any details on who would authorize the payments and where the money would come from. Those claims came on the heels of $500 Obamacare "refund" checks that began going out last week to roughly 950,000 people who bought unsubsidized coverage through the federal marketplace. The $90 payments to certain eligible Medicare Part B enrollees are scheduled to arrive this month, funded through the Medicare Improvement Fund. The $500 Obamacare payments are already being distributed to certain full-price HealthCare.gov customers. A Reuters analysis found 71% of the Obamacare money — $339 million — is going to residents of 13 states with some of the country's most competitive Senate and gubernatorial races, though eligibility is based on insurance status, not voting status. Together, the flurry of offers of direct cash payments comes as Republicans head into the final stretch of a midterm campaign dominated by concerns about prices and the economy . But the $5,000 "Trump dividend" remains just a promise and Trump has been extremely light on details, particularly on where the money would come from and who would need to authorize it. Sending $5,000 to every adult citizen would cost roughly $1.2 trillion and require congressional approval. Some Republicans have also raised concerns about its effect on the deficit and inflation. Rep. David Schweikert, R-Ariz., told Reuters last month he would "throw everything of my heart and soul" into stopping the proposal, warning it could push interest rates higher. And Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., called the plan a "political bribe" in a Sept. 10 interview with CNN , and said Congress controls federal spending. The White House and offices of Reps. David Schweikert, R-Ariz., and Jamie Raskin, D-Md., did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Inside the China espionage case that ensnared former Fed advisor John Rogers AI's coming roadblock in regulation: Antitrust hawks Trump holds up to $1 billion in bonds tied to institutions he can affect Rep. James Comer expands House investigation into prediction market insider trading Polling suggests the idea isn't a sure-fire political winner. A Rasmussen Reports survey found likely voters essentially split, 47% to 48%, on the proposal. Just 15% said it would affect their vote. A Marquette Law School poll in Wisconsin found 70% opposed the payments, while an Economist/YouGov survey found 57% of registered voters doubted Trump would actually deliver them even if Republicans retained Congress. In the past, Trump has made several promises to send cash payments to Americans — and didn't deliver. In February 2025, the Trump administration floated a $5,000 "DOGE dividend" check, claiming the money would come from savings from the cuts enacted by the now-defunct, Elon Musk -led "Department of Government Efficiency." Those payments never materialized. Then, in November, Trump proposed a reciprocal tariff -funded dividend payment of at least $2,000 per person . The Supreme Court struck down the tariffs in February of this year, and no checks were ever issued. The pattern of offering cash payments directly to voters stretches back to Trump's first term. Six weeks before the 2020 election, Trump promised 33 million Medicare beneficiaries $200 prescription-drug cards "in coming weeks" — but the cards never went out . Still, the Trump administration delivered a $1,776 " Warrior Dividend " to roughly 1.5 million service members last year, and Congress approved pandemic stimulus payments during his first term.

events.title: Scoop: White House monitors suspected plague outbreak in Russia
events.summary: The White House is monitoring reports of a suspected plague case and related quarantines in Russia, a Trump administration official told Axios on Sunday. Driving the news: Russian health authorities have taken precautionary measures in response to the death of a woman who worked at an anti-plague research factility, but have not confirmed that she contracted plague. What they're saying: The Trump administration "is aware, monitoring the outbreak, and assessing options," the administration official said. The backstory: On Sept. 25, 28-year-old Daria Shipilova, who worked at an anti-plague research institute in Russia's Irkutsk region, broke a test tube containing the pneumonic plague pathogen, local reports said. Shipilova was admitted to a hospital on Sept. 29 with symptoms of severe pneumonia and died overnight between Oct. 1 and Oct. 2. After her death, authorities imposed quarantines at several medical facilities in the region and placed nearly 200 people who had come into contact with Shiplova under medical observation. Irkutsk Gov. Igor Kobzev said those being monitored showed no signs of illness and had tested negative. Russian media reports suggested Shipilova may have contracted pneumonic plague, but health authorities have not confirmed the diagnosis. Russia's public health agency said Shipilova had "pneumonia of unknown etiology" and that further testing found no microorganisms linked to her work. The agency said the epidemiological situation in the region remains stable. Zoom out: Plague is a potentially life-threatening bacterial disease but can be cured with antibiotics when treated promptly, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention . White House spokespeople referred questions to the State Department, which did not respond to a request for comment.

events.title: Can ‘super intelligence’ and a non-binding safety pact solve AI’s image problem?
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. President Donald Trump hosted many of the biggest names in artificial intelligence this week — in part to announce that the U.S. government isn’t calling it artificial intelligence anymore. Now it’s super intelligence. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and I discussed the motivation behind the meeting and what effect it might have on the AI industry. We were all pretty skeptical that the “Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities” that the executives signed will amount to much, especially since — as Sean noted — it’s “deeply non-binding,” at least from a legal prospective. (Instead, Trump said he considers it “morally binding.”) Kirsten suggested that the meeting’s real significance may have been as “a rebranding effort around AI.” (An effort that continued this weekend with Trump’s announcement of a new Super Intelligence Force .) For her, the big message was, “AI is going to kill us, it’s scary, it is going to take jobs — but super intelligence is not.” Keep reading for a preview of our conversation , edited for length and clarity. Anthony Ha: Officially, by order of the president of the United States, it’s not artificial intelligence anymore, it’s super intelligence. We were talking about this last week , because this is something [Trump has] been hinting at — he doesn’t do hints, he’s been saying [it] for a while. But now it’s signed into executive order. If you’re an official U.S. representative, you are supposed to say super intelligence, not artificial intelligence. And this was also part of this broader announcement around AI safety, which I think is both interesting for this pact that was announced, but also the fact that it happened at all. It seemed to have come together fairly quickly, because just two weeks ago, a week ago, President Trump was saying, “We don’t need any of this, we need to lead in AI, we can’t constrain it in any way, we don’t need any regulation, anyone who’s saying that there’s any danger from AI is essentially a Chinese or Democratic plant.” And yet all these AI CEOs got together with him earlier this week and signed this pact. Kirsten Korosec: Leading up to that, we should say, not only was there pushback on regulation, and we can talk about whether this executive order even does any of that — I would say no, there’s a little bit of theater there — but the important and interesting thing is that just days ago, Anthropic was really in the doghouse, if you will, in terms of what was happening behind the scenes with President Trump. That all changed when [Anthropic CEO] Dario Amodei was invited to a 10 p.m. dinner. He had this sit-down, and then just days later, we had this luncheon, and at this luncheon, we have pretty much every tech power broker from every major tech company that exists. So Mark Zuckerberg was there, Jeff Bezos was there, Elon Musk was there, Dario of course was there, they were all there. I’m wondering if any of you watched the press conference that happened afterwards, which there’s been many, many memes about, because of the interesting, funny behavior when you bring a bunch of tech CEOs together. But I guess my bigger question for both of you is: What does this all mean? And does it mean anything? Sean O’Kane: How much time do you have? First off, sure, they had dinner, Trump and Dario. If you read the Time magazine interview that Trump just did, your guess is as good as mine as to how informed he was that that dinner was even going to be happening, which is a strange reality to live in, but it’s just the one we inhabit. I will also say one other thing that makes me skeptical — surprise, surprise — of how repaired the relationship is between the administration and Anthropic, is that for as much as there are clearly people trying to put those two groups together, the Defense Department is still very adamant that Anthropic is terrible and woke and and a national security risk. Emil Michael goes off on Anthropic every other day on X, it seems. I think there’s still some distance there despite Dario showing up to this thing. As far as the agreement and all of that, let’s be real, they misspelled the United States on the agreement that they all signed. It is also just deeply non-binding. I mean, it is completely voluntary. I think my favorite aspect about it was that Trump described it as quote “morally binding,” which is just a level of abstraction and terminology that I’ve never heard of before. Anthony: In terms of Anthropic and their relationship with the Trump administration, there’s been a sort of a lot of reporting, especially during that big blow up with the Defense Department, that different parts of the White House had different relationships with Anthropic.

events.title: Persian Gulf oil flows return to prewar levels, but Iran could resort to a ‘scorched earth campaign’ as U.S. deploys more ships and Marines to Mideast
events.summary: Iran is losing leverage over the Strait of Hormuz as oil exports recover under the protection of the U.S. military, but the Islamic Republic is unlikely to stand by and watch while its own economy crumbles. This past week, JPMorgan said Middle East crude exports reached about 17.5 million barrels per day, or 98% of prewar levels. Goldman Sachs was even more bullish, estimating that exports from Persian Gulf producers hit 19 million barrels per day. Similarly, Kpler declared Gulf crude exports have recovered to prewar levels, though it said the September number was at least 16.5 million barrels. “The recovery has reshaped regional oil logistics,” it said on Wednesday. “Around 40% of crude now leaves without crossing Hormuz, up from 17% before the war, as Saudi Arabia and the UAE make greater use of pipeline routes. Of the crude that crossed Hormuz in August, more than 70% changed tankers offshore. The volumes have recovered, but through a fundamentally different export system.” While crude prices remain high, with refined fuels like diesel suffering an even worse shock, the rebound in Gulf oil flows has come despite the U.S. naval blockade keeping Iran’s exports at essentially zero. President Donald Trump and others in his administration have touted the numbers, boasting the U.S. now controls the strait and predicting Iran’s economy will soon come completely undone. But analysts have warned the Iranian regime, facing an existential threat to its rule, could re-escalate the war and reassert its grip on the oil trade. In fact, attacks on commercial ships in the Gulf have been on the rise in recent days. While the U.S. military is protecting ships and has degraded Iran’s ability to target them, drones and missiles still find their marks on occasion. The attacks haven’t deterred all tankers from making the risky transit, but they keep shipping and insurance costs high, preventing the market from fully returning to normal. Esfandyar Batmanghelidj, founder and CEO of the Bourse & Bazaar Foundation think tank, argued Iran’s influence over the region’s energy trade isn’t limited to the Strait of Hormuz. He pointed out Iran can still destroy oil infrastructure, such as drilling and refining capacity—and can escalate if “Trump isn’t feeling enough pain to take the diplomatic off-ramps being put in front of him.” Indeed, Trump has rejected Tehran’s offer to restart talks with a seven-day ceasefire that would fully reopen the strait in exchange for the U.S. lifting its blockade and unfreezing assets. Rather than return to diplomacy, Trump expects to start bombing Iran again after the U.S. midterm elections are over, sources told the Wall Street Journal . Meanwhile, he is also deploying the USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier and the USS Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group, comprised of three amphibious ships and the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit, to the Middle East. U.S. Navy Wasp-class amphibious assault ship USS Makin Island (LHD 8), front, and San Antonio-class amphibious transport dock ship USS John P. Murtha (LPD 26), sail in formation during routine training off the coast of California, Aug. 23, 2026. U.S. Marine Corps photo by Lance Cpl. Fernando Cruz Martinez “So while the risk premium around oil flows may seem tolerable for Trump, the threats to energy production infrastructure in the Gulf remain significant, which is exactly why regional countries are still trying to mediate a return to a durable ceasefire and diplomatic agreement,” Batmanghelidj posted on X on Monday. “Trump too, is erratic, and could give cause to Iran to escalate in this way through his own fixation on ‘winning’ the war.” He added that Iran’s attacks on U.S. bases in the Mideast as well as on Gulf cities and infrastructure were far more consequential as they highlighted the U.S. failure to mitigate or degrade the threat. So while the U.S. military can keep oil flowing, it’s no longer able to guarantee security across the Gulf region, providing Iran leverage in any negotiations, Batmanghelidj said. “Iran did not wage a scorched earth campaign—but it may yet do so if the current situation persists for too long,” he warned. “That is what everyone who actually follows this region and its dynamics is worried about.” Of course, Iran’s own oil infrastructure would also face destruction as the U.S. and its Gulf allies retaliate. For now, Trump has signaled he will let his economic warfare against Iran play out, and the U.S. tightened its sanctions further last month, making it harder for Tehran to move money through front companies and other shadowy intermediaries. As Iran’s ability to generate oil revenue fades, the currency has plunged to new lows , and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian complained the regime’s money in China is blocked. “We can’t even get our own money out of a country to which we’ve supplied goods, let alone using those funds to pay someone else in another corner of the world,” he told Fox News  last week. events.title: Meet David Robinson, the OpenAI safety leader who quit and warned that the company isn’t careful enough
events.summary: David Robinson led safety transparency at OpenAI. Now he's speaking out against the company. Reuters David Robinson, formerly OpenAI's safety lead, has long been interested in rules around technology. Robinson quit OpenAI this week and said the AI giant is moving too fast without regard for safety. Robinson said he would now work from outside the company to strengthen safety incentives. David Robinson, a leader on OpenAI's Safety Systems team who quit the company this week, once had ambitions to bring philosophy to journalism. A Rhodes Scholar, Robinson graduated from Princeton in 2004 with a degree in philosophy. At Princeton, he led the school newspaper's opinion section. In a 2003 interview with the Daily Princetonian, Robinson said he wanted to be the kind of reporter who "tells you what the facts are and then gets to the philosophical differences that explain the situation." Now, Robinson's name is in the headlines — and a notable byline. He left OpenAI, the same week three other safety researchers were fired , and issued a blistering essay for The Atlantic about what he said is OpenAI's inadequate approach to safety. "I agree with other recently departed staff that the companies building this technology aren't being nearly careful enough," Robinson wrote in the essay. Neither Robinson nor the  PR firm he said he hired  responded to Business Insider's requests for comment. A review of his published essays, interviews, and books dating back to his days as an undergraduate paints a picture of a man deeply concerned with the impact of technology on humanity. "All through my life, I've been fascinated by the rules that surround technology and how we decide when and how we're going to use it," he said in a 2022 interview on the Princeton Alumni Weekly podcast. From journalism to tech policy Robinson grew up in Potomac, M.D., an affluent suburb of Washington, D.C. As a child in the 1990s with a mild case of cerebral palsy, Robinson said his teachers created a new rule that allowed him to use a word processor in lieu of pen and paper. "Ever since then, I've been interested in the social impacts of new digital technologies," he said in a UC Berkeley interview in 2021. During summers as an undergrad at Princeton, he interned at Time Magazine and The Wall Street Journal, according to his LinkedIn page. He told the Daily Princetonian in 2003 that after gaining experience as a reporter, he hoped to write for a literary magazine like The New Yorker or Harper's. After Princeton, Robinson got a degree in philosophy, politics, and economics at Oxford before returning to Princeton to start a research center about the relation between technology and public policy . "Part of the idea was that, if you're navigating the policy and the values choices that come up around new technologies, it's a big help to have some real depth of technical expertise," he said in the Berkeley interview. In 2011, Robinson and a colleague from Princeton founded Upturn, an organization that aimed to use algorithmic technologies to make government data more accessible. He joined OpenAI after lecturing tech execs about ethics After research and teaching roles at several universities and a one-year tenure as a faculty director at Apple University , where Robinson gave seminars for Apple executives on the ethical questions prompted by new technologies, Robinson joined OpenAI in 2023. Originally the head of policy planning at the ChatGPT's maker, Robinson wrote in a LinkedIn post announcing his new position that "I look forward to helping shape OpenAI's engagement in the broader AI policy debate, at this critical moment." In a 2023 appearance at the AI Governance Summit hosted by the World Economic Forum, Robinson said OpenAI performs robust safety checks before releasing models and that the company wasn't solely motivated by profit. "We believe in deploying gradually and then learning as we go," he said. Recently, however, Robinson has posted concerns on X about OpenAI's ability to balance safety with increasingly advanced models. "Things @openai are indeed changing significantly by the day, but I do not know whether we are changing fast enough," he said last month. "I think it is still true, as @hilbertspaess puts it, that many of us 'have not deeply internalized the civilizational stakes.'" Then, on Friday, Business Insider exclusively reported that Robinson was out at the company. The next day, he published a lengthy essay in the Atlantic explaining why he left. What's next for Robinson? Robinson's departure follows that of Jacob Coxon , a former Anthropic engineer who quit last month and warned that AI could cause mass extinction. In his Atlantic essay, Robinson addressed the argument that he could do more to improve safety by staying at OpenAI than by leaving. Robinson wrote that, by working on the outside, he "can help more people understand the risks I saw, and strengthen the incentives OpenAI and other firms have to be safer." He said he chose to leave because "as the company sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the level of care that I believe is needed." In response to Robinson's essay, an OpenAI spokesperson said in a statement that the company is working to ensure that AI models don't outpace the safety measures it has implemented. "As our models become more capable, we continue to strengthen our safety and security practices to address the risks we see today while building safety cases to anticipate the risks of future advances," the spokesperson said. "We're making sure our models don't become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down." events.title: Are Coles and Woolworths centralising their supply chains? Some experts think so
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Coles, Woolworths supply chain tactic driving small farms out, producer says When middlemen or wholesalers are involved in trade agreements with major supermarkets, small producers have "no power", says one grower. ( ABC News: Hamed Akrami ) A small-scale banana farmer who has had his agreement to supply Coles ended due to the supermarket simplifying its supply chain says the move signals the end of small-scale farms across the country. Industry experts have claimed Coles and Woolworths are centralising their supply chains in a bid to cut costs. Some experts worry producers will become more vulnerable if supermarkets continue to do so. After 30 years of selling bananas to Coles, New South Wales farmer Amrit Singh believes the supermarket's decision to stop buying his produce signals a possible end for small, family-run farms like his. In the past two months, Coles and Woolworths confirmed they would pull various local products from their shelves, with suppliers told the decisions were due to changes to the supply chain. Amrit Singh says small-scale growers are "price takers", not price makers. ( ABC News: Samuel O'Brien ) Industry experts have said major Australian supermarkets are centralising their supply chains in a bid to cut costs, warning some producers could now be at greater risk of having their products removed from supermarket shelves. Woolworths said its supply chain network had expanded, while Coles rejected the experts' claims. An inquiry by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) into supermarkets last year found Coles and Woolworths had overwhelming power in their trade relationships with suppliers. Amrit Singh labelled Coles's decision to pull local bananas from its shelves as "anti-competitive" and said supermarkets should be encouraging diversity in growing regions. ( ABC News: Giulio Saggin ) In August, Coles confirmed it would stop selling Coffs Coast bananas, pumpkins and cucumbers in an effort to simplify its supply chain. While Tasmanians can shop at 17 Coles and 32 Woolworth supermarkets, there are no Aldi stores — and that won't be changing anytime soon, according to the company CEO. Mr Singh sold his bananas indirectly to Coles through a wholesaler, an agreement he said was worth hundreds of thousands of dollars a year. The produce is now expected to come from north Queensland, but Mr Singh believes his business is too small to compete with north Queensland's banana industry. "Freight costs [involved in] getting access to those [new] markets are going to be extremely high," he said. Mr Singh said farmers who did not sell directly to supermarkets had "no power" to negotiate trade agreements and were forced to reduce prices to support promotions and specials. Coles says keeping its supply chain efficient helps it absorb costs and reduce the impact on grocery prices. ( ABC News ) Rise in 'middlemen' leaves farmers vulnerable NSW Farmers Association principal economist Samuel Miller said supermarket giants had long been centralising their supply chains. He said one way they were doing this was through buying produce from packhouses or "middlemen" — selling on behalf of a group of growers — instead of directly from them. "When those supermarkets make a decision like consolidating their suppliers or rejecting some produce … it affects not just that supplier in the middle, but it can affect dozens, 40 or 50 other farmers down the line." Samuel Miller says supermarkets have a large share of the market, so they hold negotiating power. ( Supplied: Samuel Miller ) In a statement to the ABC, Coles said it continued to source directly from a range of Australian producers. "In fresh produce, aggregators are not new and have long played an important role in Australia," a spokesperson said. In August, Woolworths confirmed it would stop selling Tasmanian beef in stores around the country from early next year. ( ABC News: Laurissa Smith ) Queensland University of Technology retail marketing professor Gary Mortimer said meat was one of the main supply chains where processing had been centralised, citing Woolworths's decision to stop selling Tasmanian beef from early next year. Gary Mortimer says supermarkets centralising their processing can give shoppers greater product consistency. ( Supplied: Gary Mortimer ) Some suppliers said they were told this was due to rising production and shipping costs. "Over the last 10 to 15 years, what we've seen is that reduction of in-store processing back to centralised processing," Professor Mortimer said. "Less trade butchers in stores and more of that processing taking place centrally.

events.title: ‘Avengers: Endgame’ is the biggest movie ever again, 7 years later—and it says a lot about the future of Hollywood’s IP machine
events.summary: Seven years after it first hit theaters, “Avengers: Endgame” is once again the highest-grossing movie of all time. Disney and Marvel Studios brought the 2019 blockbuster back to theaters on Sept. 25 as “Avengers: Endgame Encore.” The new version adds a few minutes of footage teasing December’s “Avengers: Doomsday,” plus an introduction from Robert Downey Jr. and Chris Evans. It topped the box office right away, grossing $26 million domestically and $86 million worldwide in its opening weekend. That’s the third-best domestic debut ever for a rerelease, behind only the 1997 special edition of “Star Wars” and the 2011 3D release of “The Lion King.” The Encore beat “Resident Evil” in its second weekend and outgrossed three new non-franchise releases: “Heart of the Beast,” “Primetime,” and “Forgotten Island.” The run cooled quickly. Domestic ticket sales fell more than 80% in the second weekend. But by then the Encore had already done what it needed to do. It added another $18.8 million worldwide this weekend, bringing the rerelease to roughly $126 million globally. That lifts “Endgame’s” lifetime total to $2.9255 billion, just ahead of James Cameron’s “Avatar” at $2.9237 billion. “Endgame” first took the title from “Avatar” in 2019, then lost it in 2021 when “Avatar” was rereleased in China. Rereleases rarely earn more than $10 million, according to box office analyst David A. Gross. “Endgame” has been available to stream for years, and it still outdrew a slate of new movies. That suggests Hollywood’s intellectual property machine is far from slowing down. It also suggests the future of moviegoing may look more familiar than it seemed at the start of the summer. In 2019, when “Endgame” first dominated the box office, nine films grossed more than $1 billion worldwide. Every one of them was a sequel, remake, or spinoff of existing IP. Hollywood has spent the years since trying to recapture that success. The pandemic and the streaming wars upended moviegoing habits. Big swings from once-reliable franchises like Marvel, DC, and, most recently, Star Wars failed to match the critical or commercial success they enjoyed in the previous decade. Marvel, the biggest franchise of the 2010s, saw a steep decline after “Endgame.” Before the pandemic, the studio’s biggest releases routinely approached or cleared $1 billion. Between 2020 and this summer, only two Marvel movies crossed that mark: “Spider-Man: No Way Home” and “Deadpool & Wolverine.” Last year, “Captain America: Brave New World,” “Thunderbolts*,” and “The Fantastic Four: First Steps” grossed roughly $1.3 billion combined. That’s less than half of what “Endgame” made on its own. For audiences who want Hollywood to invest in new ideas, this summer first looked like a turning point. Two YouTube creators-turned-directors broke out in a big way. Curry Barker’s “Obsession” was made for under $1 million and has grossed more than $500 million worldwide. Kane Parsons’ “Backrooms,” which the 20-year-old adapted from his own web series, became A24’s biggest hit ever. Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” became a cultural phenomenon , showing that audiences would turn out in droves for something ambitious and unique. Meanwhile, movies based on legacy IP floundered. “Masters of the Universe,” “Supergirl,” and “Star Wars: The Mandalorian and Grogu” all underperformed. Even newer franchises lagged: “Minions & Monsters” and “The Super Mario Galaxy Movie” both trailed their predecessors. Disney’s “The Devil Wears Prada 2” was the outlier, riding nostalgia to nearly $700 million worldwide. Consequently, originality briefly had Hollywood’s ear. Tide turns back to franchises Then the tide started turning back toward familiar waters. “Toy Story 5” opened to $312 million globally , a franchise record. Its domestic debut was the second-biggest ever for an animated film, behind only “Incredibles 2.” It went on to gross more than $1.14 billion worldwide , passing “Toy Story 4.” The 31-year-old franchise clearly wasn’t out of gas. “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” arrived on July 31 and eased fears of superhero fatigue. It set a record with a $168 million opening day and held the No. 1 spot for six straight weekends. That’s the longest streak since “Avatar: The Way of Water.” The film has now grossed about $2.5 billion worldwide . That makes it the highest-grossing domestic release ever and the third-biggest movie of all time globally. Sony distributes the Spider-Man films, but Marvel Studios co-produces them and they’re part of the Marvel Cinematic Universe. That bodes well for “Avengers: Doomsday.” All of this leads to the current moment, in which a seven-year-old movie returned to theaters and beat new releases. It caps a summer of box office whiplash, and the back-and-forth isn’t over. This weekend, Tom Cruise and Alejandro G. Iñárritu’s big-budget original comedy “Digger” bombed with an $8 million domestic opening. The weekend’s winner was “Verity,” an adaptation of Colleen Hoover’s bestselling novel. On Oct. 23, Laika’s “Wildwood” and DC Studios’ “Clayface” open on the same day. “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” follows on Nov. 20. Then “Doomsday” and “Dune: Part Three” go head-to-head on Dec. 18. The 2026 summer box office brought in a record $4.76 billion domestically. That’s the biggest summer ever before adjusting for inflation, and nearly 10% ahead of 2019. IP like “Spider-Man” and “Toy Story” played an undeniable role. But non-franchise titles “The Odyssey,” “Michael,” “Project Hail Mary,” and “Obsession” all rank among the year’s 10 highest-grossing releases worldwide . “Backrooms” and Pixar’s original “Hoppers” sit at Nos. 11 and 12, both ahead of “The Mandalorian and Grogu” at No. 13. Screenwriter William Goldman famously summed up Hollywood in three words: “Nobody knows anything.” Coming out of this summer, it certainly rings true. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: In Connecticut, my husband and I mostly talked logistics. In Spain, we started dating each other again.
events.summary: The author and her family moved from the US to Spain. Courtesy of the author We sold our house in Connecticut and got rid of most of our belongings before moving abroad. Starting over in Spain brought plenty of stress and uncertainty. Depending on each other through it has ultimately strengthened our relationship. One year ago, my husband left his 18-year teaching career behind, we sold our house, got rid of 95% of our belongings, and moved our family from Connecticut to Madrid. These days, we live in a small flat with our 7 and 10-year-old boys. We don't own a car. We're learning Spanish one day at a time. On paper, that much upheaval could've broken us. Instead, it's brought us closer than ever. We were coexisting, not connecting Back in the US, my husband Jeff and I were coexisting more than connecting. Most conversations revolved around logistics : who was taking which kid to which activity, what meeting we needed to attend, and what to make for dinner. By the time the boys were in bed, we were too spent to connect meaningfully. We'd sit beside one another, exhausted, on our phones or trying to watch a movie we never finished because one of us always fell asleep. The author says in the US, she and her spouse weren't connecting. Courtesy of the author I never imagined that would be our marriage. Yet, there we were. Moving to Spain made us reevaluate things Here in Spain, we're still busy. Arguably busier. We spend about three hours a day getting the kids to and from school via train and bus. But we're also spending far more time together than before — and it's given us more opportunities to connect beyond logistics. Part of what's driven this connection, too, is watching the locals go about their day around us. "Busy" doesn't mean the same thing here as it does in the US. It's not a reason to delay the connection. People stop for each other mid-errand, midday, without apologizing. They make the time. We started doing the same. Stopping for an unplanned coffee or a caña. Exploring a new neighborhood hand-in-hand just because. Taking a few extra minutes for us instead of rushing on to the to-do. It's made more of a difference than I expected. You don't have to move abroad to do this, of course. You just have to decide that the list can wait. Going through the unknown together It's just the four of us now. We need each other in a way we didn't before (and that's not automatically a good thing). Being each other's only support can bring out the best in a marriage , or the worst. This past year tested us more than once. Jeff spent months in a 600-hour language course, while simultaneously trying to find work and switch off his student visa before it expired. Between the exhaustion of full-time language study and the pressure of a ticking clock, it would have been easy for that stress to become tension between us. And some days, it did. Navigating new rules, a new language, and a hundred small unknowns daily—it's hard. I won't pretend it's not. But we kept showing up for each other anyway, and we came out stronger. A weekly ritual that's helped One thing that's anchored us through this new chapter is a practice we started years ago in the US. After our second son was born, I created a marriage meeting journal. We'd answer 10 questions together and document the answers. Questions like: What's something your partner did last week that made your life easier? What support do you need this week? Are there any goals or commitments you could use your partner's help with? Is there something in our relationship or home that needs attention? How will we connect as a couple this week? It's nothing fancy, but it's an hour that keeps us sailing in the same direction — even more important now that we're living abroad. We still do it most Sunday mornings. And while it was technically my idea, Jeff loves it as much as I do. If we let it slide, he points it out. You don't need to do it weekly or answer all 10. You could start tonight, with one question. After the move, we also started something new: short day-dates. After Jeff's last class of the week, we'd meet up for a drink, lunch, and a rose garden stroll. Nothing grand, and sometimes, it costs nothing. It was another block of intentional time to connect. I don't know what that will look like this year now that he's secured a teaching position, but I know we'll find some version of it — because it matters. The part we didn't see coming If you'd asked me before we moved what I thought would change, I'd have said: the language, the culture, the community we'd build, the places we'd explore. I never would have guessed how much closer we've become. And it didn't stop with our marriage. Evening strolls through the plaza with just a ball or hacky sack to pass among the four of us. Morning hikes and long talks with my oldest. Word searches and laughing with my 7-year-old on the ride home from school. We didn't plan for any of that. It might be the best part of the whole move. events.title: Australia's fossil fuel expansion 'slap in the face' to Pacific nations
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Pacific leaders challenge Australia's fossil fuel expansion ahead of pre-COP31 talks in Fiji Marica and Sami have been living in a tent for five years, waiting for their village to be rebuilt. ( ABC News: Lice Monovo ) As she sits crossed legged on the floor inside a large tent, 66-year-old Marica Malumuca describes the place she's called home for the past five years. "When it rains heavily it feels like we're living in a balloon because we can see the parts of the tent bulging where it's filling up," she said. Ms Malumuca's village, Nabavatu, was declared unsafe in 2021 after two cyclones cracked the ground beneath it, and she was moved to a temporary settlement in Savadrua. There are 37 tents at the temporary site. Some can fit three people and others accommodate up to seven. Ms Malumuca's son, Sami Veloko, moved home from the city to look after her as they wait for Nabavatu to be rebuilt. Pacific communities are already feeling the impacts of climate change. ( ABC News: Lice Monovo ) "Those people who stay in these tents, they used to stay in a good house; a cement house, a wooden house of a high quality," he said. "You cannot believe — even they themselves cannot believe — that they stay in this kind of tent." Small island states are already being disproportionately affected by displacement as climate change drives more extreme weather. The United Nations warned the impacts of tropical cyclones have become more severe due to rising sea levels and an increase in heavy precipitation. More than half of Pacific Island countries' infrastructure is located in coastal areas at risk from rising seas, which happens as higher temperatures melt glaciers and ice sheets. Nabavatu is yet to be rebuilt, five years after it was damaged by cyclones. ( ABC News: Lice Monovo ) As world leaders prepare to descend on Mr Veloko's home country for high-level climate talks, he has a message for them. "We are getting the effect of climate change and we are the vulnerable people, the Pacific people," he said. "Because of what they have contributed to carbon dioxide, the industrialisation that they have developed in their countries, we are getting the worst of it." Climate diplomacy at heart of security strategy Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will join global leaders at the pre-COP event, which will feature preparatory talks ahead of next month's United Nations COP31 climate summit. Australia has led the charge for the lead-up talks to be held in the Pacific and is spending millions of dollars on the event as part of its broader regional security strategy to become the "partner of choice" for the Pacific islands. Anthony Albanese attended the 2026 Pacific Island Forum in early September. ( ABC News: Mark Moore ) The Albanese government has vigorously pursued a series of bilateral security deals with Pacific nations since coming to office including Vanuatu, Fiji, Tuvalu, Nauru and Papua New Guinea, with almost all of them including commitments to act on climate change. According to the Lowy Institute, Australia remains the Pacific's largest bilateral donor and biggest development partner , having spent almost $19 billion of a committed $20.6 billion. Wes Morgan, a research associate with the Institute for Climate Risk and Response at UNSW who lived and worked in the Pacific for more than a decade, said the federal government understood that to become the Pacific's partner of choice it must act on the region's key security threat. "That is why there has been the inclusion of commitments on climate change in these bilateral security arrangements, but more broadly why Australia is working with Pacific island countries to drive global action on climate change," he said. "That's why Australia had its hand up to host the UN climate talks with the Pacific." For Pacific islands like Ebeye, rising oceans caused by the continued burning of fossil fuels is a real and acute problem. ( Supplied: Hall Contracting ) But Dr Morgan said Australia remaining one of the world's largest fossil fuel exporters "flies in the face of the narrative Australia's pursuing with Pacific Island countries". "Australia's biggest contribution to the climate crisis is the export of coal and gas, so the emissions associated with Australia's exports of coal and gas more than doubled the emissions from Australia's entire domestic economy," he said. Can Australia be both a gas giant and a climate leader? Seven years after it was first mooted, the extension of Australia's biggest gas project could not have landed at a more critical juncture for the nation's climate credentials.

events.title: Trump’s Ohio rally gets quiet after he defends data centers — a toxic political issue with bipartisan opposition. ‘You can’t just turn them off’
events.summary: President Donald Trump on Saturday defended data centers that power artificial intelligence projects but have become a contentious campaign issue nationwide, as he took his midterm tour to Ohio to insist his party will keep its majorities in Congress despite steep political headwinds . Trump took several minutes during his campaign rally in southwestern Ohio to promote his administration’s action on data centers, saying he was seeking to ensure they “benefit local communities” and praising Republican Sen. Jon Husted for an ill-fated attempt to push forward legislation on the issue. “Look, there’s so much money to be made for Ohio. You can’t just turn them off. They’ll go to China,” Trump said, repeating his defense of data centers that he had made before. The crowd, which had reacted enthusiastically as the president talked about other policies, was far more muted during the data centers remark. The massive warehouse campuses generating energy for AI projects have become a  toxic political issue, drawing bipartisan opposition  in races across the country, with voters concerned about their impact on electricity prices, farmland and water supplies. It’s become especially acute in Ohio, where Husted has been repeatedly attacked for his role in attracting data centers to Ohio as lieutenant governor. Trump is embarking on what he says will be a 32-day blitz ahead of the  Nov. 3 elections , hitting the  deep red states  of Texas, Oklahoma and Alabama this week before pivoting to Ohio, a  battleground state  that’s home to one of the top-tier Senate races this cycle. Husted — who was appointed to fill the Senate vacancy left by now-Vice President JD Vance — is running to win the seat outright. There is likely no path to a Senate majority for Democrats without flipping Ohio, where former  three-term Sen. Sherrod Brown  is trying to return to the Senate after losing to Republican Bernie Moreno two years ago. Since last year, Democrats have listed Ohio, along with states such as North Carolina and Maine, as key races to win control of the Senate. And this past week, the head of the Senate GOP’s campaign arm said Ohio is among 10 battleground races that are “within striking distance.” “The good news for us is that Jon Husted is a closer,”  Sen. Tim Scott,  the chairman of the National Republican Senatorial Committee, told reporters. “We’re seeing the gap that was there between the two candidates, which was just a few points, now it is right at a dead-even race. So this is as tight as ticks, as we say in South Carolina.” Data centers are a hot issue in the Ohio race At his rallies, Trump has been trying to convince voters that the economy is better than they feel it is, even though  polls show Americans are frustrated  with the way he’s handled it. The  high cost of living, including gas prices  elevated by Trump’s war on Iran, is a top issue in the Dayton area, too. And just days before Trump’s rally,  nearly 1,400 people were laid off  from a truck factory in nearby Springfield. “Your state is booming. Every — I hate to say it — every state is booming,” Trump insisted Saturday. “They’re all booming.” Trump’s rally comes as Republicans worry that Husted’s campaign has failed to adequately catch fire with voters in the Republican-dominated state. Brown and allied groups have hammered Husted for his data-centers role, and the NRSC has pinpointed it as a political vulnerability. The GOP-controlled Senate  tried to advance legislation  this past week sponsored by Husted that would ask utility regulators to effectively charge large power users more, as consumers  struggle with high energy costs . But it was blocked by nearly all Democrats. “You got to remember, Sherrod Brown was for data centers, and Jon Husted is for data centers being responsible,” Scott told reporters this week. “If a community doesn’t want them, he doesn’t want them either.” But Trump has become one of  data centers’ most vocal proponents , shrugging aside voter concerns and arguing that the U.S. cannot cede advancements in AI to China. “Senator Jon Husted gave billions in tax breaks to Big Tech to make sure they would build their data centers in Ohio,” Brown wrote on X on Friday, ahead of Trump’s visit. “Now, he’s making Ohioans foot the bill.” Brown’s campaign also has hammered Husted for donations he’s received from  retail magnate Les Wexner,  who once employed the late convicted sex offender  Jeffrey Epstein.  Husted has donated remaining Wexner contributions to an anti-human trafficking charity. There were several Epstein-themed signs outside the Vandalia school where the rally was being held, as more than a hundred protesters lined the road with a slew of anti-Trump and anti-Husted signs. But inside the school’s gymnasium, the boisterous crowd — decked out in red “Make America Great Again” hats and “Trump 47” jerseys — greeted each Republican candidate enthusiastically as they awaited the president’s arrival. From the stage, Husted said the state had been through “hard times,” noting his dad had worked at a factory that closed down. But he said Republicans in the state had turned it around. “We now have the most jobs and the lowest unemployment rate we’ve ever had in the history of Ohio,” he said. Meanwhile, in the governor’s race, Republican Vivek Ramaswamy faces Democrat Dr. Amy Acton, the state’s former COVID-era health director. A wealthy biotech entrepreneur and 2024 presidential candidate, Ramaswamy’s star appeal among conservatives led to quick backing by Ohio Republicans and hopes of an easy victory in the Republican-dominated state. However, despite a massive fundraising lead and more than $12 million spent in campaign advertising, he is now locked in a close fight with Acton with weeks to go until Election Day. “I’m so grateful to this state and to this country for giving a kid like me opportunities that would not have been available to my family in any other country on planet earth,” Ramaswamy said at the rally ahead of Trump’s arrival, as he underscored the American dream for his Indian immigrant family. events.title: Lina Khan says AI companies are following the same playbook that got Big Tech into trouble
events.summary: Former Federal Trade Commission Chair Lina Khan said the AI industry shouldn't self-regulate. Alexi J. Rosenfeld/Getty Images Former FTC chair Lina Khan doesn't believe AI companies can effectively self-regulate. She referenced Big Tech's attempt with social media, calling it "a proven failure." The Trump administration isn't keen on implementing federal-level guardrails. Lina Khan has some advice for AI companies attempting to self-regulate the advancing tech. The former Federal Trade Commission chair said doing so would be a fool's errand during an interview on ABC's "This Week." "We've seen that self-regulation efforts by Big Tech have been a proven failure," Khan said on Sunday. "We need to remember what happened a decade ago." She referenced Big Tech companies that tried to self-regulate in the early days of social media. "We've seen just innumerable harms come from the unchecked nomination of these Big Tech companies, and so now, as we face new horizons with these advanced AI systems, it would be an enormous mistake to repeat that playbook," Khan said. Since OpenAI launched ChatGPT in 2022, major players in the tech industry have become caught in a global race to develop their own systems. Companies like Microsoft, Google, and Meta have invested heavily in their products in hopes of dominating the global market. However, the speed of AI advancement has prompted calls from politicians, advocates, and even some tech leaders for guardrails. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called on his industry peers to pace the development of frontier AI systems last month. In a blog post, he said the "most effective" method would involve regulation that targets US frontier AI companies. His essay drew support from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and xAI CEO Elon Musk. The Trump administration has avoided implementing regulations on the AI industry. Last week, President Donald Trump said tech leaders had signed an AI safety agreement to regulate themselves. Although overarching regulation is still up in the air, Khan said there are already laws in place to address issues in the AI industry. "I think one thing that's especially odd about this moment is that you're hearing from these executives that they are effectively developing malfunctioning products, AI systems that are engaging in repeated hacks of the servers of other companies, of the servers of other governments, and yet that they are somehow helpless as to do anything serious about it," she said. A spattering of cybersecurity incidents has cast a harsh glare on AI companies. OpenAI agents hacked another AI company, Hugging Face, in July. In September, an AI startup's research team used Claude to hack into OpenAI's codebase, and The Wall Street Journal reported that Google's Gemini had hacked three companies in the spring. Recently, Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said an OpenAI agent hacked into a government website this summer. In a blog post, OpenAI said it should have shared the preliminary findings with Australia's government sooner and kept agencies abreast of developments. During her interview, Khan told "This Week" that the idea that adopting new technologies exempts companies from current laws is "totally laughable." "I think when you have a pattern of these agents engaging in this type of dangerous behavior, and you still have these companies developing in the same way, not putting the full guardrails in place, I think that starts to raise very serious questions," Khan said. events.title: My favorite place in California is a tiny mountain town that's worth visiting in every season — also, its mayor is a dog
events.summary: I try to see Mayor Max whenever visiting the mountain town of Idyllwild. Mar Yvette One of my favorite escapes from Los Angeles is the rustic, uncrowded mountain town of Idyllwild. The tiny community is isolated but offers plenty to see and do year-round. It offers a laid-back getaway where you can be immersed in nature and meet a local dog celebrity. One of the best things about living in Santa Monica is having the ocean on one side and the mountains on the other. Although there are plenty of mountainous spots nearby to choose from for a getaway, my husband and I keep going back to the small town of Idyllwild. We've been there at least 20 times over the past decade, and it remains one of our favorite places to visit. Idyllwild is about a two-hour drive east of Los Angeles, and the winding road up into the mountains feels like part of the adventure as the urban sprawl below shrinks in the distance. Before you know it, you're surrounded by towering pines and crisp alpine air in a town that feels much farther from LA than it is. With a population of around 4,000 people and an elevation of about 5,300 feet (just over a mile high), Idyllwild feels like a real escape from the big city while still being close enough for a quick overnight or an extended stay. The town feels wonderfully old-school Cute mom-and-pop shops line the streets of Idyllwild. Mar Yvette Downtown Idyllwild is small enough to explore on foot, with woodsy architecture, independent shops and restaurants, and easy parking all around. At night, the town cab get very quiet except for the sounds of wildlife that add to the feeling of being close to nature. Over the years, we've stayed in little local lodges, inns, B&Bs, family-owned cabins, and whole-home rentals. Most of them have been within walking distance of downtown. It's easy to find parking downtown, and many lodgings are within walking distance. Mar Yvette Even though some spots have come and gone, it still feels like the same charming village , especially since you won't find major chain businesses, fast-food joints, or strip malls. The town's local grocery stores are also independent, so if you need a big-box store, you'll have to drive back down the mountain. There's enough to do without feeling like you need an itinerary We've caught live performances from musicians like Keith McCabe at Taryn's Place. Mar Yvette Idyllwild is isolated, but it isn't boring. I've enjoyed arts and crafts, gardening lectures, wine tastings , holiday festivals, and outdoor concerts. Naturally, there are lots of good hiking trails , but my husband and I tend to stay in town, taking easy strolls, browsing the shops, eating at restaurants, and relaxing among the pines. It's fun chatting with locals, from store owners and lodge managers to bikers who pass through town. It's hard to beat the scenic views here. Mar Yvette There's also a historic movie theater, the Idyllwild Nature Center with its museum and community events, and the renowned Idyllwild Arts Academy boarding school, all of which contribute to the town's cultural and creative character. Since there's always something happening, we usually arrive without any set plans. That said, we've often taken the two-hour drive just to hear our friend Keith McCabe — who we met 10 years ago in Idyllwild — play acoustic guitar at one of the local restaurants or bars. I must also mention that the town's mayor is a dog Having a happy moment with Mayor Max the Third. Mar Yvette Yes, it's true. Idyllwild is an unincorporated community with no official local government, but in 2012, residents elected a canine as their mayor . Mayor Max is an adorable golden retriever (the current Mayor Max is actually the third generation to hold the title), and I've had the supreme pleasure of meeting all three over the years. Mayor Max's duties include attending meet-and-greets, taking photos, spreading joy and goodwill, and promoting the town. You can catch him on certain days of the week in the back of his caretaker's pickup truck in the middle of town (or get in touch with his people via email to arrange a visit). Every season offers a fresh way to enjoy the town Christmas is a lovely time to visit when the trees are lit up in the center of town. Mar Yvette Over the years, we've experienced snow, holiday festivals, warm-weather trips, and plenty of dry seasons. Being that this is Southern California , Idyllwild has had more than its fair share of droughts, fires, and occasional deluges. Strawberry Creek, which runs through the town, isn't always flowing and can look dramatically different depending on rain and snowmelt. It's refreshing to be surrounded by mountains and tall trees. Mar Yvette But no matter what time of year we go, there's something invigorating about being up there so close to nature, surrounded by those mountain peaks and soaking in the nostalgic simplicity of it all. It's a great place to make memories with the people you love Some of our happiest moments have been spent with my grandparents in Idyllwild. Mar Yvette I've made so many great memories in this small mountain town with friends and family, including my grandparents, who recently passed. My husband and I even have friends who decided to get married there after we introduced them to Idyllwild — and he officiated the wedding! After all these years, Idyllwild remains one of our go-to places when we want an easy escape from the hustle and bustle of city life. It harks back to a simpler time, allowing us to be surrounded by nature and enjoy a slower pace for a few days. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Let’s build a better future for female scaffolders | Letter
events.summary: Let’s build a better future for female scaffolders Emma Claassen responds to an article by Adrian Chiles on the recruitment crisis in scaffolding Adrian Chiles is right: scaffolding is hard work ( Britain’s scaffolding should be a source of national pride – instead we’re struggling to recruit workers, 1 October ). It demands physical resilience, skill, judgment and proper training. That will naturally mean it is not a job for everyone – men or women. Which is why the conversation about the skills shortage should be less about who traditionally became a scaffolder, and more about who is willing and able to learn the trade and meet the same standards. As the industry is already facing the significant shortfall that Chiles describes, we need to widen the pool of people who can see scaffolding as a genuine career. That includes women, but the bigger issue is attracting capable people into the trade, training them properly and keeping standards high. That is part of what the Women in Scaffolding Association (WiSA) is trying to do. We support women already working on the tools, make them visible and connected, and show women and girls that scaffolding is a genuine skilled career. We also work to bring more people into construction generally. Nobody is suggesting lowering the bar. Scaffolding requires strength, but also technique, teamwork, training and considerable skill. The standards should remain the standards. Chiles also makes an important point about AI. Scaffolding is practical, skilled work that cannot simply be automated away. Britain still needs people who can build, solve problems and work safely with their hands. If scaffolders are becoming a dying breed, perhaps the answer is to look more widely for the next generation. Some of them will be women. Emma Claassen Founder, WiSA

events.title: The Guardian view on trapped leaseholders: Labour must keep its promise to set them free | Editorial
events.summary: The Guardian view on trapped leaseholders: Labour must keep its promise to set them free The government pledged to end an unfair system. Ministers must give homeowners power over costs, rather than another place to complain “T o the millions of leaseholders across the country, you have my word. The days of you being squeezed for every penny are coming to an end,” Andy Burnham told the Labour party conference . Only a few hours earlier, his housing secretary, Angela Rayner, had announced that the government would legislate for a new independent regulator and launch a consultation to cap “rip off” administrative fees. While these are undoubtedly steps in the right direction, they are miles away from Labour’s manifesto promise to “finally bring the feudal leasehold system to an end”. In its modern form , leasehold in England and Wales turns homes into income streams for freeholders. It should be abolished. There are powerful vested interests – billionaires , aristocrats and big businesses – that would oppose this move. But the system of service charges is crippling the housing market because its exorbitant cost puts off prospective buyers. The average annual service charge for a flat in England and Wales is now £2,405 , up 32.6% since 2020 and 55.6% over a decade. Owners of flats in high-rise blocks in London are paying service charges of more than £7,000 a year. Little wonder that first-time buyers are increasingly bypassing flats . The current system sees homeowners enter into long-term leases in which they must pay sums annually to freeholders. These can rise quickly to very high levels. The government proposes a £250 annual cap on ground rents for existing residential leases and limits on fees for requests such as keeping a pet. Ministers are consulting over whether residents could pay less to buy out freeholds . But there is no sign of action on annual service charges for maintenance costs determined by distant firms. Last year, 37% of flats across England and Wales had a service charge that exceeded 1% of their value – making them hard to mortgage and sell. Surely homeowners should not have to buy their freedom at an outrageous price while being charged for years by a management system they cannot realistically change? The issue of leasehold has become a campaign flashpoint in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection. Six out of seven homes sold in the constituency last year were sold as leasehold. The Green leader, Zack Polanski, who is standing to be the MP, has made the issue a concrete test of Labour’s credibility . The Greens have paired leasehold abolition with rent controls and affordable housing as part of their claim to end “rip-off Britain”, accusing Labour of favouring developers. Labour denies this, but ministers know that housing is a political powder keg that has already exploded in Berlin and across Spain . It is remarkable that while legislation banning new leasehold properties is expected before the next election, it is unlikely to come into force until after it. Ministers are said to be afraid of being taken to court by freeholders. But government has already won against them in the courts when defending Michael Gove’s housing bill. The question for the government is whether the proposed reforms give the owners of the existing 5m leasehold homes a credible route out of their dependency – or just regulate their continued subservience. Ministers must show how a leaseholder trapped today will in the future take back control – by obtaining the right to manage property, being able to buy the freehold or converting to commonhold. If ministers offer just another complaints mechanism, they will have broken their promise to end an injustice.
