events.title: TechCrunch Mobility: Reining in robotaxis
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility , your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility ! On an average day in San Francisco, you might see dozens (hundreds?) of Waymo robotaxis zipping around the city — and with little disruption. But, as TechCrunch has reported, there have been numerous incidents of robotaxis impeding traffic, driving into crime scenes, and interfering with first responders. And not just in the Bay Area. In some cases, companies have relied on first responders to move their robotaxis. These disruptions are occurring in the early stages of the robotaxi era. California has a new law hoping to get ahead of the problem before the next impending wave of robotaxis land. Senate Bill 1246, which was signed into law by Governor Gavin Newsom this week, sets a series of new rules for AVs designed to improve safety and response times when they become disabled or interfere with emergency responders. The law also creates ways to hold these companies accountable if they don’t. Autonomous vehicle technology companies like Tesla , Waymo , and Zoox will have to provide first responders with local, on-the-ground support when their robotaxis cause problems and could also face penalties if a robotaxi blocks police or firefighters for more than 30 minutes. The law also says AV developers can only employ remote drivers who are based in the United States and those drivers must hold a U.S. driver’s license. They must also notify cities, towns, and other local jurisdictions about the location and status of vehicles during system-wide failures and must provide “local incident technicians” who can assist with AV accidents and obstructions. There are still some details to hammer out, which the Department of Motor Vehicles will handle since it’s the main regulator of autonomous vehicles in the state. But when this law goes into effect in July 2028, will it actually keep robotaxis out of the way of emergency responders? It likely won’t, but hopefully this law reduces the chaos and raises the accountability when something does happen. Perhaps the better question is will other states follow California’s lead or wait for the federal government to weigh in? Harbinger , the EV startup, landed a $300 million deal to supply FedEx with 2,000 of its electric trucks. HyperGuest , an Israeli travel tech startup, raised $25 million from AMI, the investment arm of Apax Partners. REGENT Craft , the developer and manufacturer of the all-electric Seaglider, extended its collaboration with the U.S. Marine Corps Warfighting Lab, pushing the total value of the contract to $19.25 million. Quartermaster , an Arlington, Virginia-based maritime intelligence startup, raised $140 million in a Series B round. About $100 million came from Insight Partners, defense-focused firm Overmatch Ventures, and First Round Capital. The remaining $40 million came in the form of a debt facility from investment bank Stifel. Voltaback , a French fleet management software startup, raised €2.8 million from European investment fund Serena. When Aurora announced it would have 30,000 autonomous trucks on the road by the end of 2030, I admit that I raised at least one of my eyebrows. I interviewed CFO David Maday to find out exactly how the company plans to accomplish this and why he’s confident it will succeed. BMW unveiled its new 2027 3 Series and it’s offering essentially the same car for gas and electric. Guess which one is cheaper? DoorDash shared more about its new drone delivery business DoorDash Air, including the autonomous aircraft and its ground-based systems approach. Kodiak has landed Ikea as a customer and will begin driverless deliveries on public highways later this year. The trucks will haul Ikea products without anyone in the cab on a 219-mile stretch of Interstate 45 between Houston and Dallas, according to the company. Lyft agreed to pay $272.5 million to settle a lawsuit accusing the ride-hailing company of violating California law by misclassifying drivers as independent contractors, instead of employees. The settlement wraps up violations that occurred before Prop 22 was approved by voters, which allows companies like Uber and Lyft to classify drivers as contractors. Northeastern University tested 21 late-model vehicles from 17 automakers and 30 companion mobile apps. The upshot: cars are collecting a trove of personal data and sharing it with a lot of tech companies, including Adobe, Contentsquare, Google, Microsoft, Meta, Snap, and Yahoo. events.title: LIM Advisors founder George Long: ‘We’ve been here 30 years. We’re going to be around’
events.summary: Thirty years of Asian alternatives, from the 1997 crash to Japan activism, a smaller firm on purpose, and a caution that no asset class is perfectly safe [The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.] George Long does not talk like a man selling vision. The founder, chairman and chief investment officer of LIM Advisors is understated and unshowy. After three decades running an independent firm in Hong Kong, what comes through is a temperament suited to difficult Asian markets: calm, pragmatic and focused on protecting capital when conditions turn. Long left Barclays’ Asia Pacific asset management business in late 1995 to set up LIM Advisors, one of the longest continually running alternative investment firms in Asia. The Hang Seng had fallen 31 per cent in 1994, and clients wanted a less volatile way to manage money. “A lot of my investors said, can you create a more stable way, a more diversified way, not so much dependent on the stock market.” Convertible bonds were his answer. LIM rolled out its first fund in January 1996 focused mainly on Asian convertibles. A year later the Asian financial crisis hit. Long recalls the Hang Seng falling about 25 per cent over two years, yet “we were up about 12 per cent.” “It was really tough because no one wanted to invest in Asia at that time even though the market was extremely cheap.” The SARS pandemic in 2003 arrived before the region had fully recovered. The Hong Kong market fell nearly 18 per cent and travel almost stopped. LIM later lived through the Japanese banking crisis around 1999, the 2008 global financial crisis, Covid and the latest Iran war shock. His father did not invest at the start but after about 15 years he did. “When I set up my business, my father didn’t give me money. After 15 years he said, okay, I’ll now give you money, because you’ve proved you can survive.” “Now we’re 30 years old. We proved we can survive.” Japan is an important part of the firm’s focus. Long has covered the country for four decades. LIM has maintained a research team in Tokyo since 2002. He says it “may be the second oldest hedge fund office in Japan”. Foreign interest was thin for years and has only revived over the past three years. Precious metals and mining stocks are a major bet. Long thinks they gain from persistent inflation and a weaker dollar reserve role. The portfolio also holds copper miners. He sat on Australian mining boards in the early 2000s. He also thinks Hong Kong can become a serious gold trading centre, given storage, no capital controls and the old bullion market. The latest Policy Address sets out a gold clearing system, tax concessions for commodity trading and a larger official role for bullion. China is another large bet. “The Chinese stock market is relatively inexpensive compared to, say, the US stock market. China went through a major correction and has only partially recovered. They’re still relatively good value.” Chinese convertibles remain “an interesting niche opportunity.” He also holds Hong Kong property and financial names. The first fund has evolved over three decades. Convertible-bond and other Asian arbitrage, then high-yield, largely dried up. As those trades thinned out, the portfolio was steered towards corporate events, metals and China. The fund has since been renamed the LIM Global Opportunities Fund. “It’s a broader fund now and can invest in any liquid asset anywhere based on my 40 years of experience.” Fifteen years ago capital came more from Western institutional investors. International investors, especially Americans, lost some interest in Asia. More of the money now comes from Asian family offices, foundations and funds of funds. He will not give up Hong Kong. The city, he says, is still a major international financial centre, with a good legal system, infrastructure and talent. “But sometimes the government can take a while to change things such as the taxation of funds, but they generally move in the right direction.” Tokyo is the only other Asian office. There is a small New York office. Looking out five or ten years, he sees a rougher climate. “Interest rates are going up; inflation is in the system.” He started at a major New York bank in 1982, when US rates were high. “Most people who are even in their 50s have never seen high inflation and interest rates. I’ve seen that. I also saw a lot of commodity inflation early in my career.” No asset class, he says, is perfectly safe. The dollar is no longer as dominant as it was. Gold should hold its value, even if it fluctuates, as it did recently. Japan will still matter, and so will China. “We’ve been here for 30 years,” he says. “We’re going to be around.”

As promised, President Donald Trump has announced the formation of a new Super Intelligence Force, which he said will be led by national intelligence director Jay Clayton and other members of his administration. “The Super Intelligence Force is tasked with coordinating the effort of the Federal Government to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans,” Trump said in a Sunday morning post on his social network Truth Social. Back in September, in response to an AI safety debate that the president has largely dismissed as a hoax created by “Radical Left Dumocrats,” Trump said he would nevertheless form an AI Force and appoint an AI czar (“Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!”). Since then, Trump signed an executive order seeking to rebrand AI as “super intelligence,” a term seemingly embraced, with some stumbles , by the tech executives who gathered at the White House this week to sign a non-binding safety pledge. (The pledge included an impressive typo .) So it’s only natural that Trump’s new task force is named in accordance with this new branding. The Wall Street Journal reports that Clayton will chair the Super Intelligence Force, effectively making him the new AI/SI czar, with Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson, Undersecretary of War for Research and Engineering Emil Michael, and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor serving as vice chairs. The task force will reportedly have 120 days to create a report on the risks and opportunities presented by AI. Clayton, who previously said that it would be irresponsible for the United States to “back away” from AI while countries like China advance, made similar comments to the WSJ, insisting that one of the biggest risks is “not being first.” The task force’s charter reportedly says that it will “develop plans for responding to SI-enabled threats to our society, while preventing overregulation and regulatory capture that would stifle innovation and competition.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Fulcrum Echo promises AI text in the style of any writer, so I tested it
events.summary: Fulcrum faces an identity crisis, even as it works on creating one by enabling anyone to imitate another person's writing style. The AI startup, founded in 2025 and previously operating at fulcrumresearch.ai, now uses fulcrum.inc and could easily be confused with one of the handful of other companies named Fulcrum or some variation of that. There's Fulcrum (withfulcrum.com), Fulcrum (fulcrumapp.com), Fulcrum AI (fulcrumai.us), Fulcrum Digital (fulcrumdigital.com), Fulcrum Labs (fulcrumlabs.ai), Fulcrum (fulcrumpro.com), Fulcrum Insurance Technology (fulcruminsure.app), and perhaps more. This Fulcrum is offering a large language model called Echo, which allows you to generate text in the style of a well-known author. Fulcrum appears to have no issue with corporate echoes. It now falls to writers to decide whether they have an issue with non-corporeal imitation. "Echo can do any writing task, from literary fiction to casual chatting, in whatever style you choose," the company says, and then launches into an exploration of how the technology works without addressing whether imitating a person's writing style poses any problems. Suggestions in the Echo Playground, for generating sample text, include Paul Christiano, Emily Dickinson, and Donald Trump. So, the full gamut of literary achievement: from AI safety expert to acclaimed 19th-century poet to the wordsmith who brought us "covfefe." But Echo will echo even the style of not-so-famous scribes, such as this reporter. So I fed the model a recent op-ed to assess its copying capabilities. The result was mixed, but better than the AI-crafted pitches that have been hitting my inbox for the past few months. I asked the model, "What do you think about the possibility that AI is conscious?" Here's part of the response, notionally written in my writing style. I suspect the debate about whether AI is conscious is less consequential than the debate about whether AI is profitable. Consciousness is a word that invites philosophical speculation and TED Talk invitations. Profitability is a word that invites shareholder lawsuits if you get it wrong. If you ask Meta's latest model whether it's conscious, it will probably say something reassuringly vague, trained as it is on the corpus of human equivocation. If you ask Mark Zuckerberg whether Meta's AI is conscious, he will probably say something about how we need to focus on the future being for everyone, because that's a question that doesn't require him to discuss the ad targeting business. The evidence for AI consciousness at the moment is about as strong as the evidence for Zuck's credibility as a futurist. Which is to say, it exists mainly in press releases and earnings calls. What's clear is that software can simulate aspects of human conversation well enough to unsettle people, and that unsettled people are a valuable audience. If you can convince users that your chatbot understands them – or might, someday – you can sell them subscriptions, or better, harvest their attention for advertisers. The style is familiar but makes a lot of choices I wouldn't have made. I wouldn't begin with "I suspect…" – commit or go home. The consciousness/profitability parallel construction is clumsy. "TED Talk invitations" bets on alliteration at the expense of coherence – "discourse" or "chatter" would work better than "invitations." I wouldn't have written "corpus of human equivocation" – a nice turn of phrase, but an unnecessary shot at training data when the point is the model's response rather than the provenance of that response. Though off-topic, Echo did a passable job of reproducing my op-ed's skepticism of Meta and its CEO. The paragraph that begins "The evidence for AI consciousness at the moment…" is succinct and sounds good. It just doesn't make much sense because there's nothing in the text that addresses Zuckerberg's predictions about the future or whether they're credible. And that's not really relevant to the prompt about AI and consciousness – a subject about which I'd be far more dismissive if opining. As AI research, Echo is an improvement on the text emitted by many AI models. But whether the beneficial uses of this technology outweigh the harms is less clear. Generative AI models that imitate artists' visual styles remain controversial and are the subject of ongoing litigation. And voice imitation has also raised questions about publicity rights and the risk of deception. Such concerns have prompted US lawmakers to propose the NO FAKES Act, which would create federal protections against certain unauthorized AI-generated replicas of a person's voice or visual likeness. If writers generally have no copyright in their writing style itself, and limited practical means to stop unwanted automated imitation of it when their published work is publicly accessible, then the surest defense against Echo may be silence.®

events.title: I left my dream life in London to move back in with my dads at 41. I have no regrets.
events.summary: The author moved home to Colorado after living abroad for many years. Courtesy of Jen Kaarlo. I left my home in Colorado more than two decades ago and eventually built a life in London. When I turned 40, I started to think more and more about the distance between me and my dads. Soon after, I moved home and a year later, I'm still happy with that decision. When I think back to how my life looked this time last year, I can't help but laugh out loud. Last August, I was sipping cocktails by the pool at White City House with London illuminated in the background, wondering if I was ready to let this life go. I was chatting to a friend-of-a-friend, a woman around my age, who was aghast at the idea that I was abandoning my life in the British capital to move halfway across the world to live with my two dads in Denver. So much so that her perfectly manicured hand almost dropped her spicy margarita when I told her the news. She wasn't alone. Most people were flummoxed as to why I would swap a charming flat in the heart of Marylebone and a thriving social calendar to live in our family house smack dab in the middle of America. The author (left) pictured with her dad and step-dad after returning home to Colorado to be closer to them. Courtesy of Jen Kaarlo, By many definitions, you could say I had made it I left the Mile High City over two decades ago and called Miami, NYC, and London home for varying lengths of time. I had a stacked résumé and traveled to over 50 countries, many of them solo. Though none of that seemed to matter as much after I turned 40. What mattered most to me was that I didn't want to take time with my family for granted. As an expat , I always find myself coming back to a cost-to-closeness ratio. Many moons ago, I was having dinner with a new friend I'd been introduced to through mutual friends in Paris. Over escargots and red wine, he told me all about the glamorous adventures he had embarked upon, seemingly plucked right from the scenes of "The Devil Wears Prada." What stuck out to me all these years later is not how he knew every designer under the sun, but how he spoke about the calculations behind his trips back to the States. He suggested that we were both in our 30s and that, if we were lucky, we could manage two trips back home a year, but some years it might be just one. If we were even luckier, we would have our parents with us for at least another 25 years. His grand takeaway was: if the experiences you're living while you're abroad no longer make your heart sing, then was living so far away worth it? Time with family became perilously finite So, one Sunday afternoon after a deliberate bout of hemming and hawing, not to mention a few pints at my local, I called my dad and said I was coming home. Unlike many of my peers, I didn't look at the move as a step back . Instead, I chose to look at the adventure as my "Glitter Gap Year," as I called it. Besides, if all else failed, I had my UK citizenship and could always move back. The author said moving back to the US has been a better experience than she expected. Courtesy of Jen Kaarlo. It's been nearly a year since I hopped on that plane back to my beloved cow town, and it's been a robust adjustment, but oddly, an even better experience than I could have ever dreamt up. Sure, there are times when I miss my independence and wish I could catch a last-minute showing in the West End as I often did, but there is a beautiful luxury to seeing my two dads at the start and end of every day that few things can compare to. What I've learned to appreciate are the small moments. Getting to chat about the state of the garden, shaking my head at ridiculous dad jokes, and relishing in every single hug. events.title: Nigel Farage questioned by standards commissioner over £5m gift
events.summary: Reform UK leader was interviewed for half an hour last month over money from crypto billionaire Nigel Farage has been interviewed by the standards commissioner for an investigation into whether he should have declared a £5m gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne . The Reform UK leader spent about half an hour being questioned over the money, the Sunday Times reported. Farage maintains the gift was for his personal security. The interview conducted last month is a sign the process is nearing a conclusion, although Reform UK is not believed to have been informed that the report is finished. An MP under investigation is usually notified before the conclusion of the process. If the commissioner finds that there has been a serious breach of the rules, the matter is passed to the standards committee of MPs and lay members, which can ask for further evidence. The committee can recommend a sanction or override the report. If it suggests more than a 10-day suspension from the Commons – and parliament agrees – the Reform UK leader could find himself facing a recall petition and second byelection in his Clacton constituency. Farage has been under investigation over the gift since shortly after the Guardian revealed in May that Harborne had given him £5m just before the last election in 2024. The Reform leader has said it was a personal matter , not political, and the money did not need to be declared. The rules state that financial support related to an MP’s job needs to be registered if given in the 12 months before they enter parliament. After a slide in the polls over the summer, Reform is about to embark on a major reorganisation at its headquarters to try to revive its fortunes. Insiders said it would involve a big shake-up of staffing, in addition to the suspensions of James Orr, the party’s head of policy, and Dan Jukes, Farage’s close aide. The pair are facing an internal investigation into whether they encouraged illegal foreign donations during an undercover investigation by reporters from Verbatim. The inquiry is being carried out by lawyers who are expected to reach their conclusions soon. The matter is also the subject of a police inquiry. The party is working out how to spend £72m in donations from Harborne and another crypto billionaire, Ben Delo. The huge sums have prompted calls from political rivals for a donation cap. Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning A possible use of the money is the relaunch of a TV channel that produces Reform-related video coverage and a show fronted by Farage. Farage told the Sunday Times he thought the reaction to the donations would be “far worse” but had produced “some grudging respect – the fact that I managed to pull off a coup of that magnitude, I think people were quite impressed”. It is not clear whether the donations fall within the rules because the government is putting forward legislation to ban overseas donors from giving more than £100,000 in a calendar year – backdated to March this year. Harborne joined the UK electoral register only this summer and Delo has been largely based in Hong Kong, although on the register for some years. If the donations are ruled impermissible, Reform could have to hand them back, a prospect that is likely to lead to court action.

events.summary: Yemeni government forces backed by Saudi Arabia launched a counteroffensive against the Houthis on Sunday in an effort to win back territory from the rebel group, the head of Yemen's presidential council said in a speech. "We have exhausted all opportunities for deescalation with the Houthi militias," Rashad al-Alimi said . Why it matters: One of the key objectives of the operation is to regain control over the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a vital artery for global trade and Saudi oil exports. When the Houthis took over territory on the Red Sea coast close to the strait, it gave them — and Iran, which backs them — powerful leverage over the U.S., its Gulf allies and the world economy. Despite pleas from Saudi Arabia, the U.S. is not getting involved in direct combat against the Houthis for now. It is providing intelligence and targeting support, U.S. officials say. Driving the news: The counteroffensive has been planned for many weeks by Yemen's internationally recognized government and Saudi Arabia. Tens of thousands of ground troops loyal to the Yemeni government are participating. The Saudi military is mainly providing air cover for Yemeni forces and conducting airstrikes against Houthi targets. The goal is to retake the Yemeni capital of Sanaa, which has been under Houthi control for several years. The Houthis continued launching missiles at Saudi targets over the weekend, including at facilities of state-owned oil giant Aramco. The intrigue: President Trump is caught between wanting to help Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, his friend and ally, and avoiding getting entangled in a new front in the Middle East. U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) also had serious reservations about launching strikes in Yemen, viewing it as a distraction from its focus on Iran, a U.S. official said. On Thursday, Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman called Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to brief him on the planned operation and ask again for U.S. airstrikes against Houthi targets, the official said. A second U.S. official said that the U.S. "is not going to take kinetic action for now," but stressed that could change if the operation runs into problems. What to watch: On Friday, Trump's top cabinet members huddled for hours at Camp David to discuss next steps in the Iran war and the conflict in Yemen, Axios first reported. It's unclear whether the meeting ended with new policy recommendations for the president regarding Yemen.

events.title: Dubai to expand CommerCity in push for digital economy growth
events.summary: Dubai CommerCity (DCC) , the free zone dedicated to digital commerce in Dubai, is launching the second phase of its expansion programme with Dh1.8 billion ($272.2 million) investment that will help the emirate grow its digital economy . The free zone is set to deliver the expansion project in phases between the first quarter of 2027 and the fourth quarter of 2028, Dubai Media Office said in a statement on Sunday. “Phase two of Dubai CommerCity comes at a time when Dubai continues to demonstrate its ability to grow and expand despite the changes and challenges facing the global economy,” Sheikh Ahmed bin Saeed, Chairman of Dubai Integrated Economic Zones Authority (Diez), said. The free zone, which is a joint venture between Diez and Wasl Group, will add a series of projects across its three districts: the Business Cluster, Logistics Cluster, and Social Cluster. On aggregate, the projects will add more than 91,000 square metres of new office space, increasing the free zone’s capacity and expanding its integrated ecosystem to serve companies operating in digital commerce and technology sectors. The push to expand the free zone builds upon Dubai CommerCity’s record demand, with occupancy reaching nearly 96 per cent across its office, logistics, and retail spaces. Investor confidence “This expansion reflects the growing investor confidence in Dubai’s economic ecosystem and its ability to attract high-quality investments while providing an advanced economic infrastructure that responds to rapid shifts in emerging sectors,” Sheikh Ahmed said. The move, he added, aligns with the Dubai Economic Agenda, D33, objectives and helps strengthen Dubai's position as a global hub for the digital economy and future commerce. Launched in January, D33 aims to double the size of Dubai’s economy , with a target of reaching Dh32 trillion by 2033 and establishing the emirate among the top three global cities. The plan envisages a programme to support 30 private companies to achieve unicorn status – worth more than $1 billion. Other business incubators will support the growth of private companies, with 400 of the most promising identified. The expansion of the Business Cluster and the Social Cluster will add 86,000 square metres of new space, which will add to options available to local, regional and global companies that are looking to become a part of the Dubai CommerCity ecosystem, the Media Office said. The Business Cluster will include additional office space across six new buildings, including shell-and-core offices, fully fitted workspaces, and flexible plug-and-play solutions. Within the Logistics Cluster, the phase two expansion will add The Hive, a 5,600 square metre facility that will provide an alternative logistics model. It will feature 181 flexible units, alongside climate-controlled fulfilment areas, as well as digitally managed loading and unloading zones, the Media Office said.

events.title: This NYC startup requires 4 days in office but just let everyone work remote for a whole month
events.summary: Work 'Doomjobbing’ can hurt your job search and worsen anxiety, experts say: Why it happens and how to avoid it Work Forcing workers to use AI can be counterproductive—3 tips for a better approach Work AI is making a mess of how humans interact at work Psychology and Relationships For young Americans, the workplace is the new phoneless frontier Side Hustles NASA engineer spent $200 to start side hustle from closet—it brings in $32K/mo Bruno Solari spent his August traveling all around Spain, starting with a week in Ibiza, continuing on to Madrid, Málaga, Marbella and Barcelona, before finally returning to Ibiza for a bachelor party. He also managed to squeeze in a few meetings and client calls all throughout. Solari, founder and CEO of the New York City-based PR firm SolComms, was among his company's 53 employees enjoying their inaugural "Work from Anywhere August." Other employees logged on from all over the U.S. (the Jersey Shore, the Hamptons, Florida) and the world (Berlin, Prague, London, Portugal). "I was in Spain the entire month of August, and I would have felt like a hypocrite if I was going to be there and making my team be in-office," Solari, 33, tells CNBC Make It. "So I thought, 'OK, I'm doing this myself. I'm going to grant that flexibility to the entire agency.'" The end-of-summer experiment felt like a worthwhile risk to the 3-year-old startup: Employee surveys of the trial indicate boosted productivity, work-life balance and happiness, while the business also saw a modest revenue boost. It also runs counter to several big companies scaling back on remote-work flexibility in a job market where employers have the upper hand. "I think people were surprised that I went for it," Solari says. Four weeks of fully remote work from anywhere in the world is a bold move for the millennial founder, who came up in PR agencies at the height of the hustle culture era and says he holds more "traditional" workplace values, like building company culture through in-person interactions rather than "through a screen" of fully remote work. Since its founding in 2023, SolComms has operated with a four days in-office requirement, with Fridays at home that end at 3 p.m. most weeks (and 12 p.m. during the summer). Some 25% of full-time U.S. workers work in a hybrid arrangement, with the most common requirements being three days in the office, followed by four, according to a recent report from Owl Labs , a video-conferencing technology company, which surveyed 2,000 people in July. Most, 65%, work onsite full time, and 10% work remotely full time. Solari says every year his company surveys its own employees about the perks and benefits they want, and every year they ask for more work-from-home days. Wary of granting another remote working day during the week, Solari thought to offer 100% flexibility within a one-month period instead. He and his leadership team came up with the idea in January, announced it to employees in February, and spent the next six months coming up with best practices to make sure everyone was set up for remote success. Among those guidelines: Stick to 9 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. EST working hours, keep cameras on for all meetings, dress for meetings as if you were going into the office, use Slack status updates liberally, take lunch and other breaks, and no sensitive calls or screens in public spaces. SolComms also communicated their remote-August plans to the agency's 80-plus clients across healthcare, tech and AI, and consumer brands, says Natalie Valicenti, 30, the company's associate vice president of operations, who split her remote month across Rhode Island and Minnesota. Businesses are scaling back workplace flexibility The SolComms benefit comes at a time when many company leaders are scaling back on employee flexibility and benefits, and during a tightening labor market where employers have the upper-hand. In September, Uber announced plans to cut about 3,300 corporate jobs, as well as scale down its remote workforce and tighten in-office rules. Disney said it would require more employees to report to the office four days a week and later announced layoffs of about 300 employees. The five-day return-to-office creep has been growing for several years. The share of Fortune 500 companies requiring five days in the office nearly doubled from mid-2024 to mid-2025, from 13% to 24%, according to research from Flex Index , a resource within the advisory firm Work Forward that analyzes office requirements data. But for SolComms, the risks of loosening office requirements for a month seem to have paid off. Twenty-one employees answered a survey following the inaugural remote month, with 76% saying they were more productive, 90% saying they maintained high work-life balance, and 100% saying they want Work from Anywhere August back next year, according to documents reviewed by Make It.

events.title: I'm a matchmaker for people over 50. The couples who end up in the happiest relationships don't look for chemistry first.
events.summary: Brigitte Weil is a matchmaker who works with older clients. Photo Credit: Andrew French Brigitte Weil is a matchmaker based in Manhattan, working with the 50+ crowd. She says superficial details like looks and finances become less important with age. Widowed clients focus on what they want, while divorced clients focus on what they don't want. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Brigitte Weil . It has been edited for length and clarity . My parents have been married for 62 years, and my grandparents were married for 76. I've always been surrounded by longevity in relationships , and it's something that captivates me. Becoming a matchmaker who works with older adults was a natural fit. Dating in your 70s or older is radically different from dating in your 30s or even 50s. Younger people are looking for someone to build a life with, but older people are seeking someone who can share a life that's already been created. Lifestyle compatibility becomes critical with age When I match older clients, I need to know that their lifestyles will mesh well. We're talking less about chemistry, or someone who checks all the boxes, and more about how their lifestyles can be shared. Older clients care less about a man's height or a woman's appearance in a bikini. Even finances play a smaller role. Instead, geography becomes a big issue: many people don't want to move and give up their community and family connections. To find long-term love , clients must share values on topics such as grandchildren and travel. People know their nonnegotiables Finding lifestyle compatibility can be a challenge. People become wiser with age, and they know themselves. They know what they're willing to compromise on, and what they're not. Take my client Sol , who at 96 is by far the oldest person I've worked with. Sol wants a woman to wake up next to every morning. He's not alone — most of my clients want cohabitation, even as marriage becomes less important to many of them. Sol's been on some great dates, but many of the women his age aren't interested in moving house. They already have their routines. She says her older clients know what they want in a partner. Photo Credit: Andrew French My clients are building on their experience with love Rarely do I work with someone who's never been married before; Most of my clients are divorced or widowed. Widowed clients usually start by telling me exactly what they want in a relationship. They've experienced a loving partner, and know what qualities and traits matter most to them. Divorced people , on the other hand, tend to tell me what they don't want. They're looking to make different choices this time around and create a healthier, happier relationship than the one they left behind. Both types of clients often need a little encouragement. They need to know it's possible for them to fall in love again. I teach them they're not starting over; they're building on all the experiences they've had. A date gone wrong led to love One of my favorite success stories is of a couple who were both right around 70 when they met. For both of them, going on this date was a big deal. I was excited for them, but the day of the date, the man called to say the lady didn't show. That was unlike her. A moment later, my phone rang. My client was frantic — she'd gotten a flat tire on the New Jersey Turnpike, and was waiting for AAA to come replace it. When I told her date, he insisted on going to wait with her. She was frazzled, her hairstyle and makeup drooping, but she appreciated the gesture. He waited with her until the fire was fixed, then they headed home. A week or so later, he asked her out on a proper date. Now, they travel the world together , sending me pictures from all these beautiful locations. I'm getting married this fall Lots of people want to know about the matchmaker's love life . I'm divorced, and was single for about 10 years. I did a fair amount of dating, but dating as a matchmaker was hard. I was constantly exposed to so many wonderful single people. Yet, that reminded me that there's not just one great person out there. I met my now-fiancé, Michael, through my matchmaking network about five years ago. We were absolutely meant to meet when we did. I really admire Michael for the choices he's made in raising his own family. That admiration just melted me. We're getting married in November. events.title: CDL’s Lucerne Grand launch moves 61% of 570 units at average $2,480 psf
events.summary: CDL said all unit types have been well received, with two-, three- and four-bedroom premium units being the most popular. City Developments’ Lucerne Grand in Jurong sold 61% of 570 units at an average price of $2,480 psf during its launch weekend. The development is linked to Lakeside MRT, includes retail space, and is near the future Jurong Lake District business hub. Strong demand is supported by nearby schools, a large local population, and the project's appeal to Singaporean buyers upgrading from HDB flats. SINGAPORE – City Developments Limited’s (CDL) Jurong condominium project Lucerne Grand sold 61% of its 570 units at its weekend launch, according to the developer. A total of 350 units were sold as at 6pm on Oct 4 in the project that was priced on average at $2,480 per square foot (psf). Approximately 93% of the buyers are Singaporeans, while the remaining 7% are permanent residents from countries such as Malaysia, China and India. Prices at the 99-year Jurong Lakeside project started from $1.5 million for a two-bedroom unit, $2 million for a three-bedroom unit and $2.8 million for a four-bedroom unit, which PropNex CEO Kelvin Fong said was “relatively affordable”. “All unit types were well received, with two-, three- and four-bedroom premium units being the most popular,” said CDL in a news release. The development has a commercial space on the ground floor and is directly linked to Lakeside MRT, located on the East-West Line. CDL clinched the plot of land in June 2025 for $608 million, or $1,132.08 psf per plot ratio. The take-up puts Lucerne Grand within range of the five mixed-use projects launched in 2026, said Nicholas Mak, chief research officer at Mogul.sg. The launch-weekend sales of the mixed-use projects ranged from 56.9% at Newport Residences to 98.8% at Tengah Garden Residences, he noted. Analysts attributed the “healthy” take-up rates partly to the proximity to the MRT station. “The location provides residents with excellent accessibility and convenience to one of the most heavily used MRT lines,” said Mak. He noted that the recently launched Amberwood at Holland, which sold only 11% of 212 units, is about 1.5km or a 20-minute walk to its nearest MRT station. Justin Quek, deputy group CEO of Realion, said that buyers were also “enticed” by the provision of retail space within the development, boosting convenience for residents. The development’s location near the Jurong Lake District, which is envisioned to become Singapore’s largest business district outside the city centre, also provided a positive long-term backdrop, said PropNex’s Fong. CDL group CEO Sherman Kwek said: “We are encouraged by the healthy response at Lucerne Grand, which reflects home buyers’ appreciation for its distinctive combination of connectivity, convenience and nature.” Demand could have been driven by the presence of a broad range of educational institutions, said Mohan Sandrasegeran, head of research and data analytics at SRI. Mak noted that there are seven primary schools within a 2km radius of the project. Sandarasegeran also pointed out that the last private residential launch in Jurong West was in 2016. Mak added that there is a large population of some 598,160 people living in the areas surrounding Lucerne Grand, such as Jurong East, Jurong West, Clementi and Bukit Batok. “The substantial population forms a large catchment of home buyers and HDB upgraders,” he said. events.title: Top Wall Street analysts are upbeat about the prospects for these 3 stocks
events.summary: September ended on a mixed note, with the S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average falling 0.5% and 4.3%, respectively, while the Nasdaq Composite climbed 1.9%. Markets remained on edge with higher oil prices and Treasury yields weighing on investor sentiment and triggering fears of additional interest rate hikes. In this climate, investors with a long-term horizon can track recommendations from top Wall Street analysts to find stocks with solid growth prospects. Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance. Neocloud company CoreWeave ( CRWV ) is benefiting from robust AI-driven demand for cloud computing. Recently, JPMorgan analyst Samik Chatterjee upgraded CoreWeave to buy from hold, raising his price target to $125 from $120. The analyst cited favorable pricing, driven by solid demand, for the upgrade. Chatterjee said CoreWeave is now more willing to sign premium priced, shorter-term contracts, which lift his revenue and margin estimates. CRWV stock performance has been underwhelming as investors worry about high capital spending, the analyst noted. That said, he believes that higher prices and increased margins will more than offset the rise in debt to fund capital spending, improving the stock's valuation. Chatterjee noted the 25% price hike in July across CoreWeave's product offerings and frequent price increases by rivals like Nebius (NBIS), adding that some peers are charging nearly three times more for short-term compute contracts than what CoreWeave charges on longer-term deals. "CoreWeave's leverage of the opportunity [is] evident in its recent press release highlighting contracts signed in F3Q at ~$40M/MW," said Chatterjee. JPMorgan said higher pricing is already contributing 5-10 percentage points to contract margins versus earlier deals. Chatterjee ranks No. 4 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 75% of the time, delivering an average return of 55.3%. See CoreWeave Statistics on TipRanks. Palo Alto Networks ( PANW ) is a provider of cybersecurity solutions across network, cloud, security operations, AI and identity. Following a discussion with management, BTIG analyst Gray Powell reiterated a buy rating on PANW and raised his price target to $425 from $404. After a review of Palo Alto's product-level growth catalysts, Powell sees clear upside to both revenue and next-generation security (NGS) annual recurring revenue (ARR) in fiscal 2027. He expects PANW to deliver pro forma revenue growth of more than 17%, above the consensus estimate of 14.6%, and NGS ARR growth of more than 26% versus the Street's expectation of 24.5%. Over the past five years, the Palo Alto business mix, has moved to higher-growth product areas and new markets. from what was earlier viewed as a hardware-centric network security company, Powell said. The 5-star analyst estimates that hardware firewalls and attached subscriptions now account for less than 50% of revenue. Meanwhile, high-growth solutions, including Prisma SASE, software firewalls, Cortex XSIAM, Chronosphere and Idira now represent more than 35% of PANW's revenue. "Investors may not fully realize the growth potential within PANW's platform story," Powell said. BTIG is optimistic about the prospects of Chronosphere in observability, CyberArk in identity and software firewalls and Prisma AIRS in the network and AI security business. Powell ranks No. 320 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 61% of the time, delivering an average return of 17.3%. See Palo Alto Networks KPIs on TipRanks. In a research note on September 30, Rosenblatt analyst Scott Devitt reiterated a buy rating on e-commerce and cloud computing platform Amazon ( AMZN ), raising his price target to $360 from $335. Fears that agentic commerce poses a major threat to Amazon's advertising business seem "overstated," he said. Devitt noted that the growing adoption of personal agents and AI shopping assistants has sparked concern about displacement of Amazon's retail media business. But the 5-star analyst remains bullish, given Amazon's ability to adapt to changing consumer behavior, as it's done in the past. Additionally, Devitt argues that even if an AI agent helps a shopper discover a product, Amazon can still handle the purchase and delivery, keeping much of the transaction value. He highlighted that management believes that existing Amazon shoppers will likely continue to start their shopping journey on the platform because it has better personalization, accurate pricing and inventory information that third-party agents still lack. Overall, Devitt expects Amazon's retail business to prove a net beneficiary of agentic commerce. Fewer clicks would not hurt the company if the value of each remaining click and overall volumes keep rising, he said.

events.title: I ranked the signature burgers from McDonald's, Wendy's, and Burger King. My favorite surprised me.
events.summary: I tried the signature burgers from three fast-food chains: McDonald's, Wendy's, and Burger King. Erin McDowell/Business Insider I tried the signature burgers from three fast-food chains: McDonald's, Wendy's, and Burger King. I thought McDonald's Big Mac was underwhelming and needed more sauce. I liked the smoky flavor of Burger King's Whopper and the chain's  recent upgrades . As a food reporter, I've tried and tested many burgers over the years. But for my latest taste test, I decided to go back to basics. While I've compared the biggest burgers at fast-food chains and practically every fast-food double cheeseburger , I wanted to see if the signature burgers from three of America's most beloved chains really are classics. I tried the McDonald's Big Mac, the Wendy's Dave's Single, and the Burger King Whopper to determine which is best in terms of taste and value. Even though they're menu mainstays, not all the burgers have remained unchanged: Burger King recently updated its signature  Whopper , and it's already helping boost the brand. Inspired by customer complaints that the burger was often squished during transit — it used to be simply wrapped in paper — the fast-food chain updated the Whopper in February with new box packaging, a new bun, and new, "creamier" mayonnaise. In August, the chain reported that US same-store sales jumped 8.5% in the second quarter, a surge that company president Tom Curtis attributed to the updated burger and new family-focused promotions, such as Burger King's Mandalorian meal collab, showing the power a signature burger can have. Here's how the three burgers compared and how I ranked them, from least to most favorite. My least favorite of the signature burgers I tried was McDonald's Big Mac. Erin McDowell/Business Insider Arguably the most iconic fast-food burger, the Big Mac is a staple on McDonald's menu. Created by owner-operator Jim Delligatti of Pittsburgh in 1967, the first "Big Mac" featured a triple-decker burger and sold for 45 cents, according to McDonald's. The burger rolled out across the US in 1968 and quickly became the chain's signature burger. Today, an estimated 900 million Big Macs are sold each year around the world. A Big Mac comes with two 1.6-ounce beef patties, pickles, shredded lettuce, chopped onions, a slice of American cheese, and layers of Big Mac sauce on a sesame-seed bun. Erin McDowell/Business Insider The Big Mac cost me $8.39, excluding tax, at my local McDonald's in Brooklyn, New York. Right away, I wasn't obsessed with the flavors or texture of this burger. Erin McDowell/Business Insider The burger I received was mostly lettuce, which covered up the flavors of the cheese, meat, and sauce. I wanted more of a tangy flavor from ketchup, mustard, or simply more Big Mac sauce. I thought it could have used an extra layer of sauce or cheese on top of the burger. Erin McDowell/Business Insider The burger tasted dry to me — I think a lot of that could be remedied if the burger wasn't so bottom-heavy with its toppings. The cheese and layers of Big Mac sauce were all toward the bottom of the burger, rather than the top, which meant the dry bun and burger were hitting the roof of my mouth with little to no flavor or moisture happening. While I understand that this is the most iconic burger on the McDonald's menu — and that preparation can vary slightly by location — it is by no means my favorite. Next time, I'll order a Quarter Pounder . My second-favorite burger was the Dave's Single from Wendy's. Erin McDowell/Business Insider Named after Wendy's founder, Dave Thomas, Dave's Single is Wendy's signature burger. It is available in multiple sizes, from a single to a triple-stacked burger . It features one of Wendy's signature square patties and is the chain's take on a classic cheeseburger.  The Dave's Single burger comes with a quarter-pound beef patty, a slice of American cheese, lettuce, tomato, pickles, ketchup, mayo, mustard, and onions on a potato bun. Erin McDowell/Business Insider The burger cost me $8.74, excluding tax, at my local Wendy's in Brooklyn. The burger was noticeably saucier than both the Whopper and the Big Mac. Erin McDowell/Business Insider It was practically dripping with sauces, which I didn't necessarily mind. Some of the flavors were slightly masked by the two condiments, but I thought the cheese was tangy and the onions cut through the burger's sweeter elements. There was also a generous serving of pickles and a large slice of tomato. Overall, I thought this was a good, classic cheeseburger. Erin McDowell/Business Insider If I had to change one thing, I might remove or ask for a half-serving of mayonnaise. But I thought it was an overall solid choice for a late-night snack. My favorite burger was the Whopper with cheese from Burger King. Erin McDowell/Business Insider Burger King's signature burger has been around for decades. Released in 1957, just four years after the chain opened, the Whopper was 37 cents compared to Burger King's original burger, which cost 18 cents. Whoppers — and all Burger King burgers, for that matter — are flame-grilled, giving their burgers a distinct smoky flavor. You can order a Whopper with or without cheese. Erin McDowell/Business Insider For the sake of this experiment, I decided to order a Whopper with cheese to ensure a fair comparison with the other signature burgers.  The Whopper cost me $9.18, excluding tax, at my local Burger King in Brooklyn. A Whopper comes with a quarter-pound beef patty, pickles, onions, lettuce, tomato, ketchup, and mayonnaise on a sesame-seed bun. Erin McDowell/Business Insider Burger King updated the Whopper to include a new premium mayonnaise and a new bun, and now serves it in a clamshell box instead of wrapping it in paper. The thicker, fluffier bun gave the burger more heft, which held in the generous amount of toppings. The flavorful burger was my favorite for both taste and texture. Erin McDowell/Business Insider The lettuce, tomatoes, and onions all tasted very fresh, adding a delicious crunch to the burger. The patties had a smoky, savory flavor that made the burger taste freshly grilled. Their wider, flatter shape also made the sandwich easier to eat than some of the thicker burgers I tried. The new, creamier mayonnaise had more flavor, without making the burger a soggy mess. Overall, I thought the burger was worth its higher price tag, which surprised me. Comparing the three signature burgers made me feel like a fast-food Goldilocks: One was too dry, one was too juicy, and this one was just right. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Are my gen X peers the influencers the world has been waiting for? | Emma Beddington
events.summary: Are my gen X peers the influencers the world has been waiting for? Their careers are peaking, they’re rich in money and time – and young people think they’re cool. But maybe it’s not as simple as that ‘S top sleeping on gen X.” I heard this on TikTok recently. I misinterpreted it, with a guilty start, as: “Stop sleeping, gen X,” because I am 51 (peak X), so always tired; while not sleeping at the time, I may have been resting my eyes. In fact, Joel Marlinarson, a marketing guru , was suggesting my generation have become a powerful, if underrated, force online. Aged between 46 and 61, gen Xers with proper jobs are peaking, career-wise (although it’s a different story for those out of work, as a report last month on the struggles of over-50s jobseekers made plain). We’re more likely to own homes than the following generations ; we’re emerging from the trenches of childrearing and, the argument goes, ready to indulge in some me-time. “If gen X were a country, it would be the world’s second-largest consumer market,” the World Economic Forum reported last year , with gen X women in particular influencing 70% to 80% of all consumer spending. That makes us great customers – witness the tidal wave of menopause-washed wellness guff (Which? reported last month that many pricey supplements were no better than a cheap multivitamin ) and beauty brands for people suddenly horrified by their necks . But does it give us content-creating clout? We’re supposed to be (or at least meme lore presents us as ) the forgotten generation, low-key, countercultural slackers on the sidelines in the grudge match between millennials and boomers; aspiration and self-promotion aren’t really part of our brand. Sure, kids are scrambling for Oasis tickets and rediscovering zines ; US Vogue called us “the cool ones” and the New York Times went further with “the greatest generation”. I get the argument that it’s our time to shine. But real gen Xers have a lot on their plate and it doesn’t necessarily lend itself to fun, aspirational content. Being peak career means peak responsibility: our parents are faltering (I’m writing this as my mother-in-law is moving into sheltered accommodation) and our kids are facing awful geopolitical and economic prospects that undermine their mental health and chances of independence. We’re falling apart physically: for women, the sorting hat of perimenopause doles out a set of grim symptoms, while men are wondering what will fell them next – heart, stomach, back or knees? Who wants to hear about that? And who can be arsed to make perky TikToks? I’ll tell you who: Kathryn Turner . I was introduced to Turner, M&S Food’s director of product development, by Marlinarson, for whom she is evidence that over-50s employees are “ the next biggest influencers ”. Turner, a cheery woman in smart trousers who exudes quiet competence, has worked for M&S since 1995. She launched her account in May, but her TikToks already garner up to 2m views and her nearly 250,000 fans are devoted: “Would follow that woman into war,” commented one . “Why did we give Andy Burnham the job over her,” asked another . “ I love you Kathryn turner [sic],” wrote an account claiming to be the Heartstopper actor Joe Locke . I love her, too: Turner’s calm sunniness, as she talks viewers through innovations in the picky bits space, is a balm in a fractious world. Turner isn’t Kate Moss, Miranda July or any of the other impossibly glamorous gen X figureheads – she seems like a normal, middle-aged woman who knows her stuff and does it well. I love that she’s popping up on TikTok and I get it – I’m projecting, but I bet Turner’s great in a crisis, her desk drawer and handbag well stocked with protein-rich treats, blister plasters and ibuprofen. Maybe this is our online USP. Could watching grownups quietly bossing their busy, complex lives be the next ASMR? Because, mostly, gen X aren’t the “cool ones”: they’re the knackered ones, dealing with life, death, work and frozen shoulders. I don’t know any Mosses or Chloë Sevignys, but I know lots of Turners and I, too, would follow them into war, or at least get a dopamine hit from watching them be extremely competent in short-form videos. No one would want to watch me staring at a screen then breaking to fold some pants, obviously, but I’d love to see more of my capable peers ditch the self-deprecation (very gen X) and shine online. events.title: New York has a socialist mayor. Los Angeles may be next
events.summary: LOS ANGELES — Voters could make history next month by giving the two largest U.S. cities something in common: South Asian immigrant democratic socialist mayors. Why it matters: Such a pairing would capture two forces reshaping urban America — its growing diversity and the Democratic Party's shifting ideological boundaries. New York, the nation's largest city, is already led by democratic socialist Mayor Zohran Mamdani . The challenger in Los Angeles is Nithya Raman, an Indian-born urban planner and two-term City Council member who is trying to unseat Democratic Mayor Karen Bass on Nov. 3. Bass, elected in 2022, is the first woman to serve as mayor of Los Angeles. State of play: Raman became the first Asian American woman and first South Asian elected to the L.A. City Council in 2020. A Harvard and MIT graduate, she entered politics after working on homelessness and neighborhood organizing. A September Berkeley IGS/L.A. Times poll found Raman at 39% among likely voters, Bass at 28% and 33% undecided. The intrigue: The Berkeley poll had Raman ahead 66%-4% among likely voters under 30, while 56% rated Bass' response to the Palisades Fire poor or very poor. It also found an even wider gap among likely Latino voters : Raman led Bass 45%-21%, with 34% undecided. What they're saying: "I'm getting a little emotional thinking about it," Raman told Axios and Noticias Telemundo on Wednesday at Visionarios when asked what it would mean if she and Mamdani led the country's two largest cities. Raman, who immigrated to the U.S. as a child, said her family came to America seeking opportunities they didn't have in India. She contrasted the welcome her family received with what she sees as a harsher moment for immigrants today under the Trump administration. "The idea of this city welcoming an immigrant as its mayor ... is just so deeply moving to me at this moment." The other side: Bass strategist Julie Chavez Rodriguez told Axios and Noticias Telemundo that voters are talking about rent, affordable housing, public safety and whether they can afford to raise families in Los Angeles. Rodriguez credited Bass with accelerating nearly 47,000 affordable housing units, a figure also cited by the mayor's office for units in the city's pipeline. She also defended Bass' response to federal immigration raids, pointing to lawsuits and restrictions on using city property to assist immigration enforcement. Zoom in: Raman's version of democratic socialism sounds less revolutionary than municipal. She told Axios that Americans are pushing back against an establishment they believe favors wealthy and politically connected interests. Her alternative: make City Hall deliver basic services and prove government can work for ordinary people. Raman called it "sewer socialism" or "pothole politics," adding: "I just want government to work for the people." Zoom out: Mamdani has made a similar ideological bet in New York, declaring at his inauguration that he was elected as a democratic socialist and would govern as one. Yes, but: Raman isn't simply the West Coast version of Mamdani. She calls herself an independent leader and has repeatedly split with Democratic Socialists of America-LA — accepting a pro-Israel group's endorsement that earned her a DSA censure . She also backed Jim McDonnell for LAPD chief over the group's objections and sought changes to L.A.'s voter-approved mansion tax that housing activists opposed.

events.title: Scoop: A powerful new model from startup Reflection is set to shake up the AI race
events.summary: A closely watched Nvidia-backed startup called Reflection is preparing to shake up the AI race with a powerful open-weight system that could threaten Chinese upstarts and U.S. AI giants alike. Why it matters : The marriage of an American open-weight model and Nvidia GPUs would give individuals and companies a new, cheaper alternative to Anthropic, OpenAI and Google. Open models, designed to compete with Chinese rivals, can be harder to monitor and regulate than the Big Three so-called frontier models. Supporters of such ecosystems say their widespread availability and transparency also bring security advantages. Reflection's first model is set to be joined by other open-weight models from other Western players this month, sources tell Axios. That will bring a new competitive dimension to the AI boom. State of play : Reflection's model, set to be released soon, is expected to initially lag behind the most cutting-edge U.S. models and be competitive with top Chinese open-weight models. Sources tell Axios it will still boast powerful intelligence — capable enough to help companies build their own proprietary, low-cost AI systems. Combining a lower-tier open model with high-quality company data can yield results that rival the most expensive frontier AI systems in certain situations. A Reflection spokesperson declined to comment. The big picture : Open-weight models, the most powerful of which are almost uniformly made in China, have taken Silicon Valley by storm. As opposed to closed models like Claude and ChatGPT, open-weight models like Reflection's are generally available to be downloaded freely and can be used and customized by anyone. On platforms that serve many models, their combined market share at times has surged to take up a majority of usage. However, in the far higher-spending arena of enterprise use, which is typically handled through API and corporate billing, open-weight models account for a small proportion of usage, AI execs and analysts say. Zoom in : Reflection's ultimate goal is to pioneer the "AI factory" — a product allowing institutions to spin up their own localized AI ecosystems. A company, for example, would take its own proprietary data, use Reflection's models and secure its own computing firepower to build a highly customized, cheap AI system. Some institutions, particularly hedge funds and trading firms, are already eager to build proprietary AI systems using their own highly guarded data. The startup has already begun testing this concept, announcing a sovereign AI factory partnership with Shinsegae Group in South Korea. Behind the scenes : In preparation for the launch, Reflection has held discussions with interested parties in Washington and elsewhere in recent weeks to detail its model release and explain how the AI factory will work, sources told Axios. It is also aggressively locking up the compute capacity required to scale. In recent weeks, the startup signed massive deals with Nebius and SpaceX to rent Nvidia AI servers. What they're saying : Reflection CEO Misha Laskin has indicated it will take time for its models to reach the most advanced capabilities. "They're kind of like rocket ships," Laskin, a Russian–Israeli researcher who previously worked at Google, told CNBC . "To build a big rocket ship, it takes time." The Nvidia factor : The AI factory has been a core vision of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang for years. He has described a scenario combining computing hardware with open-source models, allowing enterprises to retain ownership of their data. Top AI users in Western business and government, such as banks or the Pentagon, balk at using highly capable Chinese models due to security risks. Reflection and other Western players are trying to fill that void. For years, Huang has sought to strengthen the open AI ecosystem and has been strongly supportive of Reflection's move toward building a top open system, according to stories in The Wall Street Journal and The Information . The bottom line : Reflection's release, and the startup's close ties to Nvidia, will bring a renewed focus on open-weight models, combining with other coming offerings to shake up the AI race.

events.title: My husband and I finally took a trip without our 5 kids. It didn't go at all how we expected.
events.summary: Our adults-only trip away from our kids didn't go the way I expected it to, but I'm still glad we gave it a try. Alexandra Frost My husband and I wanted to take a trip away from our five kids, so we planned a 4-day beach getaway . I didn't relax much, and it felt impossible to disconnect even though the kids had a trusted sitter. I missed my kids more than I expected, but I enjoyed being able to talk to my husband uninterrupted. My husband and I both work and parent our five kids, and some days the rat wheel of events and responsibilities feels endless. So, during a particularly tough season, we started scheming about whether it would actually be possible to "get away." First, we tried to plan a little weekend cabin retreat nearby, but I knew I'd just come right back if something went wrong, and it didn't feel like a real getaway without sand and water. How hard could it be, really, to hand off our day-to-day responsibilities to a fully qualified adult babysitter who is also a local teacher in our area? Once we planned to travel further, we started a spreadsheet to help us map out a few logistics. Four pages later, we were able to see the load we'd been carrying and how complex it would be to transfer it over. Yet, we did it. We headed to Florida from Ohio for a four-day beach getaway, hoping for the best. It didn't go as planned. Trying to relax was challenging even before all the messages began Let's just say toes in the water doesn't cure it all. Alexandra Frost I'm not someone who typically has a tough time being away from my kids. I don't struggle when we're separated at day-care drop-off , on date night, or during their occasional overnight stay at grandma's. However, as our plane landed several states away, anxiety started to build around how complicated it would be to get back in an emergency, and whether the sitter would really be able to handle five kids. It took a good 24 hours to calm down about it, which unfortunately was 25% of the vacation. I did notice that it was nice to be able to think about my own needs first for a bit. What did I want for dinner? What would be fun for us to do? These mini luxuries helped me start to understand why rediscovering yourself on getaways is necessary. But when you run your own seven-person three-ring circus, you can't really just turn off your phone, or it might all come crashing down. So I left it on, and couldn't really disconnect. The messages and notifications wouldn't stop. It started with a forgotten uniform. Soon after, it morphed into a disagreement with the babysitter about the rules. A grandparent wondered what time something was happening. A practice was canceled on the app that only I could see. A few beachside cocktails were a little bit helpful to get in the vacation spirit, but this didn't feel the same as a real vacation. I found this incredibly frustrating — we'd worked hard and paid a good amount of money to make it happen, and I couldn't calm down about my kids over 1,000 miles away? Everything's a little less cool when you can't show your kids — but uninterrupted time with my husband made the trip worth it It was nice for my husband and me to speak to each other without being interrupted by our kids. Alexandra Frost We found a nest of bunnies living next to the beach, which was the most shell-covered beach I'd ever seen. I wanted to show my kids, and I missed them. I'd head into the tourist shops to buy them shell necklaces, and feel nostalgic watching other families dig on the beach. I was sad they were missing this trip, and no amount of logic about how we really needed a break seemed to counteract the feeling. How ridiculous, I'd think to myself, that I spend time with them hoping to get a break away from them with my husband, and a break with my husband wishing they were there. I guess this is motherhood? Despite the crises with my kids — which kept getting more severe and distracting, from behavior issues to logistics problems — one bright spot in the vacation was some uninterrupted conversation. I learned that my husband and I actually have a great time together when we can finish a dang sentence. That made me excited for future trips where the kids are a little more self-sufficient and a couple's only getaway can feel a little more like that — a getaway. Until then, I'm already planning to head back to the beach with the kids, where I'll probably spend a lot of moments wishing I were able to get out of my head and enjoy an adults-only trip . events.title: The demands of Welsh devolution are simple: just give us what Scotland has | Will Hayward
events.summary: The demands of Welsh devolution are simple: just give us what Scotland has Andy Burnham is a Westminster leader whom Welsh nationalists could finally work with - but only if he stands up to the devo-sceptics in UK Labour A s I sat in the first Plaid Cymru conference since the party won the Welsh election and started leading the Welsh government, I heard things I had never heard before. I have been to a lot of Plaid conferences and not once have I heard people being really positive about a UK Labour leader. But there was no mistaking it: the Welsh nationalist party feels that Andy Burnham is a man it can work with. When I interviewed Welsh first minister Rhun ap Iorwerth , he indicated he was hopeful – in a way he never was under Keir Starmer – that there was a prime minister who had a genuine desire to give Wales meaningful concessions when it comes to additional powers. In his speech in Llandudno, the first minister said that the prime minister had “looked me in the eyes and promised he would not [bypass the Senedd]”. He said he had written to Burnham with a “formal ask” for “a new deal for Wales”. There were five demands from the Welsh government to Westminster: powers over policing and justice, powers over rail infrastructure, control over the crown estate , “fiscal fairness” and control of welfare. Seems like a pretty long shopping list, right? Well, it can actually be summarised in just five words: “Give us what Scotland has.” The Scots have control of the crown estate, a better funding settlement, with more money through the Barnett formula , heavy rail is devolved , and the Scottish government controls policing and justice, as well as having partial control of welfare spending . When you look at it from that perspective, it’s not as if the Welsh government is asking for something unprecedented. The UK government only has to look north to see the precedent. You don’t have to be a Welsh nationalist to think it’s unfair that Wales’s government is equipped with fewer tools than its Scottish counterparts to meaningfully tackle Wales’s challenges. Wales has less borrowing capacity than a local council and, as mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham had more power over policing in his area than the first minister of Wales does. The stars are aligning for Wales to get more parity with Scotland. If Burnham follows his own devolution logic – that decisions should be taken closer to the people they impact –then how could he defend a region of England getting more autonomy than a nation? Though figures within Plaid clearly believe that Burnham is genuinely open to giving Wales more powers, they have real concerns that the more devo-sceptic figures within both the UK Labour party and the civil service will hinder their attempts. These fears are not unfounded. A leaked memo from Starmer revealed that he warned his cabinet against being “overly deferential” to devolved governments. In December 2025, 11 Labour Senedd members wrote to the then PM accusing him of “rolling back” devolution. This fear led to one of the better lines in ap Iorwerth’s speech, where he said that if Burnham fails to give Cymru concessions: “Wales will know again that our best interests will never be served by Westminster, and that it matters little whether who lives in No 10 Downing Street is an Evertonian or an Old Etonian.” With all the talk of “the Burnham bounce”, one thing that I think is being missed in the wider media is the total collapse of Labour’s status in Wales. Before the Senedd election in May, Welsh Labour was the most successful democratic party in history, having been the largest party in Wales at every general and Senedd election since 1922 . Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more When Labour was struggling in England and Scotland against the Tories, led by both David Cameron and Boris Johnson, Welsh Labour was winning election after election. But now Labour’s dominance in Wales is over. In a 96-seat Welsh parliament, Labour now has just nine seats . At Labour conference in Liverpool, speaking to people on both the Welsh and UK sides of the party, it was clear to me that they were facing very different trajectories. UK Labour members were full of hope, optimism and excitement for what is to come: the conference was like an engagement party, to celebrate a union with their new partner. Meanwhile, Welsh Labour members had just broken up with their partner of 27 years and were totally cut up about the divorce. They were at the engagement party, trying to keep a stiff upper lip while nursing a can of strong lager and wondering how they were going to afford to furnish their new one-bed flat. But this is a very bad time for Welsh Labour to have an identity crisis. All of the demands made by Plaid to Burnham are longstanding Welsh Labour policies . For so long, Welsh Labour and devolution were synonymous with each other, but now the mood music is very different.
