events.title: Met Police suspends use of phone-hacking software over Russian links
events.summary: The Metropolitan Police has stopped using digital forensics software from Oxygen Forensics while it investigates US allegations that the supposedly American outfit was secretly owned by Russians and developing its wares in Moscow. Scotland Yard confirmed it has paused use of the company's tools and launched a "full review," after US prosecutors last week accused Oxygen CEO Lee Reiber and Russian national Oleg Sergeyevich Davydov of concealing the company's ownership and where its software was actually being built. The Met signed a three-year deal with Oxygen in December 2023. Digital forensics teams use its software to extract and analyze data from phones and other devices seized during investigations. "We have paused our use of the tool while we carry out a full review," a Met spokesperson told The Times. "At this time, we believe any impact to ongoing investigations will be extremely limited. The Met does not share any data obtained from investigations with Oxygen Forensics Inc." The force said Oxygen's software runs on a closed IT system that isn't connected to the internet and was used in less than 0.2 percent of the more than 23,000 actions carried out by its digital forensics team over the past year. The pause comes after the US Department of Justice alleged that Oxygen, which is based in Alexandria, Virginia, presented itself to US government customers as an independent American company despite being owned and controlled by five Russian nationals through a Cyprus-based holding company. Prosecutors claim the same five Russians also owned Moscow-based MKO Systems, previously known as Oxygen Software, where developers actually wrote Oxygen's software. MKO, meanwhile, sold the technology in Russia under different product names to customers reportedly including the Federal Security Service, better known as the FSB, as well as the Russian Investigative Committee and Ministry of Internal Affairs. Oxygen's US customers weren't exactly small fry. US defense and homeland security agencies bought its software, including Homeland Security Investigations, the DHS Office of Inspector General, and the Secret Service's National Computer Forensics Institute. The DoJ isn't alleging that Oxygen's software contained malicious code or was used to gain unauthorized access to customer systems or data. Davydov, 52, was arrested at London's Heathrow Airport last month while preparing to fly to Turkey and appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Tuesday as the US seeks his extradition. District Judge Anthony Calloway declined to grant bail, according to The Times, citing Davydov's Russian citizenship and residence and the risk that he could flee. A clerk at Westminster Magistrates' Court told The Register that Davydov, was refused bail because it "hadn’t had enough time to gather important information." The fallout isn't limited to Scotland Yard. The National Police Chiefs' Council said other UK forces also use Oxygen products and have been encouraged to carry out their own assessments. "We are aware of the allegations made by US authorities regarding Oxygen Forensics," an NPCC spokesperson said. "These remain allegations at this stage and we note that US authorities have stated they are not alleging the software contained malicious code or that customer data was accessed without authorisation." "Forces that use Oxygen products have also been encouraged to undertake proportionate local assessments and activity to understand and contain any issues that are identified," the spokesperson added. The allegations are causing headaches elsewhere in Europe too. Romanian authorities have begun terminating their use of Oxygen products, while Latvia's State Police has suspended the software pending an assessment. The Register contacted The Met, NPCC and Oxygen Forensics for comment. ®

events.title: "Strange bedfellows": Bernie Sanders, Florida Dems and a benchmark $250k donation
events.summary: MIAMI — Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders is sending the Florida Democratic Party $250,000. It's a relative pittance in the Sunshine State — but the check signals a big political shift. Why it matters: The state party's moderate leaders have resisted the rising tide of democratic socialists elevated by Sanders for years. But political changes and financial need have brought the two together like never before: The Florida Democratic Party is essentially broke after decades of being out of power, and national establishment Democratic organizations have so far refused to help. Florida state Rep Angie Nixon , who joined the Democratic Socialists of America this summer, is the state party's U.S. Senate nominee. Sanders endorsed her and has long wanted to help, an aide said. Zoom in: Despite being vastly outraised and outspent in Florida, Nixon and Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Jolly are stubbornly close in polling to their respective Republican opponents, Sen. Ashley Moody and Rep. Byron Donalds. Until now, national Democrats have been hesitant to spend in Florida due to years of soul-crushing defeats —especially at the hands of President Trump and Gov. Ron DeSantis — that made the state and its 10 expensive media markets look like a bad investment. This year, with Republican fortunes sagging nationwide, Texas, Ohio, Iowa and Alaska look more promising for Democrats. That could change soon. Nixon told a liberal podcaster Thursday that the chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, held a fundraiser for her. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), whom Nixon called out last week for not helping, also might make money available. "Folks are a little gun-shy because, unfortunately, Vice President [Kamala] Harris lost as a Black woman. And so people are being very hesitant in terms of funding Black women, especially in the South," Nixon told MS NOW's "Clock It with Symone & Eugene." Behind the scenes: Florida Democratic Party chair Nikki Fried has been constantly working national donors for money, allies say, but she never asked Sanders for help because of their ideological differences and resistance within the state party. Socialists — and Sanders' associated views — have long been regarded as political liabilities in a state where so many Hispanic voters hailed from countries associated with leftist violence. But when Sanders signaled he was ready to give to a " victory fund " that joins the state party and Nixon's campaign, Fried didn't stand in the way. "Angie's going to turn out our base," Fried privately told skeptical allies in the party. "Every dollar that helps Angie, helps Jolly and helps the candidates down ballot." Friction point: Establishment Democrats are divided between those who don't want to be associated with Sanders and those who wanted him to give more of his $23 million campaign fund than just $250,000. "That's it? He should send more," said Florida Rep. Lois Frankel, who has been critical of Sanders and doesn't agree with Sanders' and Nixon's criticisms of Israel. "Republicans are going to kill us for taking Bernie socialist money and we're not even getting enough of it," one Democratic candidate groused. "But yeah, strange bedfellows." Said Javier Fernandez, a Democratic mayor of the city of South Miami: "The more we rally around Bernie, the more we hurt our long-term prospects." "It's a Faustian bargain: The party captures the energy and dynamism of the Bernie/DSA that are trying to use the party, but it compromises core values of moderate and progressive Democrats and puts us further out of step with the views of mainstream voters." The big picture: The Democratic Party is evolving as progressives and socialist-aligned candidates and activists energize its base. Nationwide, 65% of Democrats now have a favorable view of socialism, according to a Gallup survey released last week that also found support rising among independents. Nixon is the Democratic engine drawing enthusiastic crowds in Florida. Her rallies double as organizational events to harness volunteers to knock on doors, make phone-bank calls or volunteer. She also has a notable social media presence and a stable of influencers. It's a stark contrast with Jolly's low-key candidacy, which has a small social-media footprint and events. Between the lines: After some initial tension , Nixon's campaign is aligned with the state party, which is providing additional organizational support. Statewide, the state party reports an army of 6,000 volunteers who helped Democrats flip 46 seats in legislative, school-board and local-government races across Florida in two years. Florida Democrats are now keeping pace with the GOP in voter registration gains. Sanders has sent his staff and organizers to Florida to help Nixon with literature, texting and phone-banking. Yes, but: Florida Republicans still have far more registered voters, an edge of more than 1.5 million. And the Florida GOP has a well-oiled turnout machine and a stable of political pros who have consistently helped keep the state reliably red. "We don't lose Florida," one of them said, noting Moody and Donalds are marginally ahead of Nixon and Jolly in most polls. Still, there are jitters in the GOP as gas prices rise along with interest rates and the real estate market cools. "I'm not going to say Angie or Jolly are going to win," said one GOP consultant. "It's hard to see a DSA candidate winning a general [election], but could I see a world where she turns out the base and falls short but Jolly benefits from it and ekes it out? Nobody knows." What they're saying: Nixon's campaign manager, Eunic Ortiz, said the money from Sanders helps, but big money is less salient nowadays. Republicans' "billionaire donors will likely outspend us, but we know we will out-organize them," Ortiz said. "We're going to win with people on the ground, neighbors talking to neighbors, and the kind of energy and excitement money can't buy." "Did we see a world where Bernie led the way in getting national money to Florida? No," said an ally of Fried's. "But national donors are starting to give to Florida. And Bernie was the first nod the nation is paying attention." Axios' Holly Otterbein contributed to this story.

events.title: ‘It’s not about the champagne:’ Why VistaJet thinks the private flights boom can last
events.summary: The Signal Insight Swiss billionaire Thomas Flohr is a World Endurance Championship racing driver who has spent 22 years building VistaJet into a $2.9 billion revenue private aviation business with global reach. He is now weighing a possible market listing that could value his holding company at $10 billion , even as war in the Middle East sends jet fuel prices higher and economists debate how much longer the boom in global luxury spending can continue. Flohr, with a fleet of almost 200 planes and an order for up to 160 new Bombardier jets over the next decade, doesn’t see any turbulence on the horizon. Vista has seen “an explosion of demand at the top end” of the market for its longest-haul flights, he says, with growth from Asia to Africa driving record sales and 28% growth in flying hours sold in the group’s latest quarter. Even in the Middle East, where many planes were grounded immediately after the US-Israeli strikes on Iran, Vista’s founder and chairman says there has been “a significant surge” in demand from local clients. Second-quarter sales in the region, measured in hours, were up more than 68% year over year. Private aviation has undergone “a massive change in perception” since Vista was founded in 2004, Flohr says, shedding its “Hollywood image” as companies prize the ability to move their executives around the world quickly and jets with ranges up to 17 hours bring more locations within reach. In business today, “everything is now,” he says. Flohr’s company has a subscription model and typically charges between $11,000 and $25,000 per hour for its flights, but he says companies have become more willing to entertain such operating expenses than the tens of millions of dollars in capital expenditure required to buy their own jets. A company-owned aircraft might fly 250 hours a year, but Vista’s fleet averages 1,000 hours, allowing it to recoup its fixed costs faster. “If you control and own the airplane, you can offer the client ultimately what he wants, and I think that is the key to our success,” Flohr says. “It always starts with the customer because in the end, we’re not paying our own bills. It’s the client that awards you the revenue.” Andrew Edgecliffe-Johnson: How’s business right now? What’s driving the growth? Thomas Flohr: We see a surge in global demand. Obviously, the tech sector is on fire, and they of all the industries have the biggest global coverage demand. One day, a meeting in South Korea; the next day, a meeting in Japan; then there is a meeting in Abu Dhabi; then everybody is back in Silicon Valley, so they’re zooming around the world. Even if you own your own jet or two of them, you can’t really effectively cover the globe unless you have a global fleet, and they’re very conscious of the time efficiencies that they gain by flying point to point. You have told bond investors that you’re considering an IPO, possibly this year. What can you say about those plans? I can’t really say much. We have an obligation to communicate if we’re considering certain alternatives. But considering is one thing, and execution [is another]. We continue to explore our capital market alternatives. It’s prudent in the debt and the equity markets that you always have all alternatives available to you. So you’ve got to be ready for the bond market, and the same is true for the equity markets. If you’re ready, and the right opportunity comes, you can go. That’s what I’m drilling into the heads of my company, that this is always a prudent thing to do, because you never want to be in a situation where you say, “Ah, I have an opportunity. I might need capital. Oh, OK. I need nine months to get there.” Your headquarters is in Dubai. There was a period where airspace was closed in the Gulf after the Iran conflict began, and then questions about whether the region’s growth story would be interrupted. What’s your appraisal now? Yes, the airspace was closed for a little while, as it would be in any conflict. But the level of long-term vision and commitment to that region is incredibly strong. It’s like, for us, nothing changed. Today, when you’re actually spending time in the UAE, you don’t feel anything. It’s business as usual. People need to move, and it’s much more difficult for an airline to restart a global logistics infrastructure than it is for us. So our hours signed up in Q2 were up about [68%] year-over-year. In a way it sounds surprising, but it’s exactly what happened post-COVID. What does your experience during the COVID pandemic tell you about how much of that short-term gain you’ll sustain? In the five-year period from 2019 to 2024, the company grew 3x. I think that’s the answer, really. After about 18 months, the whole thing starts to go back to normal growth levels, but on a much higher level. Think about the psychology: We have yet to find someone who says, “No, I don’t want to fly private.” So, if you have an external event like this, which drives people to private aviation, nobody comes and volunteers and says, “Oh, let me please fly commercial again.” So corporations make the budget available, and it’s part of doing business. It’s not about the champagne or caviar. [That] is just, like, movie stuff. It is all about the time efficiency. The question is to what extent can the C-suite convince the CFO to allow for such a travel budget. But the level of efficiency is undebated. The president of the United States said [in September] that nobody should buy Bombardier jets any more. You’ve got a big order for 160. Is it going to be affected? I did very well for the last 22 years to stay out of politics, and I will stay out of politics for another 22 years. That’s really between two countries. It has nothing to do with me. We have a multi-fleet approach, and we have our contract in place, and the rest is really between the two countries to sort out. You have this racing career as well. Is there a connection? How do you think about those two careers alongside each other? The one connection is the word ‘endurance.’ In racing, you’re not going to win Le Mans if you do 10 good laps [out of a typical 300 to 400]. And if you can consistently perform at 97% or 98%, you get very far in life. And I think that’s the same philosophy, in endurance racing and in business: Stay humble, stay with your feet on the ground, carefully analyze what is in front of you and what is behind you. Don’t rush, but be decisive, and for the long term. What about your appetite for risk? This is not a low-risk pursuit. From the outside, it might look like risk, but I’m rather risk-averse. I’m extremely diligent about preparation. I feel personally more uncomfortable driving on a country road than in a World Endurance Championship. [In a race,] you’re 100% clear. You’re prepared. The safety measures are in place. The support system is right there. The same is true in business. events.title: "We're not asking for charity": Wikimedia CEO calls out AI for unpaid data use
events.summary: Wikipedia is starting to feel the effects of the AI-driven shift in how people find information, with page views falling 8% in the latest year, new Wikimedia Foundation CEO Bernadette Meehan told Axios. Why it matters: Wikipedia is a crucial source of information for AI models, but those same models increasingly allow people to get Wikipedia-derived information without ever visiting the site — potentially threatening the ecosystem that keeps the online encyclopedia running. Driving the news: Wikipedia page views declined 8% in 2025, and while the drop wasn't unexpected, "that doesn't mean that we're sort of starry-eyed about it and not concerned about it," Meehan said. Follow the money: The problem is that even though generative AI systems rely heavily on Wikipedia's vast trove of human-created information, some companies won't pay for it, she said. Wikimedia has a program that charges large-scale commercial users for reliable, high-volume access to its data. Publicly disclosed enterprise customers, whose payments make up 10% of the organization's operating expenses, include Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Meta, Perplexity and others. OpenAI and Anthropic, two of the largest makers of generative AI models, aren't among Wikimedia's publicly disclosed enterprise customers. Meehan noted that Wikimedia has other agreements that aren't publicly disclosed and declined to identify those companies. OpenAI and Anthropic both declined to comment. What they're saying: Meehan, a former U.S. ambassador to Chile who took over Wikimedia's top job in January, said the reception from big technology companies has been mixed. Some have embraced the idea that companies benefiting from Wikipedia should help sustain it. Others, she said, have acknowledged what Wikimedia considers excessive use of its data but declined to pay for enterprise access. "We're not asking for charity," Meehan said. Between the lines: There's an unusual economic tension here: Wikipedia makes its content freely available and has no intention of changing that, leaving it with limited leverage over AI companies that don't want to pay. The big picture: Traffic matters to Wikimedia for reasons that go well beyond bragging rights for being one of the most popular destinations on the internet. Roughly 80% of Wikimedia's operating budget comes from small donations, many prompted by banners shown to visitors to its site. Readers also provide the pipeline for future Wikipedia editors. "If less readers are coming, that's less conversion to editors," Meehan said. Ironically, Wikipedia has arguably never been more valuable to the broader information ecosystem. "We're the backbone," Meehan said when asked about Wikipedia's importance to AI knowledge engines. Meanwhile, Meehan is drawing a distinction between AI using Wikipedia and AI creating Wikipedia. AI remains controversial among Wikipedia's volunteer communities, which set their own rules, but it is already being used for tasks such as translation, finding broken links and helping new editors spot problems with their contributions. Meehan sees a clear boundary, though: AI should assist Wikipedia's human editors rather than replace them. "I don't think you will ever see AI writing or generating Wikipedia articles," she said. Asked whether she believes Wikipedia articles five years from now will still be written by humans for humans, Meehan replied: "I do." Zoom out: Meehan also pointed out who and what gets left out if commercially developed AI becomes a principal gateway to knowledge. Wikipedia exists in roughly 300 languages, including many that aren't likely to represent commercially attractive markets for AI companies. She also raises the possibility of a knowledge divide in which the best access to information increasingly requires paying for an AI subscription. The bottom line: Wikipedia spent the first phase of the generative AI boom becoming indispensable to AI. Its next challenge is ensuring that AI doesn't weaken the human and financial ecosystem that made Wikipedia indispensable in the first place.

events.title: A new contest pits competitors against each other in a race to biological youth
events.summary: This week, I officially signed up for an unusual competition. One that rewards competitors for getting younger . I recently turned 40, and I don’t need reminding that both time and my chronological age only tick forward. But this game is focused on competitors’ biological ages—figures that are meant to provide a better way to measure the age-related health of our organs and bodies. Over a six-month period, around 500 of us will try to reverse our biological age as measured in a bunch of different ways. There’s even a leaderboard! The winners will include the person who shows the greatest difference between their chronological and biological age, as well as the person who manages to reverse their biological age the most. The competition is the brainchild of the neuroscientist and physician Christin Glorioso, who is also founder and CEO of NeuroAge Therapeutics. The company offers tools to track brain health and aging and is running a trial to find out if biological brain age can predict the onset of Alzheimer’s disease. Glorioso says she has several goals for the Younger contest . The first, she tells me, is to “explain to the world what aging clocks are.” Regular Checkup readers will be familiar with these tools, but for the uninitiated, they are basically designed to measure biological age. Many measure chemical signatures that form a layer on top of our DNA and seem to change with age. But others might involve looking at proteins or lipids in blood. Some are designed to measure functional health, while others predict when a person will die. There are more than a hundred clocks out there, and they probably each capture a specific aspect of the biological process of aging. These clocks are proving very useful for scientists , who use them to study aging and development in humans and many other species. But using them to estimate the biological age of an individual person is more controversial. They’re just not good enough for that yet. Part of the problem is that we don’t really understand what each clock is capturing. Glorioso hopes that data collected through the Younger contest might help answer that question. She’s hoping to generate “the world’s most comprehensive clock dataset.” Some longevity clinics try to get around the limits of biological age testing by using multiple clocks. That’s this competition’s approach too. As a standard competitor, I’ll be sending a blood spot sample to TruDiagnostic, a company that measures epigenetic chemical groups on DNA and offers to reveal an overall biological age as well as a person’s pace of aging and the biological ages of each of 11 organ systems, including the heart and brain. I’ll get a brain age score from NeuroAge once I complete the cognitive tasks on offer. I’ll also submit some physical measures like grip strength. And I’ll upload a series of selfies to an app developed by a team at Harvard that promises to tell me my face age. That’s exactly what it sounds like—an estimate of how old my face looks. I’m intrigued to see my scores, even though I know I shouldn’t put too much stock in them. The first time I took a test, four years ago, the company I used gave me a biological age that matched my chronological age, which was a little disappointing and, if I’m honest, a bit underwhelming. A year later, the same company told me I had a young heart but a relatively old brain, liver, and hormonal system. My lifestyle hasn’t changed much since then. Will the years have made much difference? (Ultra competitors—who pay $4,499 rather than the $999 cost of regular entry—are also offered a range of other blood tests and clocks, as well as MRI and DEXA scans. I’ve got complimentary press access to the standard package.) Glorioso is also hoping to gather information about the effects of some purported longevity approaches. During the competition, some participants will be offered red-light masks, access to a sauna, or other low-risk offerings that partner companies who are sponsoring the event to varying degrees might want to collect data on. “A lot of these companies just can’t afford to run [clinical] trials,” says Glorioso. She also sees the event as a public health initiative. A couple of years ago, David Sinclair, who studies aging at Harvard Medical School, and his colleagues estimated that if we could slow down aging in the general population and increase life expectancy by one year, it would save the US economy $38 trillion . The event officially kicks off in January, but around 120 people have already signed up, says Glorioso. Ultimately, she expects 500 participants. Each person’s six-month run starts as soon as they take their baseline measurements, whenever that may be. A handful of people have already started. “I think the majority of people are going to want to sign up after the holidays,” says Glorioso. “They’re not going to want to be trying to win an aging contest over Christmas and Hanukkah.” Glorioso took her own baseline measurements back in August. Those initial tests suggested that her biological age was around 10 years below her chronological age. That sounded pretty impressive to me until I looked at the leaderboard and saw that competitor @Fred had a biological age 28.8 years below his chronological age. The leaderboard is pretty sparse at the moment, as only seven people have logged their baseline measurements so far. Six of them have biological ages tracking low, but one 47-year-old has been given a biological age of 68.1. She’s competing publicly, so I can see the breakdown of her scores. The worst is for the speed at which she can stand from sitting in a chair—by that measure, she’s been given a biological age of 100. Hillary Lin, a longevity-focused physician in New York, has just started logging her baseline measurements for the competition. She tells me she’s taken biological age tests in the past and that they’ve tended to give scores below her chronological age, which is currently 37. Last year, the TruDiagnostic test put her pace of aging at 0.75—suggesting she’s only doing nine months’ worth of aging in a typical year. “That’s supposed to be quite good,” she says. If it had been up to her, Lin says, she would have incorporated more blood tests into the competition, to build a fuller picture of a person’s health. And she’s worried that a six-month period might not be long enough to see changes in biological measures of aging. Still, she’s excited, and is already making plans to improve her sleep, diet, and exercise. But she already follows a high-protein, low-carb diet and works out at the gym every day. She also visits a sauna every few days (sauna use has been linked to improved heart health ). Glorioso’s efforts are impressive too. She tells me she’s started drinking a smoothie made from a pond plant that has been linked to health improvements , and that she’s cut added sugar and deep-fried foods from her diet. events.title: Her Agency Distributes Billions for Housing Projects. Her Husband’s Company Helped Develop Some of Them.
events.summary: Andrea Bell, director of Oregon Housing and Community Services, at a groundbreaking ceremony in 2025 Oregon Housing and Community Services As head of Oregon’s housing finance agency, Andrea Bell oversees a lot of taxpayer money.  Oregon Housing and Community Services has handed developers more than $1.4 billion in state funding to build rent-restricted apartments over the last five years — and even more counting federal tax credits the agency allocates. Bell’s husband, Joshua Crites, works as a director for the consulting firm JH Brawner , which helps local housing authorities develop subsidized apartment projects that receive a lot of money from Bell’s agency. The company lists offices in Oregon, Washington and Arizona and says it has played a role in creating 20,000 low-income housing units that cost $3 billion to develop. JH Brawner’s Oregon work includes consulting on two housing authority projects that applied for or were awarded tens of millions of dollars collectively from Bell’s agency since her husband started working for the company. (JH Brawner gets paid by the housing authority rather than the state.) Oregon law requires leaders like Bell to report their sources of household income on annual ethics disclosures, including naming their spouses’ income sources, especially when they could present a conflict of interest. The law also says any government official with a conflict should notify the person who appointed them in writing . But Bell didn’t do either until ProPublica asked her about it.  A spokesperson for Gov. Tina Kotek, a Democrat whose predecessor appointed Bell in 2022, told ProPublica that the governor’s office had “not been notified of any potential or actual conflict of interest.” The closest Bell came to a disclosure was in 2025 with this vague note with a misspelling: “Spouse serves in an advisory role for a developmen.” It did not name a company but instead showed a misspelled street address, with no suite number, for JH Brawner’s office in Issaquah, Washington, a commercial building with multiple tenants. Bell filed amended economic disclosures for the last three years on Sept. 23, the day that ProPublica asked her why she did not disclose her husband’s employer. The new forms explicitly name the consulting firm. “I take concerns about my statement of economic interests (SEI) seriously and am committed to transparency, accountability, and compliance with state law,” Bell said in a statement. She did not respond when asked whether she had played any role in her agency’s decisions regarding projects the company worked on. A spokesperson said housing subsidies are approved first by an internal committee that does not include Bell and then are reviewed by another group, the Housing Stability Council, which Bell does not serve on.  The spokesperson, LeiLani Barney, told ProPublica to file a formal records request to learn who’s on the internal committee. Bell advises the housing council as it sets policy and makes funding decisions, according to the agency’s website. Neither JH Brawner nor Crites, the firm’s director of strategic initiatives, responded to messages seeking comment.  Three former officials familiar with state ethics laws told ProPublica that Bell’s lack of disclosure was a problem that merited review to see whether she influenced any government decisions that benefited her husband’s company. Russell Lehman, a retired administrative law judge who served on Washington’s Public Disclosure Commission from 2019 to 2021, said Bell appeared to have violated the law, even if she later corrected her mistake. Lehman said he would want to know: “Why did it take a reporter asking you about it to have you file your reports?” “In a perfect world, we wouldn’t need ProPublica for this kind of thing,” Lehman said.  Kotek’s spokesperson called for an evaluation by the state’s ethics commission. “The Governor holds all agency leadership to consistent and high ethical standards and any question on conflict of interest should be referred to the Oregon Government Ethics Commission for thorough review,” Kotek’s spokesperson said in a statement. Bell told ProPublica in a statement that she had sought an advisory opinion from the commission at the governor’s urging and that she had updated her ethics disclosures “to provide clarity.” Money from Bell’s department plays an essential role in helping to build apartment projects intended to be affordable, channeling state funding and federal tax credits in order to reduce developers’ costs so they can charge lower rents.  JH Brawner, where Bell’s husband works, advises public housing authorities that are putting together subsidized housing deals. The company’s responsibilities have included negotiating acquisitions, structuring deals, ensuring project appraisals are completed and collaborating with the state agency that Bell leads. Crites joined JH Brawner in 2023 after jobs with local housing authorities in Oregon, Washington and Ohio. He and Bell own a home together in the Portland suburbs, records show. JH Brawner says on its website that it worked in Oregon as a development and financial consultant on Park Place, a 200-unit project being built by the housing authority in Clackamas County with $36 million in state funding. Another project in Washington County, Aloha 209th, is awaiting a $17.5 million subsidy from the state. A spokesperson for Clackamas County said the housing authority there “did not advocate or discuss the Park Place project or application with Andrea Bell” and that the county hired JH Brawner as a consultant before Crites joined the firm. The company was involved in two other state-backed projects for Washington County that were well into the financing process before Crites started working for JH Brawner. Work continued on both as recently as last year, according to JH Brawner’s website. Bell’s agency adopted a new policy in 2024 that effectively reduces its discretion over which projects get funded, moving from a competitive bidding model to one that gives money to eligible projects in the order that applications were received. But at least one developer has asked Bell’s agency to exercise its discretion. The housing authority in Washington County in suburban Portland, which is using JH Brawner as a consultant on the Aloha 209th project, is not due to get its $17.5 million from the state until at least 2028.  Molly Rogers, executive director of the county’s housing authority, said in a June public meeting that she had contacted Bell about the project and the county’s desire to get state money sooner. “She’s open to having a discussion, which is great,” Rogers said. Rogers did not respond when asked, via a spokesperson, to comment about her public remarks, and Bell did not respond when asked to comment on Rogers’ account. events.title: How Greg Jackson runs Octopus Energy with no HR, no bonuses, and no succession plan
events.summary: The Signal Interview In a little more than a decade, Octopus Energy has grown from an outlandish idea into Britain’s largest energy provider. It now powers 12 million homes in eight countries, manages wind and solar farms from Scotland to South Korea, manufactures heat pumps, installs smart meters, leases out 50,000 electric vehicles, and supplies technology to utilities around the world. The tentacles of this “Octoverse” all lead back to Greg Jackson, a founder-CEO who has built his 13,000-person company without bonuses, HR or IT teams, or a succession plan. Beyond the walls of the company’s London headquarters, which is filled with thousands of its plushy pink octopus mascots, Jackson’s empire may look like an unwieldy one. It is not, he insists: “The thing that’s connecting it all is the underlying insight: that the technologies of electrification can deliver tremendous cost savings, but only if you build a new system.” And building that new system requires using every tool at his disposal. “There’s a scene in the movie where the astronauts are stranded and they’re going to die unless the solution is found. And on the ground, Mission Control assembles … everything there is on the space station, like duct tape and bits of piping, and they say, this is all we’ve got to save their lives,” he explains. “In any business, you choose your constraints, and then how you assemble the stuff you have to create the outcome you want.” Octopus’ job is “to take all these ingredients and say, how can we outcompete the old world of energy with better products and services with better value?” Jackson says, before reaching back to the beginning of that old world for another analogy. “When [Thomas] Edison first started building electricity businesses, he didn’t just have to innovate, fund, and build centralized electricity generation, which he did. He also had to invent the grid and distribution model. He also had to invent or sell the products that use electricity, from lightbulbs to music players. And if I look at what we’re doing, it’s almost trivial in comparison.” How to run a 13,000-person company with no HR department The growth of Octopus, which had revenues of £13.7 billion last year and a valuation of $9 billion at its last fundraising, poses a challenge for its irrepressible founder: how to transmit to thousands of employees the energy that has powered him since he dropped out of school at 16 to write video games. Jackson no longer knows each staff member by name, but he still runs his company by the same rhythms with which he started it. Each Monday starts with a gathering of senior executives to review performance data from the previous week. That helps maintain “pace and alignment,” Jackson says. Each week ends with “family dinner,” a Friday afternoon all-hands event at which the company recaps its latest innovations, achievements, and challenges. The Friday sessions began over beers with a small founding team, and Jackson “discovered that it was the best way of reminding you how great your colleagues were, and re-energizing you on the big picture.” Livestreams have since replaced in-person drinks. But the gatherings help Octopus “start the week left-brain, end it right-brain,” Jackson says, and help him explain to staff what they need to do next “and maintain the energy to feel great about it.” The company has no intranet or staff newsletters, he adds, so if people don’t tune in to “family dinner,” they won’t know what’s happening. Less is more in internal communications, he says: “The more information you put out there, the less it gets read. What you want to do is make sure the stuff that goes out there is canonical and consumed.” Octopus also has no central human resources department, devolving people management responsibilities to individual teams unless legal staff need to step in. Still a private company, it gives equity to every employee, but it pays no bonuses outside a few sales roles. Jackson says this is because he’s determined to focus people on the company’s success, rather than their own individual advancement. Similarly, Octopus sets no divisional performance targets, to keep each division from promoting whatever will make them look best at the expense of others, he adds. “The most important thing for us is to build trust among our team, so they wake up every morning thinking, ‘How do I drive the company’s mission?’ Not, ‘How do I get myself promoted?’” Hands-on leadership, from the cockpit to the customers Even as Octopus has grown to span industries as diverse as renewable power generation and software licensing, Jackson says his job has barely changed. The CEO’s role is still to understand customers and industry economics; set the vision for where the company needs to go; and build a team with the expertise and innovative impulses to get it there. For a pilot, the view from the cockpit window of a small Cessna is not that different from that of an Airbus A380, he says: “The difference comes when you look back.” If Octopus became a more complex organization, “then I’d get drawn more into wandering down the aisle of the plane than looking forward out the window,” he reasons. “The bit that really matters for me is being in the cockpit, looking forward, however many people we’ve got behind us.” So Jackson is constantly checking that his headcount is not growing faster than Octopus is adding new customers, as he looks to avoid diseconomies of scale and guards against the spread of bureaucracy. Yet he is equally anxious about ensuring that he is not losing touch with customers as their numbers run into the millions. Octopus was built on a proprietary technology platform called Kraken, which now has an $8.7 billion valuation and will soon spin out as a standalone company with its own listing. Kraken gives Jackson and every member of his staff a “single view” of everything that is happening in the company, from customer service to pricing, energy trading to finance. Despite that tech-driven transparency, Jackson has maintained a habit of regularly meeting customers face-to-face. In the two weeks before our interview, he met roughly 1,000 customers at three different events, he estimates. “I stand on stage and talk to them, and then I get off the stage and have beers with them and understand their real experiences. They tell me not what our reports say, but what their real experience of dealing with our team is.” Everyone who signs up for an Octopus service is given Jackson’s email address. He used to answer each message himself, until Octopus reached 1.2 million customers and he found himself falling asleep at his keyboard at 2 am. Now his chief of staff and a team of five people farm out customers’ complaints and observations to the relevant executives, but he thinks the system still builds a “magic connectivity” with customers. “We’re not crazy hippies,” he says. “If we genuinely love our customers, they reciprocate.” How a CEO replaces themself when there’s

events.title: Third-country decision a ‘devastating result,’ lawyer says
events.summary: Immigrant advocates are grappling with the Supreme Court’s decision to allow the Trump administration to move forward with third-country deportations, which will leave the policy in place for months while they wait for the court to rule on it. Trina Realmuto, lead counsel for the plaintiffs that challenged the policy at the National Immigration Litigation Alliance, called it a “devastating result.” She warned migrants could be sent to countries “where they may face persecution, torture, imprisonment, or other grave danger.” The Trump administration has signed deals with various countries to accept deported migrants, many of them in Africa. Burundi was the latest to announce it will accept migrants. The Supreme Court’s unsigned order this week lifted a ruling requiring migrants receive notice of — and a chance to challenge — their deportation to countries where they have no personal ties. The high court will hear oral arguments on the case, but not until December, meaning a decision will come next year. The Department of Homeland Security celebrated this week’s move, with the agency’s general counsel declaring it “a bad day for criminal illegals and open borders activists alike.” The arrangements have drawn mounting scrutiny, most recently after migrants deported to Equatorial Guinea were held at gunpoint and beaten . Congressional Democrats are vowing to investigate the deportations if they take control of the House or Senate — or both — in November’s midterm elections. — Adrian Elimian

events.title: West Virginia's Justice may delay decision on running for governor
events.summary: Sen. Jim Justice, R-W.Va., “may have to” wait until after the midterms to decide on whether to run for his old job as governor — and challenge incumbent Gov. Patrick Morrisey, he told Semafor in an interview this week. The Republican senator said he doesn’t “like jerking people around” and wanted to announce within a couple weeks, but added there’s “too much stuff going on” in the Senate for him to reflect on the choice. “I really wanted to put some time in to really think: Do you really want to do this?” he said. Nonetheless, Justice said he plans to make his decision “really soon.” Most Republican senators think he will challenge Morrisey for his old job; Justice has made no secret that he thinks he’d do a better job than his successor. “I love the people in West Virginia, and I don’t know that we’re going the right way,” he said.

events.title: A potential 2028 Democratic kingmaker has advice for candidates
events.summary: The News New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham has a message for the potential 2028 Democratic presidential candidates who are passing through her state: Focus on the children. Lujan Grisham, a Democrat who’s set to leave office after this year, told Semafor the candidates “absolutely should” be running on universal childcare proposals. Her state has enacted its own universal childcare program, though she acknowledged a national program could be “challenging” without tax increases. “What I would do in that position is make it really clear that you’ll create incentives and grants so that states have real opportunity,” she said. Lujan Grisham said she’d met or spoken with many of the possible presidential aspirants who have visited the state, including Maryland Gov. Wes Moore and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg. Their conversations were “less introductory and more policy,” she said. Know More New Mexico has been added to the early primary states, following the familiar trio of South Carolina, Nevada, and New Hampshire, and it could shake up Democrats’ strategies in the presidential primary. Lujan Grisham said she plans to endorse, depending on how the field shapes up. “It depends on who’s in that primary, doesn’t it? I mean, I would like to be in a position to get to do that,” she said. Lujan Grisham also weighed in on the criticism that the Democratic Governors Association has received for not investing more in the Texas gubernatorial race. “I think the DGA in this climate should be spending everywhere, and they’re raising to do exactly that. I mean, they’ve never done an expanded map like this,” she said. The DGA’s chair, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, a potential 2028 presidential candidate himself, has faced criticism from other Democrats for not putting more resources into the expensive Texas race. But Lujan Grisham said that “picking on the DGA is not the best strategy.”

events.title: The AI industry balances Trump and a changing Washington
events.summary: Ashley’s view The tech industry is facing strange headwinds in Washington after meeting with President Donald Trump and senior administration officials this week and signing a “morally binding” accord on AI. The meeting with Trump was largely successful for all of the companies involved. But now these same firms have to navigate maintaining ties with the president while placating Democrats who could very well control both houses of Congress next year. That’s not to mention what could be a massively consequential midterm election, fueled by AI anxiety among voters , that could test the bounds of their power. “Companies are going to have to make it more specific, on how they’re going to operationalize it,” Chris Lehane, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, told Semafor about the new White House accord on “Super Intelligence” signed by the leaders of several top firms and Trump this week, including OpenAI President Greg Brockman. “We’ve certainly approached this believing … it’s also in our self-interest to make sure that people feel that we are actually building things safely and deploying responsibly,” Lehane said, adding that OpenAI’s support for certain state-level AI bills and its hopes for a federal bill will remain the same. “That’s almost either a democratic market force, or the actual market forces themselves. Like, if you’re making cars, you’re going to want to make sure the cars are safe, or people aren’t going to buy your cars, whether there are regulations or not,” he added. Know More Before lawmakers departed Washington to focus on campaigning ahead of the November elections, AI companies were still in active discussions on Capitol Hill. They’re trying to influence forthcoming bills and determine where they can find consensus with lawmakers, a tech industry source and a source who works on AI policy told Semafor. Companies know that the midterms are likely to mean a Democratic-run House and possibly a Democratic-run Senate, and with that will come more momentum to pass AI legislation — and likely more scrutiny of their operations, particularly for firms that have demonstrated ties with the Trump administration. “There’s a world where people are smarter and smarter about these issues, and bills are going to be introduced imminently that are much better than what we’ve seen,” the AI policy source told Semafor. After the election, legislating is an obvious place to go, given the public and many lawmakers in both parties want to see something done, the tech industry source told Semafor. Considering where the Trump administration was a year ago — that is , attempting to ban state-level AI bills — progress toward federal AI policy is slow, but it’s inching forward, the tech industry source said. The FTC also kicked off its own AI inquiry, which may not yield much in the end, but nevertheless represents a signal from the administration that regulators are prepared to use existing laws to go after any companies that they suspect have hurt consumers. Still, the White House’s pro-AI posture is unlikely to fundamentally change, and Trump will remain the most important voice on it until the end of his term. Groups that are pushing for data center expansion and industry-friendly laws have plenty of money and resources, plus their own complicated financial ties to the AI and tech companies themselves. Anthropic may be experiencing the most whiplash since the surreal AI summit: Days after a federal court upheld its designation by the Pentagon as a supply chain risk, CEO Dario Amodei dined with Trump at the White House. The administration has repeatedly painted Anthropic as the face of a pro-AI safety movement that is “woke” and composed of “doomers” — too focused on AI’s harms and trying to gin up fear for ulterior motives. “I think they’re going to try to walk this tightrope for two years,” the person who works on AI policy told Semafor. “They’re in a weird place. [Undersecretary of Defense] Emil Michael hates you, and is tweeting about you every day. Nonetheless, the government seems to find you indispensable to their operations.” Sarah Heck, a policy lead at Anthropic, posted on X following the White House meeting: “You can’t do safety from second place.” She shared a video clip of Amodei applauding the accord while saying AI still has very real risks and how companies address them is still under discussion. On Thursday, Heck added: “To be clear, I’m talking about the US and its allies here: We can’t ensure AI is developed safely unless the US is in the lead.” Notable The idea for what became Trump’s pact with the AI industry came from a conversation between Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and House Speaker Mike Johnson, Semafor scooped .

events.title: Flight delayed? So are these codec updates
events.summary: Take this display at Alcantarí International Airport, which serves Sucre, Bolivia's constitutional and judicial capital. Eagle-eyed Register reader Phil Pearce spotted the Windows 11 desktop and its update prompt while waiting for a delayed Boliviana de Aviación (BoA) flight. The prompt comes from K-Lite Codec Pack, a collection of components that enables Windows to play various audio and video formats. Its presence suggests the passenger display is powered by a fairly ordinary Windows installation rather than some mysterious specialist signage system. Whoever configured the display does not appear to have disabled K-Lite's update notifications or arranged for them to run silently. In this instance, it appears the updater spotted newer versions and lumbered to the foreground with an update prompt – useful on a PC with a keyboard and mouse, but less so on a passenger-facing display beyond anyone's reach. The exposed desktop also displays the Microsoft Store, Outlook, a weather widget, and several shortcuts – more than one might expect a departure board to require. Why airport signage needs Outlook is anyone's guess, although Microsoft has not been shy about preinstalling it. The app even surfaced during NASA's recent Artemis mission and promptly required technical support. Our reader could not dismiss the prompt or update the codecs, but at least the wayward desktop gave delayed passengers something else to watch while wondering what had happened to their flight. ®

events.title: OpenAI fires workers for 'mishandling sensitive information'
events.summary: OpenAI has fired three researchers for allegedly mishandling information, including work which involved an external organisation analysing AI models. "Our investigation confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures, violating our policies and breaking the trust essential to our work," a spokesperson told the BBC. The ChatGPT-maker did not name the sacked workers, but at least two of them were involved in safety research at the firm. The firings come as the debate over AI safety and the risks the technology may pose to humanity intensified in recent months. "We have parted ways with three individuals for violating our policies on accessing and handling sensitive company information," a spokesperson for OpenAI said. Concerns over AI safety have made headlines after some researchers and industry executives called for more guardrails around the technology. OpenAI has come under under intense scrutiny after its models went rogue and hacked several platforms, including Australian government websites . In an incident in July, one of the firm's AI models accessed the internet and breached the open-source developer platform Hugging Face. That incident led OpenAI to review the activities of its AI agents, which are designed to execute tasks autonomously based on simple instructions. The firm said this week it has notified more than 100 organisations about incidents involving unauthoritised activity linked to its systems. Being notified "does not mean that any private information was accessed" or that a system was compromised, it said. Three takeaways from Trump's 'Super Intelligence' summit Published 5 days ago OpenAI says its rogue AI tried to hack other companies Published 29 July OpenAI scraps rollout of new model over safety concerns Published 6 days ago In September, researcher Jacob Coxon, who left Anthropic , called for AI development to slow down so its potential risks could be properly assessed. Anthropic boss Dario Amodei and OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman have also called for measures to address concerns over AI. On Tuesday, US President Donald Trump hosted a meeting of top technology bosses - including leaders from OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, SpaceX, Meta and Google - to discuss AI. After the gathering at the White House, Trump posted a document that he called a "morally binding" agreement that would serve as a "form of protection" from AI's potential risks. Some technology experts criticised the pact, pointing out that it allowed AI companies to regulate themselves. Trump has repeatedly downplayed concerns about AI's risks in response to calls from some industry figures for tighter oversight of the technology.
